parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illa, nominative feminine singular of ille.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of first conjugation verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of first conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish -ar, French -er, Italian -are, etc.

parole.significato: used to form adjectives expressing a tendency or inclination to the action of the root verb; -ish, -y
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ax. Doublet of -ace, which was borrowed.

parole.significato: used to form collective nouns with some words
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ālia, the neuter plural of -ālis. Compare Aromanian -alji. It is no longer a productive suffix and only found in some words.

parole.significato: -al; of or pertaining to, forms adjectives from nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -alis. Compare French -al, Italian -ale.

parole.significato: used to form collective nouns with some words
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āmen. Compare Aromanian -ame.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives and nouns describing things and characteristics of a city, region, or country; -an
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -anus. Doublet of -ân

parole.significato: Added to a word to denote a profession or craft; -er
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ārium, accusative of -ārius.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the masculine singular past participle of regular -a (first conjugation) verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātus, from Proto-Italic *-ātos.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the feminine plural past participle of regular -a (first conjugation) verbs. (e.g. lăsate, măs…
parole.testo: Feminine plural of -at; from Latin -ātae, feminine nominative plural of -ātus.

parole.significato: Used to form some adjectives (and sometimes nouns derived from them) meaning "of", "like", "characteristic of", etc.
parole.testo: From the older form -atec, from Latin -āticus. No longer a productive suffix in Romanian. Compare Aromanian -atic.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the feminine singular past participle of -a (first conjugation) verbs. (e.g. botezată, îngheța…
parole.testo: Feminine form of -at; from Latin -āta(m), feminine of -ātus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the masculine plural past participle of regular -a (first conjugation) verbs. (e.g. adunați, s…
parole.testo: Masculine plural of -at; from Latin -ātī, masculine nominative plural of -ātus.

parole.significato: -able, -ible (forms adjectives with the meaning "able to be" from verbs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -abilis, Italian -abile; cf. French -able.

parole.significato: roughly equivalent to -tion; was used to form a noun when added to a verb root, describing that action or state related…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -tiō, -tiōnem, and found in terms inherited from Latin as well those formed before the mid 19th century, but is otherwise no longer productive. Most modern words or neologisms use the borrowed doublets -ție or occasionally -țiune.
Inherited from Latin -ae (“first-declension ending”).
Inherited from Latin -e (“second-declension vocative ending”).

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of many verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ere, the ending of the present active infinitive form of third conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish -er, Italian -ere, etc.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of many verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of second conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish -er, Italian -ere, etc.

parole.significato: Used to form the feminine diminutive of a word
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ella.

parole.significato: suffix forming placenames and feminine surnames
parole.testo: From -easă + -a (definite article). For place names possibly Inherited from Latin -ēnsis with a relatively common change in declension.

parole.significato: Used to make feminine forms of some masculine nouns, or to indicate the wife of a man with a certain profession; -ess
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa). Cf. also the doublet -esă, a neologism borrowed from French.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular present and third-person plural present indicatives of some -a (firs…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izat. Doublet of -ez. Compare also Aromanian -eadzã.

parole.significato: -ness, -ity; used to form nouns from adjectives
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itia(m). Compare Aromanian -eatsã.
From Latin illaei.

parole.significato: used to form a masculine diminutive of a word (e.g. băiat (“boy”) + -el → băiețel (“little boy”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ellus.

parole.significato: A suffix forming the nominative-accusative definite plural for nouns ending in -ă.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illae.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the first-person singular and third-person plural present of most regular -i (fourth conjugati…
parole.testo: A form of the infix -esc-, from Latin -ēscō (and -ēscunt in the case of the third-person plural). Cognates include Aromanian -escu, Italian -isco, -iscono, Spanish -ezco, -ecen, Catalan -eixo, -eixen.

parole.significato: suffix forming many Romanian surnames, e.g. Ionescu, Petrescu, Popescu, Georgescu, Marinescu, Niculescu, Constantinescu…
parole.testo: From the suffix -esc, from Latin -iscus. Compare Italian -eschi.

parole.significato: Used with plant or tree names to form names of orchards, woods, forests, or groves.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ētum. Cognate with Italian -eto, French -aie.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns derived from the action of some verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itus. No longer productive.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular present of some -a (first conjugation) verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izō. Used as an infix in Romanian verb conjugations (similarly to how Spanish and Portuguese use the unrelated -ecer from Latin -escere, from -escō (as in parecer, padecer, merecer, etc). The suffix does not appear in the infinitive form of the verb in Romanian. However, t

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular present of some -a (first conjugation) verbs. E.g. lucrezi from luc…
parole.testo: Form of the infix -ez-; probably from a Vulgar Latin *-idiās or *-izās, conjugated forms of *-idiō, *-izō, ultimately from Ancient Greek -ίζειν (-ízein), used in Romanian conjugated forms of verbs. See -ez.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the third-person singular present of most regular -i (fourth conjugation) verbs. E.g. unește,…
parole.testo: A form of the infix -esc-, from Latin -ēscō, in this case -ēscit. Cognates include Aromanian -eashti, Italian -isce, Spanish -ece.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the second-person singular present of most regular -i (fourth conjugation) verbs. E.g. unești,…
parole.testo: A form of the infix -esc-, from Latin -ēscō, in this case -ēscis. Cognates include Italian -isci, Spanish -eces.

parole.significato: used to form adjectives from nouns or verbs denoting propensity or likeness, being inclined toward, or having the quali…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -icius ~ -itius (cf. Romanian -eață < Latin -itia). Its occasional use to form nouns may have originated with adjectives that were later substantivized/nominalized over time.

parole.significato: Forms the indefinite plural of masculine nouns and many feminine nouns.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ī (second-declension plural ending).

parole.significato: masculine plural, nominative and accusative definite article
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of fourth conjugation verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of fourth conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish and French -ir, Italian -ire, etc.

parole.significato: forms adjectives with the meaning "of or pertaining to"
parole.testo: From Latin -icus.

parole.significato: adjectival suffix roughly equivalent to -ous or -ish
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itiōsus; cf. -ōsus.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to create a (usually abstract) noun relating to it; can be compared to -ship, -hood, -ness, -ity, etc.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin -īlia, neuter plural of -īlis. Less likely from Latin -ia. Compare Aromanian -ilji, -ilje. In borrowed words, derived from Latin Latin -ia, French -ie and Old Church Slavonic -иѥ (-ije), further obscuring the etymology.
From Latin suffix -ificō.

parole.significato: from adjectives forms nouns denoting quality or state of. -ness, -ity, -hood, -ship, -dom
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īmen. Compare also Aromanian -imi.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the gerund of -i (fourth conjugation) verbs, as well as a minority of -a (first conjugation) a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -(i)endus.

parole.significato: Having the state or condition of; -ence, -ance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -entia. Compare Aromanian -intsã, French -ance, -ence, Italian -enza, Portuguese -ença, -ência, Spanish -enza, -encia, Friulian -ince. Compare -ență, -anță, borrowed from French.
Inherited from Latin -olus.
Borrowed from Latin -ismus, French -isme, ultimately from Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós).
Borrowed from Latin -itātem. This particular form of the suffix is used in neologisms, and based on French -ité. The inherited form -ătate is found in older words.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives denoting characteristics or qualities, especially relating to color; roughly equivalent to -ive or som…
parole.testo: Probably from Latin -īvus. Mostly found in older, popular words; compare the neological borrowing -iv.
From Latin -io, -ionis.
Inherited from Latin -īcius.

Suffixed form of ăl (inherited from Latin illum) which originally followed the noun and became attached to it as an inflection, unlike the definite articles in the other major Romance languages, which go before the noun.
Inherited from Latin -ae (“first-declension ending”), with intrusive l.
Inherited from Latin illae, nominative feminine plural of ille.
Inherited from Latin illōrum, from ille.

parole.significato: Forms nouns that indicate the action or result of a verb; -ment
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -mentum, from Latin -menta.

parole.significato: augmentative suffix for some feminine nouns (e.g. casă (“house”) + -oaie → căsoaie (“big house, pantry, larder, lumber…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ōnea, -ōnia, feminine of -ōneus. Rare and largely unused in modern Romanian (cf. -oaică, which is common). Compare the Aromanian equivalent -oanji, -oanje, -onje, which is more often used, as well as Albanian -onjë, likely borrowed from the same Latin root. See also the masculi

parole.significato: Used to form abstract nouns from adjectives, past participles and verbs; -ness.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -or, ōris, with some cases possibly influenced by Latin -oria. See -toare.

parole.significato: augmentative suffix, used to indicate a larger version of (e.g. piatră (“rock”) + -oi → pietroi (“boulder”), furcă (“pi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ōneus, -ōnius. See also the feminine -oaie. Compare Aromanian -onj, -onjiu. Additionally, cf. Italian -one, Spanish -ón, which are also augmentative suffixes.
Inherited from Latin -ōsus (“full (of)”).

parole.significato: Attached to the ends of verb infinitives to form nouns, meaning "the action or result of"; -ing, -ation
parole.testo: From the Latin infinitive endings (-are, -ere, -ire). Used in Romanian with a verb to form the "long infinitive", which is a verbal noun. See also the short infinitive forms of Romanian verbs, -a, -ea, -e, and -i.
Inherited from Latin -tātem, accusative of -tās, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts.

Inherited from Latin -tor (through a Vulgar Latin form *-torius, and feminine -toare from *-toria). With some neologisms based on French -teur. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr < *-tor-s.
Inherited from Latin -tōrius.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns relating to some action; -ure, -ing
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -tūra, and in some words based on French -(t)ure.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives denoting characteristics or qualities, especially relating to color, and often with the meaning of -is…
parole.testo: Probably from Latin -uneus, cf. -eus.

parole.significato: Suffix forming abstract nouns from adjectives.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ura.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to mark the past participle of second-conjugation verbs and regular third-conjugation verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ūtus.

parole.significato: Forms masculine diminutives of nouns and adjectives.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin -uceum or -ucium. Compare Aromanian -uts, Italian -uccio, Sicilian -uzzu.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives and nouns describing things and characteristics of a city, region, or country; -an
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -anus. This suffix is no longer productive in Romanian, largely being replaced by -an.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the gerund in -a (first conjugation), -ea (second conjugation), and -e (third conjugation) ver…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -andus, -endus. Compare Italian -ando, -endo, Spanish -ando, -iendo.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of many verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of fourth conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish ir and French -ir, Italian -ire, etc.
Inherited from Latin -am, from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂.

parole.significato: Forms nouns or adjectives indicating propensity or likeness, being inclined toward, or having the quality of; can be ro…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -āricius. Once created only nouns in older Romanian, some of which became adjectives over time.

parole.significato: Added to nouns to form other nouns meaning "place of" (an art, craft, or practice).
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āria, feminine of -ārius. Compare Italian -eria.

Shortened form of -țiune, itself a borrowing based on Latin -tiō. Compare also the Polish suffix -cja, Russian -ция (-cija) (borrowed ultimately from the same source), which may have influenced it. Also compare the inherited -ciune.

Longer form of -ție, borrowed from Latin -tiō, -tiōnem and based partially on the older inherited form -ciune, now only found in certain older words and constructions, or as part of terms inherited from Latin.
From Latin ad, from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“near; at”).
From Proto-Romanian, from a late Vulgar Latin *ae(t), from Latin habet.

parole.significato: to stray (often figuratively in a moral sense), derogate, deviate, divert from, digress
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.
Borrowed from Latin abbatissa.
Borrowed from Latin abdōmen.
Borrowed from Latin abecedārium.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad vix, from ad + vix. The original form was abi, a variant found in some dialects; the final -a was added by analogy with adverbs like aci(a), aiure(a), acole(a). This suffixation coincided with diphthongisation, turning the stressed -i into a glide. In Banat, however,
Borrowed from Latin abjudicare. By surface analysis, ab- + judeca.
Borrowed from Latin ablactare.
Borrowed from Latin ablactare.
Borrowed from Latin abnegāre.
Borrowed from Latin abolitio. By surface analysis, aboli + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin abbreviare.
Borrowed from Latin abbreviātiō, French abréviation. By surface analysis, abrevia + -ție.

parole.significato: to rescind, to repeal, to annul
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abrogare or French abroger.
Borrowed from Latin abrogatio. Equivalent to abroga + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin abstractus, German Abstrakt.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *aboricāre, derivative of Latin orior. Compare urca.
Inherited from Latin acus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).

parole.significato: shrubs or trees of the genus Acacia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acacia or French acacia. Doublet of acaț (“black locust”).
From ac + -ar, or possibly Latin ac(u)ārius. The final sense was based on French aiguilleur.

parole.significato: ratite (any bird of the order Struthioniformes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acarinatus.
Univerbation of a + casă. Alternatively, from Latin ad casam.
Borrowed from Latin acceptātiō. By surface analysis, accepta + -ție.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, a compound of Latin eccum and ille. Compare Aromanian atsel, Italian quello, Spanish aquel and Catalan aquell.
Inherited from Latin *acce (“there”) + ille (“that one”) + hāc (“over here”), equivalent to acel + -a. Compare ăla, ăsta, acesta.
From acela + și, which in this case represents Latin sic (“thus”).
Inherited from Latin aquila. Doublet of acvilă.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum + iste. Compare Italian questo, Old French cest, Catalan aquest, and Romansh quest.
Inherited from Latin *acce (“there”) + iste (“that one”) + hāc (“over here”), equivalent to acest + -a. Compare ăla, ăsta, acela.

Inherited from Latin apium. Having developed from an unattested *apiu. Displaying the /pʲ/ to /kʲ/ sound change as dialectally present in numerous other words, e.g: piatră > chiatră, spin > schin, etc...
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) (h)īc, from Latin eccum + hīc. Compare Italian qui, French ici, Spanish aquí, Catalan ací.
Borrowed from Latin hyacinthus.
Borrowed from Latin Acipenseridae.

Maybe from Vulgar Latin *accēnāre (“to wait until the evening”), originally meaning "to wait until the time of dinner". For the rhotacism of the intervocalic nasal, compare fereastră from Latin fenestra; however, this is uncommon in Romanian, especially without cause of dissimilation. Cf. also the r

parole.significato: hither, here, this way, in my direction
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (ec)cu(m) *hocce, from Latin hoc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) illā(c), from Latin eccum + illāc. Compare Portuguese and Galician acolá, Spanish acullá, Italian colà.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum illōc, from a compound of Latin eccum + illōc. Compare Aromanian aclo, cf. also Portuguese acolá, Ladin chiló.
Borrowed from Latin accommodatio. Equivalent to acomoda + -ție.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accoperīre, *accooperīre, from Latin ac- + cooperīre (“cover completely”). By surface analysis, a- + coperi.
Inherited from Late Latin ācrus, from Latin ācer (with a change in declension), from Proto-Italic *akris, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin acta.
Borrowed from Latin acta.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo. Informal variant of acum.
Borrowed from Latin aculeatus or French aculéate.
Borrowed from Latin aculeatus or French aculéate.
Borrowed from Latin aculeus, or via Italian aculeo, itself a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo. Compare Sardinian como.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo, from Latin eccum + modo. Variant of acum.
Borrowed from Latin accumbens.
Borrowed from Latin accumulatio or French accumulation. Equivalent to acumula + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin acutus or Italian acuto.
Borrowed from Latin aquilinus.

parole.significato: of good quality, beautiful, well-made, fit.
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from acătărea (“good; likely”), originally “any, whichever”, influenced by tare (“strong”), from Vulgar Latin *eccum talis.
Learned borrowing from Latin ad hoc.
Borrowed from Latin adagium.
Borrowed from Latin adamantinus or French adamantin.
Borrowed from Latin addenda.
Inherited from Latin ad + dē + vērum. Compare Spanish de veras, de a de veras (“for real”) and Italian davvero.

parole.significato: videlicet, viz., that is to say, in other words
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Latin adaeque or adde quod.

parole.significato: just now, a moment ago, not long ago
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ad de in illam horam, or from in illa hora, resulting in a hypothetical early Romanian *inioară, combined with de and a, as with many adverb constructions. Compare Italian allora, from illa hora and Spanish ahora, from hac hora.
Inherited from Latin ad idipsum.

parole.significato: a little while ago, not long ago
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ad dē ante.
Borrowed from Latin adjudicare, French adjuger, By surface analysis, ad- + judeca.
Borrowed from Latin adjuratio.
Borrowed from Latin administrātor. Equivalent to administra + -tor.
Borrowed from Latin admiror, based on French admirer.
Borrowed from Latin admirabilis. Equivalent to admira + -bil.
Borrowed from Latin admonere.
Borrowed from Latin adnatus or French adné.

parole.significato: to annotate (make annotations on the margins of a text)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adnotare. By surface analysis, ad- + nota.
Borrowed from Latin adnotātiō, annotātiō. By surface analysis, adnota + -ție.
Inherited from Late Latin addormīre. Compare Aromanian adurnjiri.
Inherited from Latin addūcere.

parole.significato: to sniff, scent, sense or trace through smell (an animal, person, etc.)
parole.testo: Unknown. Cognate with Aromanian ulmic, ulmicari. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *adosmicāre, from *adosmāre, from Ancient Greek ὀσμάω (osmáō), which would make sense semantically but is difficult to connect phonetically. Compare Italian ormare, Spanish husmear, husmar probably coming from a Latin
Inherited from Latin adumbrāre, with a change of conjugation that is probably relatively recent. Compare Aromanian aumbredz, aumbrari.
Inherited from Latin adūnāre.
From Latin adverbium, from ad- (“to”) + verbum (“word, verb”), French adverbe.
Inherited from Latin aduncus.
Inherited from Latin adaquāre.
Inherited from Latin ad appos(i)tum or ad depos(i)tum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adastāre, from ad- + Latin astāre (“stand at, on, by”), from stō. Compare Aromanian adastu, adãstari.

Inherited from Latin adaugēre, later turned to a first conjugation verb. The first conjugation form of the verb became preferred in Romanian (as in Aromanian adavgu, adãvgari), but other forms like adaoge using the third conjugation have also survived, though some are considered dated or archaic tod
Inherited from Latin āēr.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin aerarium.
Borrowed from Latin affabilis or French affable.
From an earlier afoară, inherited from Latin ad forās. Compare Spanish afuera, Portuguese afora, Aromanian afoarã, cf. also Italian fuori.

Inherited from Latin daphne, with loss of initial 'd', from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē, “laurel”); cf. also Calabrian afina ("laurel"). Another theory suggests Latin acinus, influenced by daphne. See also the related dafin.
Borrowed from Latin affinis.

parole.significato: to find out, get wind of
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin afflāre (“blow, breathe”), from ad- + flō (“blow, breathe”). Cognate with Portuguese achar and Spanish hallar.

parole.significato: to smoke (to preserve or prepare food by treating with smoke, as in smoked ham)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affūmāre, ultimately from Latin fūmus (“smoke”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + fum + -a. Compare Aromanian afum. Reinforcement by Italian affumare is possible.

parole.significato: to plunge, immerse, immerge, dip, sink
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affundāre, derived from Latin fundus (“bottom”). By surface analysis, a- + fund + -a. Compare Aromanian afundari.

parole.significato: to loosen, soften, or make a granular material less compact or dense, as with hay
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *affēnāre, from Latin fēnum. Compare French faner, from Vulgar Latin *fenāre.
Borrowed from Latin Agathyrsi.
Inherited from Latin agilis (“swift”). Doublet of agil, a borrowing.

parole.significato: a place along a river where the current has gathered shrubbery, branches, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin aggestus (“an accumulation”), perfect passive participle of aggerō.
Borrowed from Latin agnomen.
Borrowed from Latin agrammatos.
Borrowed from Latin agrestis or French agreste.
Borrowed from Latin agrimensura.
Inherited from Latin agrum (“field, ground”), itself from Proto-Italic *agros, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *agurāre, from Latin augurāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin agustus < Latin augustus. Mostly replaced by the reborrowing august. Cognate with Sicilian agustu.
From a- + Vulgar Latin *accaptiāre, from a- + *captiāre, from Latin captus. Compare Aromanian acats.
From Latin allium / alium.

parole.significato: ai (modal auxiliary, second-person singular form of avea, used with past participles to form perfect compus tenses)
parole.testo: From an old or proto-Romanian form ae, from Latin habēs.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *eas, from Latin habēbās.

From Vulgar Latin *ad hīcce (“to here”), from Latin hīc (“here”), from heic, from earlier forms of hic (“this”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi-ḱe (“this, here”). Compare Italian ci, Sicilian ci, Spanish aquí, Portuguese aqui, Aromanian atsia.
Inherited from Latin allectāre.
Inherited from Latin ad istum. Cf. also Aromanian aestu.

parole.significato: in or from another place, elsewhere
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin aliunde or from a + inde.

parole.significato: synonym of înainte (“forwards; in front of; before”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin ab ante. Used in written language until the 16th century, though probably remained in usage in isolated regions a while longer. Replaced by the prefixed variant înainte.
Probably from Latin aliubi (a variant of alibi) + rē + a. Compare Aromanian aljurea, French ailleurs, Occitan alhors and Portuguese alhures.

parole.significato: fast, fasting (abstaining from or eating very little food)
parole.testo: Probably from Latin iēiūnium or iēiūnus through a Vulgar Latin root *iaiūnus > *aiūnus, from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”). Compare Spanish ayuno, French jeun, jeûne, also Italian digiuno. The equivalent Aromani
Inherited from Latin adiungō (“add, join to”), from ad + iungō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Latin adiūtō (“help”).
Inherited from Latin adiūtōrium.
Inherited from Latin adiūtor.

parole.significato: of (masculine/neuter singular possessive or genitive article)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illum, from ille.
Inherited from Latin albus, from Proto-Italic *alβos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élbʰos, *álbʰos, *albʰós (“white”). Doublet of album.
Definite form of albă, from Latin alba, feminine of albus. For the sense of "dawn" or "sunrise", see Vulgar Latin *alba, whence also Spanish and Italian alba, French aube, Portuguese alva.
Borrowed from Latin alba spina, Italian albaspina. Compare French aubépine.

From a Vulgar Latin root *albaster, albastrum, derived from Latin albus (“white”). Probably originally referred to the whiteness in a lightly clouded sky. See also the formations in Italian biancastro (“whitish”), nerastro (“blackish”), French blanchâtre (“whitish”), noirâtre (“blackish”) (with the
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *albīre, from Latin albēscere. By surface analysis, alb (“white”) + -i.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alvīna (“beehive”) (compare Aromanian alghinã (“bee”), Megleno-Romanian ălbină, Istro-Romanian albire (“bee”), Venetan albina (“hive”), derived from classical Latin alvus or alveus.
Inherited from Late Latin albor, albōrem, from Latin albus. Equivalent to alb + -oare
From Latin aleatorius through French aléatoire.

parole.significato: to latch on to someone, follow them around or bother them
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin alligāre.
Inherited from Latin allegere (“choose; recruit”).

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *allargāre, from Latin largus (“abundant, plentiful”). Other theories derive it ultimately from a derivation or alteration of Latin legāre or alegāre. Compare Aromanian alag, alãgari; compare also Albanian largoj (“to leave”), Italian allargare (“to widen”).
Borrowed from Latin alias.
From a Vulgar Latin root *allenāre, possibly from Latin lenis (“smooth, gentle”).
Probably Latin aureolus. Other theories suggest Latin helleborus.
Borrowed from Latin allōdium, from Frankish *allaaud.
Borrowed from Latin alpicus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *altru, from Latin alter, alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

parole.significato: altar (flat-topped structure used for religious rites)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin altārium or altār, with the plural deriving from altāria. Compare oltar, a rare and dated variant which derives from the same source via a Slavic intermediary.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente.

Inherited from Latin allevātum, neuter of allevātus (“lifted, raised up”), past participle of allevō. Compare also French levain, Italian lievito, Spanish leudo, (a)leudar, Portuguese lêvedo, Galician lévedo.
Derived from Latin alumnus through German Alumnus or Italian alunno.

Inherited from Latin lūbricāre (“make slippery”). The original form was the now-obsolete lureca as intervocalic -r- and -n- are occasionally mixed in Romanian phonological evolution (cf. senin from serēnus and mărunt from minūtus), probably the result of anti-rhotacism in response to rhoticism in Tr

From a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from Latin longē. Other theories suggest it deriving straight from Latin ēlongāre. Compare Italian allungare, Catalan allunyar (“move away, remove, distance onself”), French éloigner, allonger, Galician alongar (“move away”), Spanish alongar and Portuguese alonga
From a Vulgar Latin root *abellona, from Latin abellāna, from a city in Italy known as Abella or Avella. Compare Aromanian alunã, Occitan aulana, Portuguese avelã, Spanish avellana.
Borrowed from Latin alluvium.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad lātera, variant of ad latus (“along”) (compare Italian allato, Dalmatian a lič), from Latin ad (“to, at”) + latus (“side”); compare Old French lez (“along”), Spanish al lado (“next to”).

parole.significato: am (modal auxiliary, first-person singular form of avea, used with past participles to form perfect compus tenses)
parole.testo: From old Romanian amu, presumably from an earlier (proto-) Romanian form aemu (attested in Aromanian), from Latin habēmus. The original first-person singular in proto-Romanian was aibu, from Latin habeō, but was changed to am(u) by analogy with the first-person plural. The form with -v- (avem) in th

parole.significato: am (modal auxiliary, first-person plural form of avea, used with infinitives to form conditional tenses)
parole.testo: Presumably from a Vulgar Latin *eamus, from Latin habēbāmus.
Inherited from Latin amārus (“bitter”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃- (“to be hot”).
Borrowed from Latin amarantus.
Borrowed from Latin ambiguus.

From a Vulgar Latin root *ammināciāre, *admināciāre, < *mināciō (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”), from the neuter plural of mināx (“threatening”), from minārī (“threaten”). Compare Catalan amenaçar, French menacer, Italian minacciare, Occitan amenaçar, Portuguese ameaçar, Sicilian amminazzari,

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ammixticāre, from ad- + *mixticāre, from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscere (“mix”). Compare Aromanian ameastic, amisticari, Italian mesticare, Dalmatian mescur; also Italian mestare, Asturian amestar, Romansh maschadar, Friulian mesedâ, from a related root.

From amiazăzi, from Latin ad mediam diem. Compare Latin meridies, Italian mezzodì, French midi, Catalan migdia, Occitan mieidia, Portuguese meio-dia, Spanish mediodía. Alternatively, from Latin medīdiē, variant of the standard merīdiēs (compare Italian meriggio).
Borrowed from Latin amicabilis. By surface analysis, amic + -abil.
Borrowed from Latin amicitia, Italian amicizia.
Borrowed from Latin amica, Italian amica.
Borrowed from Latin amōrem, French amour, Italian amore.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”). Compare Aromanian amurtsãri.
Borrowed from Latin amplexio.
Borrowed from Latin amplificare or French amplifier. By surface analysis, amplu + -ifica.
Borrowed from Latin amplitudo. Equivalent to amplu + -itudine.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad modo (compare Dalmatian jamo (“now”), Aromanian amo, acmo). Informal counterpart to acum.
Borrowed from Latin amusia.

Probably from mâine (compare the variant form mâne), possibly based on a Latin construction ad māne, or on a hypothetical adverbial form *amâne in Romanian. Compare Aromanian amãn, amãnari. Similar semantic development in French ajourner.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amendoi, from ambī duī, from Latin ambō (“both”) + duī, from duo (“two”). Compare Aromanian amindoilji, andoilji. Cf. also Old Italian amendue, Engadine amenduos, Old French andui, Occitan amdui.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ammagīre from *magīre, *magāre, from Ancient Greek μαγεύω (mageúō, “cast a spell; bewitch”), from μάγος (mágos, “magical”); cf. also Latin magus. May be related to Catalan amagar (“hide”) and Spanish amagar (“threaten”), Portuguese esmagar, Sicilian ammagari, although th
From the verb amărî (“to embitter”), from Latin amarire, from amarus (“bitter”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *amarīre, from Latin amarēscere, from amarus (“bitter”).
From amar + -ăcios, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *amāritiōsus, from amāritiēs (cf. amăreață).
From Latin annus (“year”), from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”). Compare Megleno-Romanian an and Aromanian an.
Borrowed from Latin anceps.

parole.significato: anchor (tool to hook a vessel into sea bottom)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ancora. Replaced the older anghiră from Greek άγκυρα (ágkyra). Cf. also Aromanian angurã.
Borrowed from Latin anguīlla.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *annināre (“to rock”), from *ninna (“cradle”), from an infantile sound. Compare Italian ninnare (“lull or rock to sleep”), Romansh niner (“to rock”), Occitan nina, Albanian ninuljë. This verb refers to hanging something in an unfixed way, allowing it to rock or dang
Borrowed from Latin ante bellicus.
Borrowed from Latin antemeridianus.
Borrowed from Latin anterior and French antérieur.
Borrowed from Latin antigraphum.
By analogy with postum, using Latin ante.
Borrowed from Latin ānus (“ring, anus”)
Inherited from Latin annō tertiō. Compare Aromanian antsãrtsu / antserts.
Inherited from Latin ad + horam.
Either from apă + -ar or from the Latin aquārius. Compare the borrowed doublet acvariu.
Borrowed from Latin aquaeductus, adapted after apă (“water”).
Borrowed from Latin apex.
Borrowed from Latin applausus or Italian applauso.

parole.significato: to bend (oneself), bend down, incline, bow, bow down, stoop, lean
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin applicāre. Doublet of the borrowed aplica.
From apleca + -ciune, possibly corresponding to Latin applicātiō, applicātiōnem. Doublet of aplicație.
Inherited from Latin ad post.
Inherited from Latin aquōsus, equivalent to apă + -os.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin apothecarius. By surface analysis, apotecă + -ar.
Uncertain. Possibly from Latin aprīcus (“sunny”) or a derivate of Latin asper (“rough”).

parole.significato: to light, to turn on (fire, light, candle, lamp)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin apprendere, alternative form of apprehendere. Doublet of the rare neologism aprehenda. See French éprendre, Tourangeau éprende and Walloon esprinde.
Inherited from Latin apprensus, variant of apprehensus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad prope, composed of ad (“to, at”) + prope (“near”). Compare Aromanian aproapea.
Borrowed from Latin approbo, approbare.
Inherited from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”). Compare Aromanian aprochiu, Megleno-Romanian prochiu.
Borrowed from Latin appropriatio. Equivalent to apropria + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin approximare.
Borrowed from Latin aptitudo. Equivalent to apt + -itudine. Doublet of atitudine.
Possibly from metathesis of a Vulgar Latin aucupāre, from Latin aucupārī. Other theories suggest Latin occupāre, with meaning influenced by or confused with the former. Compare Aromanian apuc.
Inherited from Latin appōnere.

From the past participle of the verb apune (“to fade, set”), from Latin apponere. Was the traditional word for "west", but today vest is used as the standard term. Compare also the descendants of Latin ponens in the Western Romance languages, which developed the meaning of "west".
Inherited from Latin *appausatus.
Inherited from Latin aqua, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. Compare Aromanian apã, Megleno-Romanian apu, Istro-Romanian åpę and Sardinian abba.

Inherited from Latin apparāre (“to prepare”). Compare Italian apparare (“prepare”), Spanish aparar (“prepare, arrange”). Cf. also Occitan aparar (“protect”), which may be from a different but related root.

parole.significato: to appear, show up, turn up, emerge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apparēre (19th century), with conjugation based on părea (using the model of French apparaître and paraître; cf. also Spanish aparecer).
From a Vulgar Latin root *appēsāre < *appēnsāre, from Latin pēnsō, pēnsāre (cf. Latin appēndō, appēndere from pēndō, pēndere). Compare Old French apeser, Occitan apesar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *aquatōsus, from Latin aquatus (“diluted, watered down, watery”), from aquor (“get water”), from aqua (“water”). Compare Friulian agadôs.
From older Romanian ară, are, presumably from Latin habēret (for the singular) and habērent (for the plural). See also are.
Inherited from Latin arāre, from Proto-Italic *araō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éryeti (“to plough”), from the root *h₂erh₃-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen n, derived from Latin aer-.
Inherited from Latin arātrum. Compare Aromanian aratru, arat, Spanish and Portuguese arado, Italian aratro (older form arato), Catalan arada). Largely replaced by plug.
From older arbure, from Latin arborem f. Compare Aromanian arburi. The modern form of the word, with stressed /o/, is the result of influence from Latin and various related neologisms (see below).
Inherited from Latin arborētum, equivalent to arbore + -et. Compare Aromanian arburet.
From Latin arbustum through French arbuste.
Inherited from Latin arcus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo-.
Borrowed from Latin arcuballista.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ārdĕre, from Latin ārdēre.
Borrowed from Latin ardor, through French ardeur.
Inherited from Latin aries, arietem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r-i-(e)t- (“certain domestic animal”).
Inherited from Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom.

parole.significato: person who makes or sells silver objects
parole.testo: Either from argint + -ar or from Latin argentārius. Compare Italian argentaio, French argentier, Spanish argentero, Catalan argenter.

parole.significato: containing much silver, full of silver
parole.testo: From argint + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin argentōsus.
Borrowed from Latin archidiaconatus. By surface analysis, arhi- + diaconat or arhidiacon + -at.
Borrowed from Latin archidioecesis. Equivalent to arhi- + dieceză.
Borrowed from Latin archiepiscopalis. By surface analysis, arhiepiscop + -al or arhi- + episcopal.
Borrowed from Latin archiepiscopatus. By surface analysis, arhi- + episcopat or arhiepiscop + -at.
Borrowed from Latin archipresbyter. First attested in 1817.
Inherited from Latin ārea.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *alīnus, from *alnīnus, from Latin alnus + -īnus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élsnos. Compare Aromanian anin, arinu, Megleno-Romanian rin.
Inherited from Latin arēnōsus, or from arină + -os. Compare Aromanian arinos.

Inherited from Latin arēna. Compare Italian arena, rena, Sicilian rina, Portuguese areia, Aromanian arinã. Now a regional term, mostly replaced by nisip - a Slavic borrowing. Compare arenă, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Latin alapa (“blow, slap, smack”), or ālipēs ("winged on the feet"), ultimately from āla. Compare Aromanian aripã, arpã, French aube, Spanish álabe.

parole.significato: an animal's haunch, or a thigh on a person
parole.testo: From Latin armus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join”).

parole.significato: to prepare a weapon for firing
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin armāre, French armer, or Italian armare.

parole.significato: wardrobe or closet in which clothes are kept, or cupboard for dishes or foods
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin armārium.
Past participle of arma. From Latin armātus.
Inherited from Latin armamentum.
Inherited from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

parole.significato: stud (a male animal kept for breeding)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin [equus] admissārius, probably through a later Vulgar Latin root *armessārius or *armissārius. Compare Albanian hamshor.
Inherited from Latin armāturā. By surface analysis, arma + -ătură. Doublet of armură.
Inherited from Latin ārsus, past participle of ārdeō. Compare Italian arso, Aromanian arsu.
Inherited from Late Latin ārsūra, from Latin ārsus. Equivalent to ars + -ură.
Borrowed from Latin articulus, French article.
Borrowed from Latin artificiosus. By surface analysis, artificiu + -os.
Borrowed from Latin ars, artis.
Inherited from Latin arātor, with adjectival senses derived from arātōrius.
Inherited from Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō. Compare Aromanian arãturã, Italian aratura, Friulian aradure, Old French areüre, Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish aradura.

parole.significato: Maltese cross (a plant species, (Silene chalcedonica, syn. Lychnis chalcedonica)
parole.testo: From urșinic (“silk”), from an antecedent shared with notable variant urușnic, probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *holoserinicus (“silken”), based on Latin holosēricus. Less likely, a substrate word.
Inherited from Latin [calor] arsicia, from ārdeō. Equivalent to arsus + -icia; possibly a neuter plural reanalysed as feminine.
Borrowed from Latin ascendens.
Borrowed from Latin ascēnsiō and French ascension.
Inherited from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of ausculta, a technical borrowing from Latin.
From asculta + -ător, may correspond to Latin auscultator.
Inherited from Latin abscondere (“hide”).
Inherited from Latin abscōnsus. Doublet of abscons.

Probably from Vulgar Latin root *excotīre, from Classical Latin cōs, cōtis (“whetstone”). Compare cute and cuțit (“knife”). Cognate with Megleno-Romanian ascut, scuțǫt. Cf. also the semantic evolution of Catalan esmolar (“sharpen”), from mola (“grindstone”). Was also possibly influenced by a Vulgar
Inherited from Latin assimilis.

Derived from the dated/regional form asemăra having undergone anti-rhoticism under the presumption that asemăra was a rhoticised variant. Inherited from Late Latin assimilāre, from similō, from Latin similis. Doublet of asimila and asambla.
Borrowed from Latin assessor.
Borrowed from Latin assignō or French assigner.
Borrowed from Latin assignatio or French assignation.

From alteration of the earlier variant asîn or asân (used from the 16th to 18th centuries), itself from Latin asinus. Some writers in the 19th century attempted to revive it under a more Latinized form.
Borrowed from Latin asyndetus or French asyndète.
Inherited from Latin asina.
Inherited from Latin asperum, singular accusative of asper (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”).
Borrowed from Latin astronomus, partially through French astronome. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀστρονόμος (astronómos). By surface analysis, astro- + -nom.
From a Vulgar Latin root *astruicāre, from Latin astruere (“build on, heap”).
Probably from Latin astringere or from a- + strânge.

parole.significato: to stop, close a cover, obstruct, seal, cork, stop up, plug, plug up
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *asstuppāre, from ad- + *stuppāre, from Latin stuppa. Compare Aromanian astup, astupari, Albanian shtupoj; cf. Sicilian stuppari, attuppari, Venetan stupar, Romansh stuppar, Italian stoppare, French étouper, Old Spanish estopar.

parole.significato: cunning, craftiness, cleverness, shrewdness (adeptness at using tricks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin astutia.

parole.significato: to calm down, be at ease
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *extemperāre, from Latin temperāre.
Inherited from Latin istā diē, or a compound of astă + zi.

Inherited from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-. The prefix is a later innovation carrying no semantic nor grammatical nuance, typically seen in Aromanian and less so but still occasionally in Romanian and it's regional varieties.
Inherited from Latin ad supra < ad + supra.

Ultimately from Latin tālis, possibly through a construction eccum tālem (however, compare cutare also from this source) or atque tālem, or simply with the prefix a- added. Compare Italian cotale, Old French itel (modern tel), Old Occitan aital, Old Spanish atal, (modern tal).
Borrowed from Latin attentus.
Borrowed from Latin attestatio. Equivalent to atesta + -ție.
Inherited from Latin attingere, from ad- (“to”) + tangō (“touch”).
From atot- + puternic, a calque of Latin omnipotens.
From atotputernic + -ie, after Latin omnipotentia.
Borrowed from Latin atrium.
From Latin atrox, through Italian/French atroce.
Inherited from Latin ad + *tunce, archaic form of tunc. Compare Aromanian atuntsi~atunts. More distantly related to Spanish entonces, Portuguese então, and Sicilian ntonzi.
Inherited from Latin ad + *tunce, archaic form of tunc. Compare Aromanian atuntsi~atunts. More distantly related to Spanish entonces, Portuguese então, and Sicilian ntonzi.

Either from târn (“a large broom made from brier used to sweep streets”), itself of Slavic origin, or from Latin tornāre (“to turn”) with suffix ad-. However, it would be an irregular phonetic evolution in this case (cf. turna, înturna).

parole.significato: so (to this or that extent), so much
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum tantum, from Latin eccum + tantum. (The initial syllable of *eccum- compounds regularly turns to /a-/ in Romanian.) Closely parallel to Italian cotanto and Old Catalan aitant. Compare also Old French itant, Old Spanish atanto (as well as French tant, Italian tanto,

parole.significato: au (modal auxiliary, third-person plural form of avea, used with past participles to form perfect compus tenses)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *habunt, as a conjugated form of Latin habeō.
From Latin aut.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad-hacce (from Latin hac) or Latin *ad-hocce (from Latin hoc). Compare Aromanian aoatsi.

parole.significato: audacity (insolent boldness, especially when imprudent or unconventional)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audacia.
Borrowed from Latin audiens.
Borrowed from Latin augurālis.
Borrowed from Latin augurium.
Borrowed from Latin (mensis) augustus. Compare also the inherited doublets agust and gust.
Borrowed from Latin augustinus.
Borrowed from Latin aulicus or French aulique.
Borrowed from Latin aula.
Inherited from Latin aurum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”), from *h₂ews- (“to dawn, become light, become red”).
From aur + -ar or Latin aurārius.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin aureus.
Borrowed from Latin auriculatus.
Learned borrowing from Latin auriga.
Borrowed from Latin auripigmentum.
Borrowed from Latin auscultāre. Doublet of asculta, the inherited counterpart.
Borrowed from Latin auspicium.
Inherited from Latin auster, austrum (“the south wind”). Has survived in the popular language despite being largely lost in the literary language.
Borrowed from Latin autumnalis or French automnal.
Borrowed from Latin auxilium.

parole.significato: to hear (to perceive with the ear)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”).
Past participle of auzi or from Latin audītus. Compare Italian udito, Portuguese ouvido, Spanish oído.

Inherited from Latin ūva with a protethic "a". May have been considered archaic even as early as the 17th century, but was preserved as the name of a variety of grapes in Oltenia. Replaced by strugure. However, Aromanian has preserved auã as the standard word for grape.

Probably from Latin avus, normally resulting in *au, with a diminutive suffix -uș added. Was once found in the Oltenia region but has disappeared from spoken language. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os (“grandfather”). Already present in Appendix Probi (avus non aus). Compare Aromanian a

Probably from auș (“old man”) + diminutive suffix -el. Other ideas suggest Vulgar Latin aucellus (“small bird”) (compare Italian uccello, French oiseau), from Latin avis, but this is harder to explain due to phonetic difficulties as well as the reason why a general term for bird would apply to a spe
Borrowed from Latin avaritia.
Borrowed from Latin ave.
Inherited from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”), probably from a Proto-Italic *haβēō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”).
Past participle of avea. From Vulgar Latin *habūtus, replacing Classical Latin habitus.

parole.significato: to rush at or to, dash towards
parole.testo: From avânt, from vânt. Less likely from Latin adventāre, from adventus.
Inherited from Latin hāc diē, reduced to *hadie in the local Vulgar Latin, probably through confusion with hodiē. Compare Aromanian adzã.
From Vulgar Latin habessim, from Latin habuissem. Compare Italian avessi, French eusse.

parole.significato: so (in this or that manner), thus, like that, such
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin ac sīc, or less likely *eccum sīc, in either case with paragogic /-a/ added as with some other adverbs (compare atâta < atât), the variant ași thus being the original form. Closely parallel to Aromanian ashi, Portuguese assim, Old Sicilian assì and Spanish así. Compare also
Inherited from Late Latin ascla, from Latin assula. Compare Aromanian ashclji and Albanian ashkë.
From a Vulgar Latin root *astectāre, from an alteration of Latin adspectāre, an alternative form of aspectāre. Compare Aromanian ashteptu, Italian aspettare, Sardinian aisetare, Sicilian astittari.

parole.significato: to spread or stretch over a surface (e.g. a carpet)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin asternere (“prostrate oneself, lie prone”). Compare Aromanian ashternu / ashter.

Probably from an old or proto-Romanian form aeți (with a similar form attested in Aromanian), from Latin habētis. The form with -v- (aveți) in the present form of the verb's main conjugation (as opposed to its use in this form as an auxiliary verb) may have been remade by analogy with avut; ați may
Presumably from a Vulgar Latin *eatis, from Latin habēbātis.

parole.significato: to lie in wait for someone by following them closely; lurk behind someone; stalk
parole.testo: From the variant form aținea, from Vulgar Latin *attenēre, from Latin attinēre.

parole.significato: to doze, snooze, begin to fall asleep
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *attepīre, *adtepīre, from Latin tepere (“be warm, tepid”).
Inherited from Latin acia, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).
Borrowed from Latin babylonicus. By surface analysis, Babilon + -ic.

Ultimately from Latin ba(l)neum, via the plural ba(l)nea. The stressed a in Romanian is inconsistent with râie, tămâie < Latin arānea, *thȳmānea. Hence baie may have been borrowed from Proto-Slavic *baňa; compare etymology 2 below (via Hungarian). Note also the consistent masculine gender of inherit
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *baiula, from Latin baiulus.

Uncertain. Akin to Albanian boljë, bollë, bullar. The Albanian may more likely be derived from a Latin term, alternatively, and the Romanian may be taken from it. May also have a relation to Serbo-Croatian blavor, but it is uncertain which language borrowed from which. Another theory suggests Latin

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *baba. Compare French bave, Italian bava, Spanish and Portuguese baba. The normal result, *ba, is not used as the singular has been replaced with bală through analogy.
Borrowed from Latin ballista f.

From Latin balsamum. Appears since 17th century. Probably entered Romanian through multiple routes, with the most common form from Italian balsamo, or through use in old medicinal practice. A now archaic variant form valsam derived from Greek βάλσαμο (válsamo). Cf. also German Balsam.
Possibly a substratum word (see balaur (“dragon”)), or an alternation of boală (“disease”). Other theories suggest Latin belua (“beast”), or Vulgar Latin *billa (“draught animal”).
Inherited from Latin balteus.

Unknown: * Perhaps from Medieval Latin *bannus (“communication”), perhaps through a German intermediate. * Other theories derive the word from Proto-Slavic *banъ (“master, lord”) (via Serbo-Croatian or Hungarian). * Ultimate Mongolian origin (баян (bajan, “rich lord; plutocrat”)) has also been propo
Borrowed from Medieval Latin banderium.
Borrowed from Latin baptisterium.

parole.significato: the edge of an axe or knife
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin barbula, diminutive of barba.

parole.significato: the holiday of St. Barbara's day, during which children are anointed with honey, sugar, or the juice of the guelder rose
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin Barbara (the name of the saint).
Inherited from Latin barba, Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”). Compare Aromanian barbã.
Borrowed from Latin Bastarnae.

parole.significato: to beat (repeatedly hit for various purposes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin battere, from earlier battuere. Compare Aromanian bat.
Inherited from Latin vitta.
Inherited from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti.

From a contracted Vulgar Latin form (possibly *beb(e)tus) of Late Latin bibitus (“drunk”), from Latin bibō (“drink”). Compare Spanish beodo. Doublet of băut ("beat" probably being of Transylvanian origin).
Borrowed from Latin beatitudo.

Probably from Latin vellere, with a change in conjugation. Traditionally, it was usually thought to be from Slavic bĕliti (“to whiten”); however, this presents a problem with semantics and there is already another word in Romanian derived from this source, bili, that preserved the original meaning.
Borrowed from Latin bellicosus.

parole.significato: blessing (some kind of divine or supernatural aid, or reward)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin benedictio or French bénédiction.
Borrowed from Latin benignus or French bénin.
Inherited from Late Latin berbēx, berbēce, variant of Latin vervēx. Compare Aromanian birbec. For the meanings 3 and 4, compare the evolution of Spanish cabrón.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *verucata, from Latin verruca. Often considered to be from Serbo-Croatian berikat, but this word is instead probably derived from Romanian. If so, doublet of oraș.
Borrowed from Latin betonica.

parole.significato: a blister, sore, or pustule on the tongue
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *vescella, from a contraction of *vessicella, diminutive of *vessīca, from Latin vēsīca. Cf. also vēsīcula.
Borrowed from Latin Biblia.
Borrowed from Latin bibliotheca, French bibliothèque. Equivalent to biblio- + -tecă.
Borrowed from Latin biennium.

Probably from Latin vetus (in which case it is related to bătrân (“old”)), via the extended sense of something old being in a 'poor condition'. Perhaps semantically influenced by Slavic *bědьnъ (“poor”), if not entirely derived from it. Compare Italian vieto (“old”).
Borrowed from Latin bīga.
Inherited from Latin bene.
From bine + facere. Calque of Latin benefacere.
Inherited from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ). Doublet of the borrowing bazilică. Compare Aromanian bisericã / bisearicã.
Borrowed from Latin bituminosus, French bitumineux.
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmāre. Doublet of blestema, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin blasphēmia. Compare blestem.
Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasfema, which was borrowed from Latin. Compare Aromanian blãstimari.
Inherited from Latin blandus.
Either from blând + -ețe, from -eață, or from Latin blandīties.

Inherited from Latin vōcem, accusative singular of vōx, from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs. Boace was largely supplanted by the Slavicism glas, which was itself later replaced by the borrowed doublet voce during the period of Re-Latinisation of Romanian. Cognate to Aromanian bo

Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs. Equivalent to bou + -ar. Compare Aromanian buyear, French bouvier, Italian boaro, Portuguese boieiro, Spanish boyero.

Either from Latin vapor, vaporem (which may eventually have gone through a hypothetical form *baporem before *baborem, leading to a *băoare in early Romanian and finally to its current form) or alternatively from Latin boreās (“north wind”) (compare also bură). The latter etymology seems to fit the

Uncertain. Possible etymologies: * If an internal development, augmentative of boroacă (“swelling”) inherited from Latin verrūca (“wart”), or a cognate of Italian brocca, inherited from Vulgar Latin *brocca, borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos, “vessel for water”). * Borrowed from Hungaria
Probably from Latin verrūca (thus a doublet of verucă). Uncertain if the above etymology is related.
Probably a Late Latin composition, from botum (compare Romanian bot) + Latin inflare (compare Romanian umfla). Compare Old Occitan boudenfla, Franco-Provençal budenfi, Catalan botunflat, botinflat.
From an older form *băteza, from Vulgar Latin baptidiāre, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō, “immerse, baptize”).
Inherited from Latin bōvem, accusative singular of bōs, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *bovum. Compare Aromanian bou.

Inherited from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”). It may have passed through a Vulgar Latin intermediate form or was influenced by bubulus; cf. the form bobulum. Compare also Albanian buall. Doublet of bivol, which came through a Slavic source.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain; ipotesi scartata nel testo
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from the variant boașă, possibly from Medieval Latin, Late Latin bursa (“purse”), although this is unlikely. Perhaps from Turkish boş, although this is also doubtful due to the age of the word. Compare Aromanian boashã, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian boş.
Inherited from Latin brācae, plural of brāca.
Inherited from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).
Borrowed from Latin Britanni.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *brosca, from broscus (compare Medieval Latin bruscus), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *frosk. Compare Aromanian broascã. Compare also Albanian breshkë, Old French bruesche, Italian rospo, Milanese Lombard brosco, Ladin rusk.
Literally, “shelled frog”; țestoasă is the feminine of țestos (“shelled”), derived from țest (“shell”), from Latin testum. Compare Latin testūdō, Aromanian broascã tsãstoasã.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brothācus, from Ancient Greek βροτάχος (brotákhos), from βάτραχος (bátrakhos). Compare Aromanian broatic, Albanian bretk, bretkosë.

parole.significato: November (eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Formed from brumă + ar, or inherited from Vulgar Latin brūmārius (compare Friulian brumâr (“winter”); cf. also French Brumaire, Albanian brymës (“November”)), from Latin brūma (“winter, mist”) (compare Romanian brumă (“frost”)).
Inherited from Latin brūma. Compare Aromanian brumã.
Borrowed from Latin brutus or French brut.
Inherited from Late Latin branca.
Inherited from Latin bracīle.
Inherited from Latin brachiāle, bracchiāle (“bracelet, armlet”), ultimately from bracchium (“arm”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buccata, from Latin bucca. Compare French bouchée, Italian boccata, Portuguese and Spanish bocado. Doublet of bușeu.

parole.significato: metal lining inside the hub of a wheel on a vehicle
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin buccella (“little mouth”), from bucca (whence Romanian bucă).
Inherited from Latin būcinum or būcina.
Inherited from Latin būcināre. Perhaps altered from the original form bucina based on the related bucium.
Inherited from Latin bucca.

Inherited from Late Latin būfus, probably of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate to Aromanian buf and Megleno-Romanian buf, as well as Spanish búho. The similar terms, also in the significantly less Slavic-contact language Aromanian, speak clearly in favor of a common etymology before the dispersal of Prot

parole.significato: owl (any bird of the order Strigiformes)
parole.testo: Diminutive of less common bufnă (“owl”) + -iță, from dialectal buf, bufă, from Late Latin būfus (“owl”). Compare Albanian buf, Spanish búho, and Sicilian buffa.

parole.significato: with swollen or puffed up cheeks
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *buccidus, from Latin bucca.
Unknown. Either from the verb bulbuca, or an expressive creation based partially on Latin bulbus or bulla and on the sound made by a bubble.

Probably from a Late Latin bombax or *bombacum, ultimately from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax). Compare Medieval Latin bombacium (Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (vamvákion)), from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax), Italian bambagia, Venetan bombàxo, bombàs, also Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), μπαμπάκι (bampáki), Se
Inherited from Latin bonus, from Old Latin duenos, later duonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bon, bonă, and bonus.
Inherited from Latin bonitās, bonitātem, corresponding to bun + -ătate. Compare Aromanian bunãtati.
From bună (“good”) + voință (“will”). Calque of Latin benevolentia.
Inherited from Latin bōlētus, probably through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *boletis. Ultimately from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

Inherited from Latin umbilīcus, through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *umbulicus, later separated to *un buric (compare also the development of French nombril, Catalan llombrígol). Doublet of ombilic. Compare Aromanian buric, Sicilian buddicu.

Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *umbulita (“small navel”), clipped from Vulgar Latin *umbulicus, from Latin umbilīcus (“navel”), with [um] being reanalyzed as the feminine indefinite article o at some stage as same is evidenced by related Romanian buric. The latter may have provoked such analogy. On groun

parole.significato: barrel, cask; contents of a barrel
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, probably of Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: barrel (a wood, plastic or metallic container)
parole.testo: From bute + -oi, from Late Latin buttis. Was originally an augmentative of bute, but became a synonym and largely replaced it.

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *bot(t)um, *bottia (“bump”) + -uc, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). Compare bot.

Possibly from bot or Latin botum + suffix -ză, possibly influenced by bucă, or through a confusion of Latin basium and bucca (compare bosumflat). Other theories suggest a substratum origin; it is possibly related to Albanian buzë, and is possibly derived or borrowed from it. Compare also Aromanian b

Onomatopoetic, or from a derivative of Latin balbus, balbūtīre. Compare Italian balbettare, Spanish balbucir, Albanian belbëzoj; cf. also belbët. Possibly ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root balb-.

parole.significato: To care for or feed an infant.
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *baiāre, from Latin baiulāre (“to carry a burden”). The sense was likely reinterpreted as "to bear a pregnancy" and then "to raise/care for a child." Compare Italian balia.

Most likely originated as the past participle of băia (“to care for an infant”), in which case possibly influenced by bărbat in derivation. Compare băiată (“girl”). Other theories suggest a connection to Medieval Latin balietus, from baietus (“page, serving boy”).
Inherited from Latin balteātus (“belted”), deriving from it the idea of being striped.
Inherited from Latin barbātus (“bearded”). Compare Aromanian bãrbat (“man”).
Inherited from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō. Doublet of bătălie, which entered via another language.

Inherited from a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vetrānus, syncopated form of Latin veterānus. Compare Aromanian bitãrnu, Vegliot Dalmatian vetrun, Friulian vedran, Old Venetan vetrano. Compare the borrowed veteran.
Unknown. Possibly of imitative origin, or tied to Vulgar Latin baubulāre < Latin baubor, baubari. Compare Campidanese Sardinian baulài, Piedmontese baolè.
Either from the verb bea + -tor, or from Latin bibitor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bibitūra, from Latin bibitus, from bibō (“drink”). Compare Aromanian biuturã, Sardinian bibidura, bidura.
Inherited from Latin vissīre. Compare Aromanian bes.
From bășică or possibly from Latin vēsīcāre. Compare Aromanian bishic, bishicari.
Inherited from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca. Cognate with Aromanian bishicã. Compare also the borrowed doublet vezică.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vissīna, from Latin vissīre. Compare Aromanian bishinã, Megleno-Romanian bișǫnă.
Inherited from Latin quam. The expression ca și may derive from Latin quasi.
From Latin quia.
Borrowed from Latin caballinus.
Borrowed from Latin caballinus.
Borrowed from Latin caduceum.
Borrowed from Latin caducifer.
From Latin cadus, from Ancient Greek κάδος (kádos), possibly through Proto-Slavic *kadь. Compare Aromanian cadã, Albanian kadë, Aragonese cado, cadollo, Spanish cadozo.
From a Vulgar Latin root *caiulus or *calerus, from Latin galērus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Probably; or from; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), probably of Gaulish [Term?] origin or from something further east, such as a Scythian and ultimately Proto-Iranian [Term?] origin. The Romanian word likely went through an earlier hypothetical form *căal or *caual. Com
Borrowed from Latin calamitosus.
Borrowed from Latin calathidium.
Borrowed from Latin calx, calcem.
Borrowed from Latin calculatio. Equivalent to calcula + -ție.
Inherited from Latin cal(i)dus.
Inherited from Latin callis, callem. Compare Aromanian cali, cale.
Borrowed (in this form) from Latin calendārium. Compare the inherited doublet cărindar.
Borrowed from Latin calendae or French calendes.
Borrowed from Latin Calosoma.
Inherited from Latin quam, or more likely from camai, from Latin quam magis.
Borrowed from Latin camera. Doublet of cămară, and more distantly, comoară.
Borrowed from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancelli, from cancer.
Borrowed from Latin Candida.
Borrowed from Latin canīculāris.
Borrowed from Latin canicula.
Borrowed from Latin cantabilis.
Borrowed from Latin cantor.

parole.significato: combings (fibers of wool left over from combing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cannula.
An uncommon spelling of haos, from Latin chaos.

Inherited from Late Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *káput. Plural form capete from Latin capita. Compare the doublet șef, borrowed from French.
Probably borrowed from Latin caprifolium (adapted to trifoi).
Borrowed from Latin caprimulgus.
Inherited from Latin capra, from caper, from Proto-Indo-European *kápros.
Borrowed from Latin capsa, German Kapsel or Greek κάψα (kápsa).
From an alteration of Latin capita, or a derivative of cap (“head”) through its plural capete (itself from Latin capita, plural of caput).
From Latin carrus, from Gaulish *karros. Sense 3 is influenced by French char and/or Italian carro armato.
From Latin caries or carius. Doublet of carie.
Borrowed from Latin carcer.
Borrowed from Latin Cardium.
Inherited from Latin quālis, quālem. Compare Italian quale, Provençal car, Ligurian quar and Aromanian cari, cai, care.
Borrowed from Latin carnalis. By surface analysis, carne + -al.
Inherited from Latin carnem, accusative of carō, from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”). Compare Aromanian carni, carne.
Inherited from Latin carpinus, probably from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂er- (“hard”).

Inherited from Latin charta, possibly through a hypothetical earlier Romanian intermediate form *cartă, and created from its plural (thus deriving its meaning from "many papers"). Ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Doublet of cartă, a borrowing, as well as hartă, from Greek, and hârtie,

parole.significato: shaft of a knee-high boot (the upper part that extends from the ankle to the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *calamulus, from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Compare Spanish carámbano.
Borrowed from Latin castus.

Borrowed from Latin castaneus (19th century), possibly earlier via Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă). The Aromanian (cãstãnj) and Megleno-Romanian equivalents of the word are likely directly inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin castellum (17th century).
Borrowed from Latin castellanus. By surface analysis, castel + -an. Doublet of castilian.
Borrowed from Latin castitas.
Borrowed from Latin castra or castrum (19th century).
Inherited from Latin casa. Compare Aromanian casã.
Borrowed from Latin cataphractus.
Borrowed from Latin cathedra.
Borrowed from Latin catechismus.
Borrowed from Latin catēna (“chain”). See also cătină, which may be an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin catholicus. Compare Aromanian catolic.
Inherited from Latin caucus.
Borrowed from Latin causalia. By surface analysis, cauză + -al.
Borrowed from Latin casualis.

parole.significato: a type of fresh, non-fermented and unsalted cheese
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cāseus (“cheese”), see there for more. Compare Aromanian cash.

parole.significato: a long stick with a hook at the end that shepherds use to herd sheep
parole.testo: Probably from acăță, variant of agăța. May correspond to a verbal substantive deriving from Late Latin captiāre, but this is uncertain. Compare French chasse, Italian caccia, Portuguese caça, Spanish caza.
Inherited from Latin quid, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.
Inherited from Latin cēpa. Compare Aromanian tseapã.
Inherited from Latin cēra. Compare Aromanian tsearã.
Inherited from Late Latin caecia, from classical Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”). Compare Lombard scega (“fog”), scighera (“fog”).
Borrowed from Latin cedens.
Borrowed from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros). Doublet of chedru.

Inherited from Late Latin cellārium, from Latin cella. Probably also used to mean cellar, basement (cognate to Aromanian tsilar (“cellar, basement”)), however was displaced by the Turkic beci before written attestation.
Borrowed from Latin census.
Borrowed from Latin centaurus.
Borrowed from Latin centenarius.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin centum.
Borrowed from Latin centumvir.
Borrowed from Latin centumviralis or French centumviral.
Borrowed from Latin centuriatis.
Borrowed from Latin centuria.
Borrowed from Latin centurio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cinusia, from Latin cinus, a less common variant of cinis (“ashes”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”). Compare Aromanian cinushi.
Inherited from Latin cippus, with some senses possibly influenced by Proto-Slavic *čepъ.

parole.significato: a seller or vendor of onions
parole.testo: From ceapă (“onion”) + -ar (“-er”) or from Latin caepārius.
Inherited from Latin caelum.
Inherited from Latin cerrus.
Inherited from Latin cervus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Compare Aromanian tserbu.
From cerb + -ar or possibly from Latin cervārius.
Inherited from Latin cervīcem, accusative of cervīx, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head”) and *weyk- (“to bend”). Doublet of the borrowed cervix.
Inherited from Latin circus, from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos). Compare circ, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.
Inherited from Latin circellus (“small ring”), from circus.

parole.significato: to examine, investigate, inspect, scrutinize, search
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin circitāre, from Latin circō.

Inherited from Latin quaerere (“seek, look for, desire”). In the 19th century, the older form of the simple perfect, cerșii, from Latin quaesīvī, was replaced by cerui by analogy and the old past participle, cerșit, from Latin quaesītus, was replaced by cerut. The r in these obsolete words were them
Borrowed from Latin cerebellum. Cf. creier, which may be an inherited doublet.

parole.significato: wood avens, avens, herb bennet (Geum urbanum)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cerinthus + the Romanian diminutive suffix -el.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin cerithium.
Inherited from Latin cernere, from Proto-Italic *krinō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.
From ceară + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin cērōsus. Compare Italian ceroso, French cireux.
Borrowed from Latin certus.

parole.significato: to quarrel, squabble, argue, altercate, row, argufy, wrangle, fall out with someone
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin certāre.
Borrowed from Latin certitudo. Equivalent to cert + -itudine.
From cerșii (itself from Latin quaesīvī), an older form of the simple perfect of cere (“to request, ask for”).
Borrowed from Latin caetaceum, ultimately from cētus (“whale”).
Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Originally also having the sense of city; which was displaced by the Magyarism oraș. The two can been seen used interchangeably in old texts.

parole.significato: to play the fiddle or violin
parole.testo: From ceteră. Compare local Bessarabian and Maramureș form cetereza, possibly from Latin citharizāre (compare Italian cetereggiare, citarizzare, also Old Italian ceterare).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin citera, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Compare Italian cetra. Doublet of chitară (from Italian), țiteră (from German); cf. also the related citolă (from French).
From cetate + -ean, from Latin civitatis, with meaning possibly based partly on (Old) French citezein; cf. modern citoyen.
Borrowed from Latin caesar. Doublet of țar.
Borrowed from Latin caesarinus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *clagum, from metathesis of Latin coāgulum (cf. the contracted Late Latin form quaglum, found in some manuscripts). Cognate with Aromanian cljag. A late Eastern Romance (or earlier Romanian) form was borrowed into Ukrainian ґляґ (gljag), dialectal Polish klag, dialec
Inherited from Latin clāvis, clāvem.
Inherited from Latin clāmāre, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”). Compare Aromanian cljem, cljimari, Italian chiamare, Neapolitan chiammà. Doublet of clama, which was borrowed from French.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *clautoria, from *clautus, from clavutus, ultimately from Latin clāvus.
Borrowed from Latin quaestor.

Inherited from Latin clārus, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Doublet of clar, which was a borrowing. Used almost always as an adverb in modern speech (compare Latin pure, adverb form of purus). The old adjective form is only found in old texts and in some expressions such as "di
Learned borrowing from Latin chīmia.

parole.significato: saddle girth, band, cinch, belly band
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin cingula (itself from the plural of Latin cingulum), possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *clinga, following syncopation and metathesis. Cf. Neapolitan chienga (vs. Italian cinghia).
Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.
Borrowed from Latin chirurgus, German Chirurg (19th century), earlier from Greek χειρουργός (cheirourgós); ultimately from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
Borrowed from Latin chirurgicus. By surface analysis, chirurgie + -ic.

parole.significato: cicada (any of several insects of the order Hemiptera)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cicāda. Compare cicoare, a doublet inherited through a Vulgar Latin variant.
Learned borrowing from Latin cicātrīx, cicatricem.

From Early Medieval Latin cicāla, from Latin cicāda. The hypothetical original Romanian form, *cicară, was probably influenced phonetically by the unrelated word below. Doublet of cicadă, a borrowing.
From Latin cichōria, plural of cichōrium, from Ancient Greek κιχόριον (kikhórion).
Inherited from Latin cēnāre.
Borrowed from Latin cinnamomum.

parole.significato: only used in cince de sătul (“full as a bedbug”).
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cīmicem (“bedbug”).
Inherited from Latin cīnque.

Borrowed from Latin cisalpinus or Italian cisalpino or French cisalpin.

parole.testo: From ciur, possibly corresponding to Latin crībrō, crībrāre, through a Vulgar Latin dissimilated form *cibrāre.

parole.significato: with reddish or brownish color or spots on its head

parole.testo: From coadă (“tail”) + alb (“white”), or possibly from a common Romance or Vulgar Latin source; compare Aromanian cudalbã, Sardinian codalbola.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin columna (19th century). Doublet of coloană and possibly corună.

parole.significato: name given by Romans to non-noble Dacian

Borrowed from Late Latin combīnātiō or Italian combinazione. Equivalent to combina + -ție.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *cucūta, from Latin cicūta, of Proto-Indo-European origin.

Inherited from Latin conforīre, from foriō, from foria (“diarrhea”). Compare Aromanian cufurescu, cufuriri, cf. also Portuguese and Galician forricar, esforricar.
