Inherited from Latin quantus, influenced by (conflated with) quotus (“of what number, how many”).

parole.significato: in groups of, in series of (used to indicate a collective or distributive numeral, and often used with a number)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cata, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá). The normal result in old Romanian would have been *cată, later *cate, and was influenced by cât (see the above etymology). Compare Spanish and Portuguese cada, Occitan cadun, French chacun, Italian cadauno.

parole.significato: interval between two Orthodox fasts when meat can be eaten
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cāseum ligās (literally “thou tiest the cheese”). Akin to Aromanian cãshleagã, cãshleadzi. Compare also cârneleagă.

Inherited from Latin castīgāre, with a unique semantic evolution compared to the other Romance languages: while "to punish, chastise" was a primary sense of the Latin word, one of the other senses was "to correct, amend", and related to the notion of attaining purity and virtue (see castus and chast
Inherited from Latin quod, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Compare Aromanian cã, che.

Inherited from Latin cacāre, from Proto-Italic *kak(k)āō, from Proto-Indo-European *kakka- (imitative root related to defecation). Compare Italian cagare, French chier, Spanish cagar, Portuguese cagar.

Contraction of căca + mă + aș – literally "May I shit". From Latin Latin cacāre (“to defecate”), with reflexive and conditional forms added. Used as a vulgar, expressive interjection to convey shock, annoyance, ridicule, or frustration, often followed by a humorous or insulting clause.
Past participle of the verb căca, corresponding to Latin cacātus. Compare Aromanian cãcat.
Inherited from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

parole.significato: mounted, astride of, on horseback, ahorse
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caballāris, caballārem, ultimately from Latin caballus (“horse”). Another theory suggests caballārius (cf. the old form călariu), with a change in declension. Compare Aromanian (n)cãlar, cãlari; cf. also Albanian kalëroj.
Inherited from Late Latin caballarius.
Inherited from Latin calcāre.
Inherited from Latin calcāneum.
From călca + -ătură, or possibly Latin calcatura.
Inherited from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caldūra, from Latin caldus, calidus. Compare Italian caldura, Aromanian cãldurã. By surface analysis, cald + -ură.

From a derivative of Late Latin cardellus, from Latin carduelis, from carduus; the original (expected) descendant form in Romanian, *cărdel, was later suffixed with the ending -aș, and also changed due to a mistaken association with the unrelated căldare. Compare Italian cardello, cardellino, cardel
Inherited from Late Latin caballāricius, from Latin caballus (“horse”). By surface analysis, cal + -ăreț. Compare Aromanian cãlãrets, Albanian kalorës.
From călători (“to travel”) + -ie, ultimately from Latin callis (“path, lane”).
Inherited from Late Latin camisia, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱem- (“cover, clothes”).
Borrowed from Slavic language or inherited from Latin camīnus, which both are borrowed from Greek κάμινος (káminos). Compare Bulgarian камина (kamina), Serbo-Croatian kamin.

parole.significato: the part of the bridle that goes over the horse's head
parole.testo: Probably from căpețel, either as a feminine form or reformed from its plural, căpețele. Another theory derives it from an early Romanian root *căpeț or căpăț, from Latin capitium, with the diminutive suffix -ea.

Inherited from Latin capisterium, probably through a Vulgar Latin *capisteria. The Latin further derives from Ancient Greek σκαφιστήριον (skaphistḗrion). Compare Tuscan Italian capistejo, capisteo, Abruzzese Neapolitan capistiera.
Inherited from Latin caprārius. Equivalent to capră + -ar.

parole.significato: a sheep with long and straight wool
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin caprina, feminine of caprinus.
Inherited from Latin capreolus. For secondary meanings, compare similar meanings in French chevron, Spanish cabrio; cf. also Albanian qepër.

parole.significato: a shelter, such as a hut or shed, for goats; place where goats take their rest
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caprāricia, from Latin capra (“goat”). By surface analysis, capră + -ăreață. Compare Aromanian cãpãrleatsã, cãpreatsã.
Inherited from Latin capistrum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitāre, from Latin caput. Compare Italian capitare (“happen; turn up, occur; end up”); compare also Albanian kaptoj, cf. Occitan acaptar.

parole.significato: bedside, pillow, end of the bed
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin capitāneum, neutral of capitāneus, from Latin capita. Compare Aromanian cãpitãnj, cãpitinj. Doublet of căpitan.

parole.significato: head of a dead animal cut for consumption
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin capitīna, derived from Latin caput (“head”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *carrāre, from Latin carrus. Compare Sardinian carrare. Other Romance cognates seem to have come from a root *carriāre. Related through French to English carry.

Inherited from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Akin to Aromanian cãrari, Spanish and Catalan carrera, Portuguese carreira, Occitan carrièra, French carrière (“career”) (hence the doublet carieră), charrière (“path, way”), Italian carriera (“career”), carraia (“road for carts or wagons”
Inherited from Latin carbōnārius, equivalent to cărbune + -ar.
Inherited from Latin carbōnem, accusative of carbō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”). Doublet of carbon, a borrowing from French.
Inherited from Latin calendārium. Compare also Albanian kallnor (“January”). Doublet of calendar.
Inherited from Latin carnōsus. Corresponding to carne + -os. Compare Aromanian cãrnos.
Inherited from Late Latin cānūtus, from Latin cānus. Compare Aromanian cãnut.

parole.significato: spot or mark left on the body from sweat, filth, or dirt
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carōnia, ultimately from Latin carō, perhaps influenced in Romanian by râie.
From Latin scarabaeus, see also Sardinian carrabusu, French escarbot, Greek σκαραβαίος (skaravaíos).

parole.significato: head of a family or household
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin casārius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cascāre, from Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn, gape”). Compare Aromanian hascu, cascu, Sardinian cascare, cascai.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *cascabundus, from *cascare, or a variation of *căscăun, from căsca.

parole.significato: to, toward (in the direction of, and arriving at)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin contrā. Doublet of contra.

From a lost hypothetical word *cată or *catŭ (from Late Latin catta (“cat”) / cattus), with the diminutive suffix -ușă added later. It was once attested in an old gloss with the now obsolete meaning 'cat' (now replaced by pisică in modern Romanian). Additionally, the original meaning is also preserv
Possibly from a root *cău, from Latin cavus, with the diminutive suffix -uș. Compare also zgău, gaură, găun, găoace. Also possibly an alteration of cauc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadūtus, past participle for Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *occāsionāre (possibly later changed into a form *cāssionāre, or *accāsionāre), from Latin occāsiō. Compare Italian cagionare, accagionare, Old French achoisoner (however, these may also be internally derived or formed from nouns descending from occāsiō (cf. Italian cagio
Inherited from Latin catella (“female puppy, young bitch”). Compare Portuguese cadela, Aromanian cãtsauã, cãtsau.
Inherited from Latin catellus (“little, young dog”). Compare Aromanian cãtsãl.
Inherited from Latin catīnum, from catīnus, from Proto-Italic *katinos.
From Latin dare, ultimately from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”). Compare Aromanian dau, dari, Italian dare, Spanish dar.
Borrowed from Latin Dacus, ultimately from Dacian.
Borrowed from Latin dacicus. By surface analysis, dac + -ic.
From earlier deacă, probably from Latin de quod.

parole.significato: laurel (evergreen shrub, of the genus Laurus)
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin daphinus, from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē). Also possibly from Serbo-Croatian dafina; other theories suggest this word was actually borrowed from Latin or Romanian. See also the related afin.
Borrowed from Latin dalmatica or French dalmatique.
Borrowed from Latin dalmatinus.
Borrowed from Latin Danai.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably from a compound of de and iar(ă). It may also perhaps come from an intermediate form *deară, from Latin dē vērō, or from dē eā rē. See also doar.
Borrowed from Latin dativus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *debtoriu < *dēbitōrius for Latin dēbitor (“debtor”), ultimately from dēbitum (“debt”), from dēbeō (“to owe”); influenced by the verb da (“to give”). Compare Aromanian dãtor. Doublet of the borrowing debitor.
From dator (“debtor”) + -ie, from Latin dēbitor (“debtor”). Sense 3 results from conflation with the verb da (“to give”).
Borrowed from Latin datura.
Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnom (“expense, investment”).
Inherited from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁.
Derived from Latin de facto. Literally, “of fact”.
Borrowed from Latin decanus or German Dekan.
Borrowed from Latin (mensis) december (19th century). Replaced older decemvrie, which came from the same source but through a Byzantine Greek (cf. Δεκέμβριος (Dekémvrios)) and Slavic intermediary.
Borrowed from Latin decemvir.
Borrowed from Latin decemviralis or French décemviral.
Borrowed from Latin decemviratus.
Borrowed from Latin decennium.
Borrowed from Latin decimatio. Equivalent to decima + -ție.
From Old Romanian de + cinde, the latter from Vulgar Latin *eccum inde, whence also Italian quindi.
Borrowed from Latin decuria.
Borrowed from Latin decurio.
From a Vulgar Latin root *dedāre, from Latin dēdere.

parole.significato: to dedicate (to an idea, an activity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dedicare, Italian dedicare. Compare French dédier.
Borrowed from Latin dedicativus. By surface analysis, dedica + -tiv.
Borrowed from Latin dedicatio. Equivalent to dedica + -ție.

parole.significato: to infer, deduce (to conclude by reasoning or deduction, as from premises or evidence)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deducere, French déduire, with conjugation based on duce.
From Latin fāma, probably derived from the verb diffamāre. Compare defăima.
Borrowed from Latin defectus or German Defekt.
Borrowed from Latin defendere.
Borrowed from Latin defensio.
Borrowed from Latin defoliare.
From Latin diffamāre, from fāma (“fame”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *degelāre, from dē- + gelāre. Compare Aromanian dzeadzir, dzidzirari.
Inherited from Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”). Compare Aromanian dzeadzit. Doublet of digit.
Borrowed from Latin deleatur.
Borrowed from Latin Delphicus.
Borrowed from Latin delicium and French délice.
Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum.
Borrowed from Latin delinquens.
Borrowed from Latin diluvium.
Borrowed from Latin demiurgus.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin dignus, modeled after words such as lemn, semn.
Borrowed from Latin dignitas, dignitatem. By surface analysis, demn + -itate. Doublet of dignitate.
Borrowed from Latin daemonicus. Equivalent to demon + -ic.
Borrowed from Latin denarius. Doublet of dinar.
Borrowed from Latin denegare.
Borrowed from Latin dēnigrātor.
Borrowed from Latin denuntiatio.
Borrowed from Latin depingere.
Borrowed from Latin deponens.
Borrowed from Latin deportatio. By surface analysis, deporta + -țiune.
Borrowed from Latin depositum.

parole.significato: to get used to, familiarize with, habituate, become accustomed with, acclimatize, acclimate
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dēprehendere. Compare Valencian Catalan deprendre (“to learn”), Galician deprender (“to teach”).

parole.significato: accustomed, familiarized, used to; having experienced, learned, or become familiar with; enured
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dēprensus, variant of dēprehensus.
Inherited from Latin dēpōnere. The last sense was inherited, and the other modern senses are based off French déposer as neologisms.

parole.significato: to reel on/up, wind a hank of something on a reel or bobbin
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *depānāre or *depēnāre, from Latin pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos). Compare Aromanian deapin, dipinari, Italian dipanare, Catalan debanar, Spanish devanar, Portuguese dobar, Sardinian demanare.

parole.significato: to tidy up (a house, room etc.)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *dēradicāre, from Latin dē- + radicāre (“take root”) (cf. ridica).
Inherited from Latin dēnsus (“dense; frequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”). Doublet of dens, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin de ipsa de nocte.
Borrowed from Latin descensio.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *disclāvāre or *disclāviāre (probably influenced by încheia or cheie), from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus. Compare Aromanian dishcljiedz, dishcljiari; cf. also Friulian disclavâ, French déclouer.
Inherited from Latin disclūdere. Compare Aromanian dishcljid, dishcljidiri, Italian dischiudere.
Past participle of deschide, possibly from Latin disclusus. Compare Italian dischiuso.
Inherited from Latin discingere.
Inherited from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. By surface analysis, des- + coperi.
From a Vulgar Latin root *discuneāre, from Latin cuneō, from cuneus.
From des- + încurca, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *de-obscuricare, from Latin obscurus.

parole.significato: to charm away or heal with magic words, such as an illness, or to undo or remove a spell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discantāre, from Latin dis- + cantō. Compare Aromanian discãntu, discãntari, Friulian discjantâ (“disenchant, awaken, make wiser”), Venetan descantar (“wake up, sharpen up”); cf. also French déchanter.

parole.significato: to get off a horse, dismount, alight
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discaballicāre, from dis- + Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus (“horse”). Compare Aromanian discalic, discãlicari or Albanian shkalkoj. Sense 2 may have been influenced by a migratory or nomadic Central Asian people that entered lands occupied by Romanians, as a

parole.significato: to take off or remove a shoe
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin discalceāre, from Latin dis- + calceō.
Inherited from Late Latin discarricāre, from carricō, from Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”). Compare Spanish descargar.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin disfacere, from Latin dis- + facere. Synchronically des- + face. Compare Spanish deshacer.

Unknown. One proposed etymology was a Vulgar Latin *disfabicāre. It is more likely linked to or derived from Romanian înșfăca. Cf. also Aromanian dizvoc, dizvucari (“tear to shreds, delapidate, wreck”), which may or may not be related. See also the rare and dialectal Romanian dezvoca, which may be a

Unknown. Probably from Latin dis- + fētēre (“smell bad, stink”) (compare Spanish heder (“stink, reek; upset”). The prefix dis- would indicate the opposite of the verb it modifies, thus the meaning that emerged for this word in Romanian; cf. also a similar occurrence in dezmierda. Other suggested ety
Borrowed from Latin desperatio. Equivalent to despera + -ție.
Inherited from Latin dēspicāre (“to cleave or cut the bowels (of an animal), empty a sacrificial animal”). Compare Aromanian disic, dischic, Megleno-Romanian dispic.
Inherited from Latin dēspoliāre.
Inherited from Latin dispōnere. Doublet of dispune, a borrowed word.
Inherited from Latin dispartīre. By surface analysis, des- + parte + -i.

parole.significato: (used with the dative of the reflexive pronoun) to compensate, make up for, or make amends for a wrongdoing or harm
parole.testo: From des- + toarce (or întoarce), possibly corresponding to Latin distorqueō, distorquēre (through a Vulgar Latin root *distorcere).
Borrowed from Latin detractio.

parole.significato: to fulminate, strike down by lightning, thunder
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dētonāre. Cognate with Aromanian ditun, ditunari. Doublet of the borrowed detona.

parole.significato: to devote oneself (to an idea, an activity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin devotare, compare French dévouer.
Learned borrowing from Latin dexter.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin dextra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *disglaciāre, from dis- + glaciāre. Compare Aromanian dizgljets, dizgljitsari.

parole.significato: to shell (remove outer covering or shell), husk (remove husks from), pod (remove peas from their pod), shuck.
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *disglubicāre or alternatively composed of dez- + ghioc + -a.
Borrowed from Latin desiderare.

Borrowed from Latin desideratum, possibly through the partial intermediate of German Desiderat. May also be seen as the past participle of the now rare or archaic verb dezidera (cf. also the variant obsolete inherited form deșidera).

parole.significato: to wake up from a state such as that of drunkenness, stupor, fear, powerful emotion, or dizziness; sober up
parole.testo: Unknown. One possibility may be a Vulgar Latin root *dismatticāre, from Latin mattus (“drunk”). Another etymology may be from an earlier form *desmântici, from a Latin root *de-exmenticāre, with change of conjugation (compare Italian dimenticare). Compare the verb dezmeți, and also dezmetic, possibl

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dismerdāre, a verb based on Latin merda (“faeces”). The sense evolution from "remove faeces" to "caress" appears to have occurred in the context of childcare. Compare Aromanian diznjerdu.

parole.significato: to live unrestrained, licentiously or in libertinage
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *dismētiāre, from dis- + Latin metīrī. Compare Spanish desmedirse (“to overstep the mark”).

parole.significato: to unlearn, become unfamiliar with, forget how to do something, wean from, stop or break off a habit
parole.testo: From dez- + învăța, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *disvitiāre, from *vitiāre (in the sense of "accustom, habituate, familiarize"), from Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Aromanian dizvets, dizvitsari, cf. also Italian divezzare, svezzare.
Inherited from Latin dēsertus.

parole.significato: to desire, wish or long for
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dēsīderāre. Is now archaic in Romanian. Compare Albanian dëshiroj.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin diserrāre, from dis- + serrāre. Alternatively, related to șir.

parole.significato: awake (in the sense of being wise or clever)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin de-excitus or more likely from dispectus. Also possibly a back-formation from deștepta (“to wake up”). Compare Aromanian dishteptu.

parole.significato: to awaken, to wake up, to rouse
parole.testo: Traditionally considered to be from Vulgar Latin *deexcitāre, from Latin de- + excitāre (“wake up”) (cf. Italian destare, also Dalmatian destruar), but is more likely from Latin dispectāre (frequentative of dispiciō (“look, discern, perceive, discover”) through its past participle dispectus). It is
Inherited from Latin dēscendere. Replaced by the neologism descinde (a borrowed/semi-learned doublet partly based on this word).
Borrowed from Latin dictatio. By surface analysis, dicta + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin dadascalia or Greek διδασκαλία (didaskalía).
Borrowed from Latin dignus.
Borrowed from Latin dignare.
Borrowed from Latin dignitas, dignitatem, from dignus. Doublet of demnitate.
Borrowed from Latin diligens or French diligent.

parole.significato: just now, a moment ago, not long ago
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin de una hora.

Inherited from Latin dentem, the singular accusative of dēns, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts. Compare Spanish diente, Catalan dent, French dent, Italian dente and Aromanian dinti.
Borrowed from Latin Diomedea.
Borrowed from Latin directio, French direction.
Borrowed from Latin dīrigere; after cârmui. Doublet of drege, which was inherited, and of dirija, which was borrowed through French.
Borrowed from Latin discipulus.
Borrowed from Latin discolorus.
Borrowed from Latin discriminare or Italian discriminare or French discriminer.
Borrowed from Latin discriminator or French discriminatoire.
Borrowed from Latin disertus or French disert.
Borrowed from Latin dissimilis.
Borrowed from Latin dēspērāre.
Borrowed from Latin dispersus.
Borrowed from Latin dispono. Based on pune. Doublet of despune, an inherited word.
Borrowed from Latin disputatio or French disputation. By surface analysis, disputa + -ție.
Borrowed from Late Latin disparere, Italian disparire, French disparaître, with conjugation based on părea.
Borrowed from Latin disturbatio.
Borrowed from Latin dividere.
Borrowed from Latin divitiae.
Borrowed from Latin dissolutio.
Inherited from Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ-éh₂.
Inherited from Latin Domine, vocative of Dominus (“The Lord”).

parole.significato: lady, polite term for a woman, madam, ma'am
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina. Doublet of damă.

Probably from a reduction of the variant form doară, itself probably from Latin dē hōrā. Alternative etymologies include a Vulgar Latin construction *de volat, alteration of dē velit, or that it perhaps resulted from confusion with oare, with an interrogative function, or simply that it derives from
From doagă + -ar, or possibly Latin dogārius < doga. Compare Aromanian dugar.

From a Vulgar Latin *duī (“two”, root), from Latin duo, probably formed through analogy with the usual nominative masculine plural ending in -ī. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. The similar formation of *duī also happened in Old French dui, nominative form of deus.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin dolium.
Learned borrowing from Latin dolor. Doublet of duroare.
Borrowed from Latin dolosus.
From domestic (“domesticated”), from Latin domesticus.
Borrowed from Latin domicilium or French domicile.
Borrowed from Latin dominārī, or via French dominer/Italian dominare (both borrowings from Latin).

parole.significato: mister, Mr., sir, polite term for a man
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin domnus, from Latin dominus. Cognates include Aromanian domnu, Italian donno, Spanish dueño, Portuguese dono.
Borrowed from Latin donarium.
Borrowed from Latin donativum. By surface analysis, dona + -tiv.

parole.significato: wistfulness, melancholy, nostalgia, longing; a feeling of missing someone or something
parole.testo: From Late Latin dolus (“pain, grief”), a derivative of Latin dolor (“pain”). Compare Portuguese dó (“sorrow, compassion”), Spanish duelo (“sorrow, mourning”), French deuil (“bereavement”).
Inherited from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.
Inherited from Latin dormītāre.

parole.significato: bedroom (room in a house where a bed is kept for sleeping)
parole.testo: From dormi + -tor, possibly corresponding to Latin dormītōrium (plural from dormītōria).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. This is the original and now dated Romanian word for the back - mainly replaced in common usage by the (originally popular, now standard language) alternative spate (“back”). Compare French dos and Romansh dies.
Feminine form of doi. From Latin duae, nominative feminine of duo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).

Inherited from Latin dracō (“dragon”), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Compare also Catalan and Occitan drac and the derived French drac. Doublet of dragon, which was borrowed from French. Compare Sicilian dragu, Megleno-Romanian and Aromanian drac.

parole.significato: to mend, repair, fix, doctor, restore, renew, renovate, set in order
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dīrigere. Doublet of dirigui and dirija.
From an earlier *drepănea, from a Vulgar Latin root *drepanella, diminutive of Latin drepanis.

parole.significato: right (referring to the direction or side)
parole.testo: From the older form dirept, derept, from Late Latin drictus or Vulgar Latin *dērēctus, from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct, a later borrowing.

parole.significato: a ruler or straight edge used to verify flat surfaces in construction
parole.testo: Probably from drept + -ar. Also possibly from an Latin directarium, from directus.
Probably from an earlier dreptătate, from drept + -tate. Other theories have included a Latin root *direct(it)atem, from directus, though this is unlikely. Compare Aromanian ndriptati.
Borrowed from Latin dubiōsus. By surface analysis, dubiu + -os.
Borrowed from Latin dubitare.
Borrowed from Latin dubium.
Inherited from Latin dūcere, from Proto-Italic *doukō, from Proto-Indo-European *déwketi, from the root *dewk-. Reinforcement by Italian ducere is possible.
Borrowed from Latin ductus.

From a Vulgar Latin root *doliōsus, ultimately from Latin dolor or dolēre. Compare Italian doglioso, Friulian duliôs. Also possibly from an unattested, lost Romanian word *doi, from Vulgar Latin *dolium, from Latin cordolium.
Inherited from Latin dulcem. Compare Aromanian dultsi. Reinforcement by Italian dolce is possible.
Probably from Late Latin dulcor, dulcōrem, from Latin dulcis. Equivalent to dulce + -oare
Inherited from Latin domesticus, possibly influenced later by Proto-Slavic *domaštьnъ. Today, the neologism domestic is much more common.

parole.significato: to tear, usually to drop into a liquid (milk, stew)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *dēmīcāre, from Latin mīca. Compare Aromanian dinjic, dinjicari.
Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”). Compare Aromanian Dumãnicã.

From domnia, from domn, from Latin dominus (“master”) + voastră, from Latin voster, vostra (“your”), thus initially meaning "your lordship". Compare similar constructions in Spanish usted (“you”) from vuestra merced (cf. also vuecencia), Portuguese você (“you”), Catalan vostè, etc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post. Compare Aromanian dupã, Italian dopo.
Inherited from Latin dolāre.
Borrowed from Latin dura mater.
Borrowed from Latin dura mater.
Inherited from Latin dolēre, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”).
Inherited from Latin dolōrem, from doleō + -or. Equivalent to durea + -oare
Inherited from Late Latin dolōrōsus. Replaced by dureros, a language-internal derivation from durere.
Borrowed from Latin duumvir.

parole.significato: duumviral (of or relating to the duumvirs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin duumviralis.

parole.significato: duumvirate (rank or office of a duumvir)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin duumviratus.
Feminine of dânsul. From de + însa, articulated form of însă, or possibly from Latin idem ipsa or id ipsa.

From de + însul, articulated definite form of îns, or according to another theory, based on a Latin idem ipse or id ipsum. Compare Aromanian dãs, dis, variant of nãs, the older form Italian desso, Friulian zenso.
Inherited from Latin depilāre. Compare Aromanian deapir, dipirari. See also the neological doublet depila.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Italian diramare, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

parole.significato: to tire, tire out, wear out, exhaust, overfatigue
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *derenēre or *derenāre, from Latin rēn (“kidney”). Compare Italian direnare, Spanish derrengar.
From daună. May also correspond to Latin damnāre (therefore a doublet of damna).
From daună + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin damnōsus.
From Latin et.
Inherited from Latin illa, feminine of ille.
Borrowed from Latin ebriesitas.
Borrowed from Latin ecclesia.
Borrowed from Latin edacitas or Italian edacità.
Borrowed from Latin hederaceus.
Borrowed from Latin edictum.
Borrowed from Latin edulis.
Borrowed from Latin efficacia.
Borrowed from Latin effectus, with meanings based on French effet.
Borrowed from Latin ephelis.
Borrowed from Latin ēgregius.
Borrowed from Latin egressio.
Borrowed from Latin aegritudo.

parole.significato: they (used for an all-male or mixed-sex group)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille.
Inherited from Latin illaei.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *illus, from Latin ille.
Borrowed from Latin elaterium.

parole.significato: they (for a group composed completely of females)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illae, nominative feminine plural of ille.
Borrowed from Latin eliberāre, from liberō.
Borrowed from Latin elucidatio. Equivalent to elucida + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin emendo or French émender.
Borrowed from Latin emendabilis.
Borrowed from Latin emendatio.
Borrowed from Latin eminintissimus or Italian eminentissimo or French éminentissime. By surface analysis, eminent + -isim.
Borrowed from Latin emittere.
Borrowed from Latin emittens or Italian emittente.
Borrowed from Latin epicureus.
Borrowed from Latin epistola.
Borrowed from Latin eradicare or Italian eradicare.
Borrowed from Latin erectus.
Borrowed from Latin heres or Italian erede.
Borrowed from Latin erogatio.
Borrowed from Latin erroneus.
Borrowed from Latin erumpere.
Inherited from Latin iste tempus.
Borrowed from Latin exundatio.
Borrowed from Latin aetas.
Borrowed from Latin aetās, aetatem (19th century). Compare Aromanian etã which was most likely inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin et cētera (“and the others”).
Borrowed from Latin aethereus or Italian etèreo.
Borrowed from Latin aeternus.
Borrowed from Latin ethos or Ancient Greek ἦθος (êthos).
Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.
Borrowed from Latin eugenia.
Borrowed from Latin aevum (“age, generation”).
Borrowed from Latin ēvenīre.
Borrowed from Latin ēvincere, from Latin vincō, and adapted to învinge.
Borrowed from Latin evitatio.
Borrowed from Latin evocativus.
Borrowed from Latin evocatio. By surface analysis, evoca + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin exāmen.
Borrowed from Latin exceptus.
Borrowed from Latin excludere.
Borrowed from Latin excōgitāre.
Borrowed from Latin excommunicō.
Borrowed from Latin excrescentia.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin excursus.
Borrowed from Latin excusatio.

parole.significato: to exercise, to use (e.g. one's rights)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exercitare.
Borrowed from Latin exercitatio or Italian esercitazione. By surface analysis, exercita + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin exhereditare.
Borrowed from Latin exfoliare or French exfolier.
Borrowed from Latin exigere or French exiger.
Borrowed from Latin exiguus.
Learned borrowing from Latin exitus.
Borrowed from Latin exoneratio or French exonération. Equivalent to exonera + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin exoratio or French exoration.
Borrowed from Latin exorcista.

parole.significato: exordium, beginning, commencement of a discourse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exordium.
Borrowed from Latin exhortatio. By surface analysis, exorta + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin expandō.
Borrowed from Latin expansio.
Borrowed from Latin experiens.
Borrowed from Latin experimentum.
Borrowed from Latin explicāre, French expliquer.
Borrowed from Latin expunctio.

parole.significato: to exhibit, to lay out, to expose, to make known
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exponere. Equivalent to ex- + pune, literally “to put out”. Doublet of spune, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin extemporaneus.
Borrowed from Latin extendere, based on the conjugation of întinde.
Borrowed from Latin extispicium.
Borrowed from Latin extractus.
Borrowed from Latin extrahere, based on the example of French extraire, with conjugation modeled on trage. Aromanian term astrag was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin extraneus.
Borrowed from Latin fābula. Doublet of faulă.

Inherited from Latin facere. The original past participle fapt (< Latin factus) has been replaced by an analogical form. An alternative third-person simple perfect, fece (< Latin fēcit) was also found in some dialects. The sense of “to cost” is likely a calque of Greek κάνω (káno).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *facla, from a contraction of Latin facula (“little torch”), from fax (“torch”). Doublet of făclie and faclă (borrowings through Slavic and Greek intermediates), and flacără (from a Vulgar Latin variant form).
From Latin facilitas through French facilité. Equivalent to facil + -itate.
Inherited from Latin fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech tree”).
Inherited from Latin favus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *favulus, from Latin favus, or taken from faguri, plural of fag, an older form of the word.
Inherited from Latin fāma.

parole.significato: fallacious (characterized by fallacy; false or mistaken)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fallaciosus or French fallacieux.

parole.significato: old unit of measurement (used in Moldova) in agriculture equivalent to about half a hectare, or an area of land that si…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin falx, falcem (“sickle”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelk-, *dʰelg- (“a cutting tool”). Cf. Medieval Latin falcata. See also the related form falcă (“jaw”), which underwent further semantic evolution from the original etymology of "sickle" in Latin.

Back-formation from fălci (plural), from Latin falx, falcem (“sickle”), or through a Vulgar Latin form *falca; compare Aromanian falcã; change in meaning, due to the shape of the mandible, also in Albanian felqinë (“jaw”). Compare also the semantic development of Sardinian cavanu (“jaw”) and cavana
Probably borrowed from Latin falsus (“false”). The variant form falș is from German falsch.
Borrowed from Latin falx.
From the plural of famăn, from Vulgar Latin (homo) *feminus, from Latin femina. Compare Aromanian feamin. Compare Portuguese fêmeo, Old Occitan feme.
Borrowed from Latin familia. Compare the inherited doublet femeie.
Borrowed from Latin fanum.

Inherited from Latin factum. Was once also the past participle of the verb face (“to do, make”), replaced by făcut after the 16th century through analogy with other -e ending third-conjugation verbs (i.e. cere > cerut, trece > trecut). Cognate to Italian fatto, French fait and Spanish hecho.
Inherited from Latin facta, plural of factum.
Borrowed from Latin Pharus, French phare.
Borrowed from Latin pharetra.
Inherited from Latin pharmacum, from Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”), from φαρμακίς (pharmakís, “witch”).
Borrowed from Latin fascis.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin fatum.
Inherited from Latin fēta (“woman who has just given birth”), substantivization of the adjective fētus. Compare Aromanian featã.
Inherited from Latin fābula. Doublet of fabulă, a borrowing. The semantic evolution probably developed thus: "a story" to "a recounting / description" to "an appearance".
Borrowed from Latin faunus.
Inherited from Latin fabrum, accusative singular of faber.
Inherited from Latin fascia.
Inherited from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”). Compare Aromanian fatsã.

Borrowed from Latin (mensis) februārius (19th century), and influenced by the older form of the word. Replaced older fevruarie which came from the same word but through a Slavic intermediary. The original term inherited from Latin, făurar, remains a folk term for the month.
From a Vulgar Latin *fetiola, a diminutive of Latin feta, from fetus.

parole.significato: youth, boy, child, unmarried young man
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *fētiolus, from Latin fetus. Compare Aromanian ficior.
Borrowed from Latin foederatus or French fédéré.

Inherited from Latin familia (“family”). Compare Aromanian fumealji (“family; children”), Albanian fëmijë (“child”). The old sense of "family" in Romanian is now lost, replaced by the neologism familie. Despite the phonetic and semantic similarities, is unrelated to Latin femella, and it is improbab
Borrowed from Latin fenestra.
Borrowed from Latin foeniculum, variation of fēnuculum.
Inherited from Latin fenestra, with rhotacism. Doublet of fenestra (“fenestra”).

Inherited from Latin fabricāre (which originally had to do with the forging of iron; see also fabrica, borrowed from this word and thus an etymological doublet, along with forja), and perhaps influenced by fier; another etymology links it to a Vulgar Latin root *ferricāre, from ferrum (compare Old F
Borrowed from Latin ferentarius.

Probably from Latin ferīre (“strike”), of Proto-Indo-European origin, with a related but shifted semantic development in Romanian (with the meaning seeming to derive from the reaction to being struck or attacked). Other less likely explanations include a Vulgar Latin *auferīre, from an alteration of
Inherited from Latin fēlīx, fēlīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-lw-i, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”).
From ferici (“to make happy”) + -re, from ferice, from Latin fēlīx (“happy”).
Inherited from Latin filicem, accusative singular of filix.
From farmec or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *pharmacāre, from Latin pharmacum.
Borrowed from Latin fervidus.
Borrowed from Latin festivus.
Learned borrowing from Latin fētus. Doublet of făt.
Inherited from Latin sum. The citation form and the f- conjugations come from Vulgar Latin *fīre < Latin fierī (“become”). Compare Aromanian hiu.
Inherited from Latin fera, from ferus (“wild animal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer-.

Inherited from Late Latin fīliaster, fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius. Compare Dalmatian fejustro, Italian figliastro, Spanish hijastro, Friulian fiastri, Aromanian hiljeastru. By surface analysis, fiu + -astru.
Borrowed from Latin fībula.
Inherited from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver”). Compare Aromanian hicat, hecat.
Borrowed from Latin ficus.
Inherited from Latin fīlia.
Inherited from Latin ferrum.
Inherited from Latin ferrārius, corresponding to fier + -ar.

parole.significato: to boil (heat (a liquid) until it begins to turn into a gas)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fervere < Classical Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeru- (“to be hot, boil”).
Inherited from Latin fervēntem, accusative of fervēns. Compare Friulian ferbint, Spanish hirviente, Spanish ferviente.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n. Compare Aromanian heari.

Past participle of fierbe. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fertus, contraction of *fervitus for the past participle of Latin ferveō, fervere, as with the Aromanian equivalent hertu. Compare also Apulian (dialect of Italy) fiersetu.

parole.significato: many pieces of iron or instruments made from iron
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *ferratalia, from Latin ferrum. Compare Portuguese ferratalha.
Borrowed from Latin ficus.
From the verb fi + -ință. Also, possibly based on a Vulgar Latin root *fientia (from the Latin verb fiō), a popular equivalent of Latin essentia. Compare Aromanian hiintsã.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin filioque.
Borrowed from Latin fimbria.
Inherited from Latin fīlum, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰiH-(s-)lo-.

parole.significato: of an angry disposition, choleric, furious
parole.testo: Unknown. Probably from fire possibly crossed with iretic, variant of eretic (“heretic”). Another theory suggests Latin phreneticus, influenced by fire in Romanian, or from a derivation of ferus.
Inherited from Latin fīlius. Unrelated to Hungarian fiú (of Uralic origin) despite being almost identical in pronunciation and meaning.

parole.significato: a part of the underside of a yoke
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *fībulāria, ultimately from Latin fībula.
Borrowed from Latin flabellum.
Borrowed from Latin flaccidus.
Borrowed from Latin flagellum (19th century); cf. also French flagelle.
Borrowed from Latin flagellatio.
Inherited from Latin flabrum.
Inherited from Latin flōrem, accusative of flōs, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”). Doublet of floră.
Inherited from Latin floccus.
Possibly inherited from Latin flōrus but, since its rarity, it could also be an internal constuction.
Borrowed from Latin floribundus.
Borrowed from Latin floridus.
From a Vulgar Latin root *florilia, from Latin Flōrālia, from Flōra (“goddess of flowers”), from flōs (“flower”).

parole.significato: a (large) river (large stream which drains a landmass)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluvius (19th century).

Inherited from Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). Cf. also the related folie and foliu, borrowed from the same Latin source.
Inherited from Latin follis, follem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolǵʰnis, derivative of *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).

Inherited from Latin famēs, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Italian fame and Portuguese fome. The Romanian phonetic development was unusual in this case, with the diphthong -oa- normally resulting from a Latin -o-; however, compare the aforementio

Probably from foame, or from an unknown Latin root derived from fames as a parallel formation to foame. Compare also the plural declension of words like cap > capete. Another possibility is that it was influenced in spoken Latin by fomes, fomitem. Compare Aromanian foamitã.
Inherited from Latin forficem, accusative singular of forfex. Compare Aromanian foarficã, Italian forbice, Sardinian fórfighe, fórfiga.

From the Latin adjective fortis, fortem, from Old Latin forctis, fortis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”). Compare the same semantic development in French fort, Occitan fòrça, Ligurian foart (attested in Menton, France). In older Romanian, the word was also used as a freesta
Ultimately from Latin fossa. Doublet of fosă.
Inherited from Latin focus. Compare Aromanian foc.
Borrowed from Latin folio.
Borrowed from Latin folium.
Borrowed from Latin forum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin forficāre, ultimately from Latin forfex (“scissors”). Compare Aromanian nfoarfic, nfurficari, furtichedz, Sardinian forfigare, Asturian aforfegar.
Borrowed from Latin forma, French forme.
Borrowed from Latin fornīcāre.
Borrowed from Latin Forsythia.
Borrowed from Latin fortificare or French fortifier. By surface analysis, fort + -ifica.
Borrowed from Latin forum.

parole.significato: the strawberry of the woodland strawberry or wild strawberry, Fragaria vesca (the fruit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fraga, neuter plural of fragum.
Inherited from Latin fraxinus, from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”). Compare Aromanian frapsin.
Borrowed from Latin fraternus.
Borrowed from Latin frāternitās, frāternitātem. Equivalent to fratern + -itate.
Inherited from Latin fremitus.
Borrowed from Latin frequens or French fréquent.

parole.significato: to frequent, to go to (a place)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin frequentare or French fréquenter.
Borrowed from Latin frequentativus or French fréquentatif.
Borrowed from Latin frequentia or French fréquence.
Inherited from Latin fricatura.
Inherited from Latin frīgus (“cold”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sriHgos-, *sriges-, *sriHges-.
Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
Inherited from Late Latin frīgorōsus, from Latin frīgus. Compare French frileux.
Inherited from Latin frictus, from frīgō. Compare Italian fritto.
Borrowed from Latin fructus. Compare the inherited doublet frupt. Compare Aromanian fructu.
Inherited from Latin fōrmōsus (compare Italian formoso, Portuguese formoso, Spanish hermoso, Galician fermoso).
Inherited from Latin frontale or Vulgar Latin *frontārius.
Inherited from Latin frontem f (“forehead”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰron-t-, from *bʰren- (“project”).
Inherited from Late Latin frondia n pl, a collective noun derived from Classical Latin frondeus (“leafy”). Compare Aromanian frãndzã.

parole.significato: food products deriving from animal milk; dairy
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fructus. Doublet of fruct.
Inherited from Latin fimbriātus.

parole.significato: name given in the past to a person from a western European country of Latin origin, especially from France
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin francus (“Frank”). It may have been borrowed from Italian franco (“Frank”) or Greek Φράγκος (Frágkos, “Frank, Western European”), however the phonetical form indicates an older origin. Found in 17th century. Doublet of franc.
Inherited from Latin frangere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, metathesis of Late Latin fimbria (“fringe, border, edge”), from Latin fimbriae. Compare French frange.
From a Vulgar Latin root *frānctus, from Latin frāctus. Compare Aromanian frãmtu, Italian franto, Friulian frant.

Inherited from Latin frāctura through a Vulgar Latin root *franctura (cf. also Old French frainture, Old Italian frantura), or from frânt + -ură, past participle of frânge. Compare fractură, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Latin frēnum (“bridle”)
Probably from Latin fermentāre; less likely from a Vulgar Latin *fragmentāre, from Latin fragmentum. Compare Aromanian frimintu, frimintari. Compare fermenta, a borrowed doublet.

parole.significato: ash grove, forest of ash trees
parole.testo: From Early Medieval Latin fraxinētum. By surface analysis, frasin (“ash tree”) + -et. Compare Aromanian frãpsinet.

parole.significato: to banish, expel, drive away, chase off
parole.testo: From Latin fugāre.
Borrowed from Latin fugace.
Inherited from Latin fugāx, fugacem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Compare Italian fuggire, French fuir, Portuguese fugir.
Inherited from Latin fuga.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *fulger, from Latin fulgur (“lightning”), from Proto-Italic *folgos.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fulgerāre, from Latin fulgurāre.
Inherited from Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.

parole.significato: to smoke (a cigarette, a pipe, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fūmāre, also with conjugations from Vulgar Latin *fūmizāre.
From fum + -ar, or from Latin fumārium, from fūmus (“smoke”).

parole.significato: to smoke (give off smoke when burning)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fūmigāre.
Probably from a variant of fumuriu. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *fūmulus, from Latin fūmus.
Inherited from Latin fundus. Doublet of fond, which was borrowed from French.
Borrowed from Latin fungi.
From Latin fūniculus (“cord”), diminutive of fūnis (“cord”).
Inherited from Latin fūnis, fūnem.

parole.significato: gossamer (strand of cobweb floating in the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *fūnicellus, diminutive of Latin fūnis.

Inherited from Latin fūlīginem, accusative singular of fūlīgo, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-. The expected Romanian result would have been *furigine, but was probably modified through assimilation or a hypercorrection to rhotacism.
Inherited from Latin fūr, from Proto-Italic *fōr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr, from the root *bʰer- (“to carry”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūrāre, from Latin fūror.
From furcă + -ea, or possibly from Latin furcilla, diminutive of furca.
Inherited from Latin furca.
Borrowed from Latin furia (18th century).

parole.significato: to tingle, feel pins and needles
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin formīcāre.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Italian formicaio, Portuguese formigueiro, Spanish hormiguero, Catalan formiguer, Friulian furmiâr.

From a Vulgar Latin root *furuncellus, from Latin furunculus, possibly later influenced by the furnica in Romanian. Compare Aromanian furuntsel, furnitsel. Doublet of the neological borrowing furuncul.
Inherited from Latin formīca or furmīca, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-. Compare Aragonese fornica, Aromanian furnicã.
Inherited from Latin fūrtum.
Inherited from Latin fortūna, or less likely from Greek φουρτούνα (fourtoúna). Compare also Albanian furtunë and Aromanian furtunã.
Inherited from Latin fūsus.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fusticellus, diminutive of Latin fustis.

parole.significato: to fuck (to engage in sexual intercourse, crudely)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin futuere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”). Compare Aromanian fut.

parole.significato: lance, wooden spear with an iron tip
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fustis, fustem.
Inherited from Latin fēnum, from faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fenacium or *fenaceum, from Latin fenum, or a back-formation from fânețe, plural of fâneață. Cf. also French fenasse, Catalan and Occitan fenàs, fenassa.

Inherited from Late Latin fontāna, from a substantivation of the adjective Latin fontānus, from fons. Developed phonologically in Romanian via assimilation from an earlier form *funtână (Attested in early 1900s Fărșerot Aromanian funtãnã). Compare to the more typical Aromanian fãntãnã, and also Sard

parole.significato: bosom friend, bosom buddy, very close friend or comrade
parole.testo: Possibly from the past participle of a Latin verb fratrāre (which did not survive in Romanian; however compare Aromanian nfãrtedz, nfãrtari and fãrtat), ultimately from frāter.

parole.significato: a chest or crate for storing flour or meal
parole.testo: Derived from the regional / dated form fărinar, which is from Latin farīnārius or fărină + -ar. Compare Aromanian fãrinar, French farinier, Italian farinaio, Spanish harinero.
Derived from the regional / dated form fărinos, which is Inherited from Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna, corresponding to făină + -os. Compare Aromanian fãrinos.
Derived from the dated/regional form fărină, which is inherited from Latin farīna (“flour”). Compare Aromanian fãrinã.
Inherited from Latin factūra. Compare Aromanian fãpturã; compare also Albanian fytyrë. Doublet of factură.

parole.significato: to knock, break, smash, or dash to pieces/smithereens; to crumble
parole.testo: Aphetic form of variant sfărâma, verbal derivative of sfărâmă, older variant of fărâmă (“piece, crumb”). Other theories start from the variant form sfărâma, sfărma, deriving from a Vulgar Latin root *exformāre (compare Italian sformare). See also înfărma. Compare Aromanian sãrmu, Albanian thërrmoj.
Inherited from Latin forās. Compare Aromanian fãrã.

parole.significato: February (second month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin (mensis) Februārius. Doublet of februarie.

parole.significato: Greek (of or pertaining to Greeks, the Greek language or the Greek culture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).

Inherited from Latin grandinem, accusative singular of grandō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₃d-.
Inherited from Latin grossus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *gutturālium, from Latin gutturālia, plural of gutturālis, from guttur. The variant gutunar was probably influenced by Serbian.

From găină + -ar, possibly corresponding to Latin gallīnārius. Compare Aromanian gãljinar.

Inherited from Latin gallīna. Compare Aromanian gãljinã.

Borrowed from Latin catena.

Borrowed from Latin indicium or French indice. Doublet of index and indice.

Inherited from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂no- (“ring”).

Borrowed from Latin īnfīnītus or French infini. Equivalent to in- + finit.

Borrowed from Latin municipium.

Inherited from Latin montem, accusative of mōns, from Proto-Indo-European *men-. Compare Aromanian munti.
From munte + -os or from Latin montuōsus.
Inherited from Latin mōrus, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
Borrowed from Latin mūrus (19th century). Perhaps preserved as popular in its use as a rare regionalism from Maramureș and Ardeal.
From moare (“sauerkraut brine”), probably from Latin muries, muria.
Inherited from Latin morīrī, variant of morī. Compare Aromanian mor.
Borrowed from Latin murmur or French murmure.

parole.significato: to bite and break with the teeth, crush the bones of, munch, mangle
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin morsicāre.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin mulsa, with Greek influence for the sound shift, or tied to Serbo-Croatian mrs (day of sweets). Another less likely etymology is from Latin morsa (“bite”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin mora, from Latin morum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron). Compare Italian mora, French mûre, Catalan móra, Spanish mora.
Borrowed from Latin musculatus.
Borrowed from Latin musculosus. Cf. also mușchios, which may be an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus- (“a fly”).

parole.significato: unfermented wine; grape or other fruit juice
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mustum, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”).
From Early Medieval Latin mustācium (via its plural mustācia), ultimately from Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax). Compare Aromanian mustatsã.
Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre.
Inherited from Latin mūtus, of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Latin mūtāre.
Borrowed from Latin mutuus.
Borrowed from Latin musicus.
Borrowed from Latin musica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Borrowed from Latin musa or Italian musa or French muse or German Muse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūsclus, syncopated form of Latin mūsculus (“muscle”), from mūs (“mouse”). Compare Aromanian mushclju.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūsclus, syncopated form of *mūsculus, diminutive of Latin mūscus (“moss”). Compare Italian muschio, Venetan muscio, Friulian muscli, Aromanian mushclju.
From mușchi (“muscle”) + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin musculōsus, through a Vulgar Latin *musclōsus. Compare musculos, a borrowing. Compare Aromanian mushcljos.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin musaroneus, from musaraneus (“shrew”). Compare Aromanian mushuronjiu (“mole”), Italian musaragno (“shrew”), French mûrègne (“anthill”), Venetan musiga (“mole”).
Inherited from Latin māne, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”). Compare Aromanian mãni.

parole.significato: to drive, goad, put into action (e.g. an animal, vehicle, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī. Compare Aromanian min.

parole.significato: a groove, hollow, or depression in the sole of the foot
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mancus (“maimed, crippled, defective, imperfect”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manucāre, from Latin manducāre. Compare Italian manucare, variant of manducare, itself an obsolete variant of mangiare (this form being a borrowing from French).

parole.significato: to spend the night, take shelter (for the night), put up
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin manēre, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay, stand still”).

parole.significato: to wake up in the morning
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mānicāre.
Inherited from Latin manica.
From mână + -er or from Latin manuārius. Compare Aromanian mãnar. Cf. also amnar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manganeāre or *manganiāre, from Ancient Greek μαγγανεύω (manganeúō); see μάγγανον (mánganon, “charm”).

parole.significato: rage, great anger, wrath, ire, fury, craze, mania
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía). Doublet of manie.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mana, from Latin manus f. Compare Aromanian mãnã, Megleno-Romanian mǫnă, Istro-Romanian măre, Italian and Neapolitan mana. The rest of Romance retains the original Latin form (cf. Italian mano).
Inherited from Latin marcidus.
Inherited from Latin me (accusative singular of ego), from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)me.
Either from Latin macellum or from the verb măcelări.
Inherited from Latin macellārius. Compare Italian macellaio. By surface analysis, măcel + -ar.
Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Greek. Compare Aromanian matsin, mãtsinari, Italian macinare.
Inherited from Late Latin medullāris, from Latin medulla. Compare Aromanian mãdular.
From a dated form măduă, from Latin medulla.

Inherited from Latin magister, magistrum, possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *maistrum. Doublet of magistru, borrowed from Latin, maestru, borrowed from Italian, maistru, borrowed from German, and meșter, from Hungarian.
From mai + -or, alternatively, from Latin malleolus (“little mallet”).

Inherited from Late Latin manuc(u)lus, modified ultimately from Latin manipulus. The Romanian variant mănuchi, without the nasal infix, reflects the original form. Compare Aromanian mãnuclju, mãnunclju.
Inherited from Latin mēlum, variant of mālum. Compare Aromanian mer, Romansh mail, Friulian mêl, Italian mela.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mēlus, from Latin mālus. Compare Italian melo.

parole.significato: great, splendid, magnificent, grand, grandiose, stately, imposing
parole.testo: From mare + -eț or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *maricius, from Latin mas, marem.
Inherited from Latin margella.
From mare + inimos, a calque of Latin magnanimus.
Inherited from Latin marītus.
Inherited from Latin marītāre.
From the form mănunt, from Latin minūtus. Compare the neological borrowing minut.

parole.significato: entrails, viscera, bowels, pluck, guts, intestines
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin minūtalia n pl, from Latin minūtus.

Unknown; often considered to be from a Vulgar Latin *marracīna, *marrūcīna, [Term?] derived from Latin marra (“thorn”), but possibly also from an alteration of Latin malitia, with the influence of the Romanian suffix -ciune. Compare Spanish maleza. Compare also the related Albanian mërqinje, with th
Unknown. Possibly from Latin mala signa (“bad sign”) (however with an irregular phonetic evolution; compare semn); alternatively from male sanum (“unhealthy, in poor health”).
Inherited from Latin maxilla (“jaw”). Compare Aromanian mãseauã.
Inherited from Late Latin mēnsūrāre (“to measure”).
Inherited from Latin mēnsūra.

Unknown. Possibly linked to Latin messis (“harvest”), as August is a month of harvest. Several other regional Romance languages have folk names with similar meanings or origins for months around this time of year. The variant form măselar also coincides with a separate word referring to a certain pl
Inherited from Latin mataxa. Compare Aromanian mãtasi.
Inherited from Latin mātrīcem, accusative singular of mātrīx. Doublet of matrice and of matriță.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *metula, see which for more. Compare Albanian nétull.
From Vulgar Latin *mita, from Latin amita by aphaeresis, with -ușă (diminutive suffix) added later in Romanian.
From mazăre + Latin -cla (diminutive suffix).
Inherited from Latin nāvis, nāvem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare the borrowed doublet navă.
Inherited from Latin malva, of Semitic origin. Doublet of mov, which was borrowed from French.
Borrowed from Latin nanus.
Inherited from Latin nāpus.

parole.significato: to narrate, to tell (e.g. a story)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin narrare or Italian narrare or French narrer.
Borrowed from Latin narrator.
Inherited from Latin nāris. Compare Aromanian nari.
Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

Inherited from Latin nātus, from earlier gnātus, from Proto-Italic *gnātos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós (“begotten, produced”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth”). The meaning in Romanian developed from that of "offspring" or "progeny" in relation to the parent. Compare Ar
Borrowed from Latin nativus, French natif, German nativ. Doublet of naiv.
Borrowed from Latin nātūrālis, French naturel, Italian naturale. By surface analysis, natură + -al.
Borrowed from Latin nauticus or Italian nautico.
Borrowed from Latin nauticus or Italian nautico.

parole.significato: to give birth to; to bear
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin nascere. Compare Aromanian nascu.
Borrowed from Latin nationalista. By surface analysis, național + -ist.
Borrowed from Latin nātiōnem, likely via Italian nazione or French nation.
From Vulgar Latin nīs, from Latin nos. Compare nă (old form) and Aromanian nã.
Inherited from Latin nivem, accusative singular of nix (“snow”), from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs.
Borrowed from Latin nebulositas. By surface analysis, nebulos + -itate.
Unknown. Probably an expressive creation. See râncheza. An alternate etymology proposed is a Vulgar Latin *hinnutulāre (from Latin hinnus), later influenced by râncheza.
Borrowed from Latin necromania.
Borrowed from Latin necromantia. Equivalent to necro- + -manție.
Inherited from Latin naevus. Compare the similar sound shift in fagure.
Borrowed from Latin negāre (19th century).
Most likely from neg (“wart”) + -el (diminutive suffix). An alternate and less likely etymology proposed was Latin nigellus.

Inherited from Latin negōtium. An alternative theory includes the possibility of a borrowing from Italian negozio instead; the presence of the diphthongized plural form negoațe in the 16th century, however, seems to reinforce it as an inherited term.

parole.significato: quality or attribute of being the color black; blackness, darkness
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin nigritia, or from negru + -eață.
Inherited from Latin nigrum.

parole.significato: fog (cloud that forms at a low altitude and obscures vision)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin nebula, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Aromanian negurã.
From the earlier form neguțător, from Latin negōtiātor, or from the verb neguța + -tor. Doublet of negociator.
Inherited from Latin nepōs, nepōtem, possibly through Vulgar Latin *nepōta (“niece”, root). Compare Aromanian nipoatã, Venetan neoda, Catalan neboda and Occitan neboda.
Inherited from Latin nepōs, nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare Italian nipote, French neveu, Catalan nebot, Aromanian nipot.
Borrowed from Latin Nereides or French néréide.
Borrowed from Latin nervus or Italian nervo.
Borrowed from Latin nervosus or French nerveux or Italian nervoso. By surface analysis, nerv + -os.
Inherited from Latin aestimātus, with the prefix ne- added later within Romanian. Cf. French inestimable and Latin inaestimābilis.
Inherited from Latin nitidus. Cf. also net, which is an etymological doublet, taken from French.
Borrowed from Latin neutralis or Italian neutrale. By surface analysis, neutru + -al.
Borrowed from Latin neuter.
Borrowed from Latin naevus.
Borrowed from Latin nexus.
From ne- + ști, alternatively from Latin nesciō.
From ne- + știință or nești + -ință, alternatively from Latin nescientia.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *nescio quene, from Latin nesciō quem, accusative singular of quī.
Inherited from Latin neque. Compare Aromanian nitsi.
From nici (“not even”) + când (“when”), ultimately from Latin neque quando.

From nici + un. Probably from a Latin formation neque (“and not”) or nec unus (“not even one”). Compare Old French neisune, Italian nessuno and nissuno (Tuscan), Neapolitan nisciuno, Friulian nissun, Dalmatian nenčoin, Istriot ningun, Spanish ninguno, Portuguese nenhum, Catalan ningú.
Inherited from Latin nec aliubi or nec + alibi volet.
Borrowed from Latin Nigella.
Inherited from Latin nēmō, neminem. Compare Italian nimo, Sardinian nimus, Corsican nimo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nemīca, from ne- + mīca. Compare Old French ne ... mie, Old Venetan nemiga. Compare also Italian mica.
Inherited from Latin ningere (“to snow”), present infinitive of ningit, ningo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sneygʷʰ- (“to snow”).
From ninge, Latin ninxi, from ningit.
Inherited from Latin nesciō qualem, from quālis.
Inherited from Latin nesciōquid. Compare Aromanian nishti.
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Compare Aromanian noapti.
Inherited from Latin annōtinus.
Borrowed from Latin nobilissimus.
Borrowed from Latin nobilitare.
Borrowed from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to nobil + -itate.
Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).
From nod + -os or possibly from Latin nōdōsus.
Inherited from Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs. Compare Aromanian noi.
Latin nominativus
Borrowed from Latin nonae.

From older nuar, nuăr, from Latin nūbilum, noun use of the neuter of the adjective nūbilus (“cloudy”), from Latin nūbēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)newdʰ- (“to cover”). Compare Aromanian nior, Spanish nube, Italian nuvola, Friulian nûl, Portuguese nuvem, Catalan núvol, Provençal nyiuro,
From nor + -os, perhaps corresponding to Late Latin nūbilōsus, from Latin nūbilus.
Inherited from Latin noster, nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.
Borrowed from Latin notā bene.
Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos.
Inherited from Latin novitās, novitātem, equivalent to nou + -tate.
Inherited from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
Inherited from Latin nōbīs, dative plural of ego.
Borrowed from Latin novellae.
Borrowed from Latin noxa.
Inherited from Latin nōn. Compare Aromanian nu.
Inherited from Latin nux, nucis. In Romanian, the names of nuts or fruits are usually feminine while the names of the corresponding trees or bushes are masculine; compare păr, prun, alun, măr, etc.
Inherited from Latin nucetum, equivalent to nuc + -et. Compare Italian noceto, Spanish nocedal.

From nuc, or from Latin nux, nucem, probably with later adjustment to a standard feminine form ending in -ă. In Romanian, the names of nuts or fruits are usually feminine while the names of the corresponding trees or bushes are masculine.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin nudus.
Inherited from Latin novella.
Borrowed from Latin nuelificare or French nuelifier. By surface analysis, nul + -ifica.
Inherited from Latin nōmen, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥. The presence of the -u- may indicate some influence from număr.
Borrowed from Latin numerosus or Italian numeroso. By surface analysis, număr + -os.
Borrowed from Latin numerositas. By surface analysis, numeros + -itate.
From nume (“name”) + -i, from Latin nōmen.
Inherited from Latin numerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”).
Inherited from Latin numerāre.
Inherited from Latin nomināre. Doublet of nomina, a later borrowing which has itself gone out of use.
Borrowed from Latin numerabilis or Italian numerabile. Equivalent to număra + -bil.
Inherited from Late Latin nonnus.

Probably derived as a singular form from the plural, nunți, from an earlier hypothetical *nupți, from Latin nuptiae (“wedding”), from nupta (“bride”), from nūbere (“marry”). Compare Italian nozze, Aromanian numtã.
Inherited from Latin nūtrīcium, with the ending replaced by -ĭcium.
Borrowed from Latin nūtrīre, probably borrowed at a later point in time.
Inherited from Latin nūtrīcāre. Compare Aromanian nutric, nutricari.

parole.significato: small cattle or other horned livestock or beast
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin animālia, plural of animal. Compare Friulian nemâl, French aumaille, Spanish alimaña, Aromanian nãmaljiu. Doublet of animal.
From nară, with the suffix -tos instead of -os, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *nāritōsus, from Latin nāris. Cf. also nărtilă.

Past participle of naște. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *nāscūtus, from Latin nāscor. Compare Aromanian nãscut, Catalan and Occitan nascut, Dalmatian nascoit, Friulian nassût, Ladin nascù, Romansh naschiu.
Inherited from Latin nāsūtus.
From an earlier (possibly Proto-Romanian) root *eaua, from Latin illam, accusative feminine singular of ille.
Inherited from Latin ovem, accusative of ovis, from Proto-Italic *owis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis (“sheep”) or *h₃éwis. Compare Aromanian oai.
Inherited from Latin olla, from Proto-Italic *aukslā, from Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷsleh₂, Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷ- (“cooking pot”).
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”). Compare Aromanian oarfãn, Spanish huérfano. Largely replaced by the form orfan from Greek.
Inherited from Latin hōra, from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”). Doublet of oră, which was a borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ōvāria, from Latin ovum, or less likely *avula.

Inherited from Latin hospitem, accusative singular of hospes, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European noun *gʰóstipotis (whence also gospodin), a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. See also oaste. Compare Aromanian
Inherited from Latin hostem, accusative singular of hostis (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest, stranger”).
Borrowed from Latin obediens or Italian obbediente.
Borrowed from Latin obliquus or French oblique.
Borrowed from Latin obligātōrius and French obligatoire. By surface analysis, obliga + -toriu.

parole.significato: to cloud, to obscure (one's view or memory)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obnubilare or French obnubiler.
Borrowed from Latin observatorium, French observatoire, German Observatorium.
Borrowed from Latin obsidio.
Borrowed from Latin obstinātiō and French obstination. Equivalent to obstina + -ție.
From ochi (“eye”), based on Latin ocularis. Compare Italian occhiali.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus, from Proto-Italic *okelos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Compare Italian occhio. Doublet of oculus, borrowed through French.

parole.significato: in the old days, olden times, once, formerly
parole.testo: From o + dinioară, from Latin de una hōra.
Borrowed from Latin odiosus or Italian odioso or French odieux. By surface analysis, odiu + -os.
Borrowed from Latin odium.
Borrowed from Latin odoro.
Borrowed from Latin officinalis or French officinal. By surface analysis, oficină + -al.
Borrowed from Latin officina or French officine. Doublet of uzină.
Borrowed from Latin officiolatus.

parole.significato: unofficial, but which supports the point of view of a government, party, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin officiosus or French officieux.
Probably from Latin ovīna. Cf. also Aromanian uin.
Borrowed from Latin oleaster.
Borrowed from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”). Doublet of ulei.
Inherited from Latin homō (nominative). The plural reflects Latin hominēs.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin omentum.
Borrowed from Latin omittere.
Borrowed from Latin omnipotēns.
Borrowed from Latin onania.
Borrowed from Latin honestus and Italian onesto.
Borrowed from Latin honestas.
Inherited from Latin opus. Compare Italian uopo, Old Spanish uebos, Catalan ops. Doublet of opus, a borrowing, as well as the modern sense of op, below.
Borrowed from Latin opus in the 19th century.
Borrowed from Latin oppidum.
Borrowed from Latin opinio.
Borrowed from Latin opium.
Borrowed from Latin opoponax.
Borrowed from Latin oppositio, from French opposition.
Inherited from Latin octō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Borrowed from Latin optimas.
Borrowed from Latin opponere, with conjugation based on pune.
Borrowed from Latin opuntia or French opuntia.
Borrowed from Latin orator or French orateur.
Borrowed from Latin oratoria.
Borrowed from Latin oratorius.

Borrowed from Latin oratio, possibly through Polish intermediate oracja (first appears 18th century). Compare Aromanian urãciuni, which is probably inherited (see also the now rare Romanian urăciune, which may be from the same source or may also be an internal derivation from ura).
Inherited from Latin orbus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Compare Italian orbo. Doublet of rob.
Borrowed from Latin hordeolus.
Borrowed from Latin ordinariatus or French ordinariat.
Borrowed from Latin organicus or French organique. By surface analysis, organ + -ic.
Borrowed from Latin originalis or French original. By surface analysis, origine + -al.
Borrowed from Latin ōrnātus. Compare German Ornat.
Borrowed from Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodox + -ie
Borrowed from Latin orthographia. Equivalent to orto- + -grafie.
Inherited from Latin hordeum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”).
Borrowed from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”). Cognate to the inherited doublet oară.

Inherited from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan os, French os, Italian osso, Portuguese osso, Sardinian ossu, Spanish hueso.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ossāmen, derived from Latin os.
Borrowed from Latin hospitium, French hospice, Italian ospizio. Compare the inherited doublet ospăț.
Borrowed from Latin hospitalis or Italian ospitale.
Inherited from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes.
Inherited from Latin hospitium. Compare the borrowed doublet ospiciu.

parole.significato: raw pork fat, especially from the abdominal region; lard
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin axungia, possibly through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *oxungia or the attested variant auxungia.
Borrowed from Latin othomannus or French ottoman or Italian ottomano.
Inherited from Classical Latin ōvum, possibly via Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum.
Borrowed from Latin ovarium or French ovaire.
Borrowed from Latin ovatus.
Borrowed from Latin otiosus.
Inherited from Latin pācem, accusative of pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.
Borrowed from Latin patiēns, patientis, French patient, German Patient, Italian paciente.
Borrowed from Latin patientia.
Borrowed from Latin pacificus or French pacifique or Italian pacifico. By surface analysis, pace + -ific.
Borrowed from Latin pachyderma.

parole.significato: straw (a dried stalk of a cereal plant)
parole.testo: Back-formation from paie, from Latin palea, considered as a plural. Compare Aromanian palj, paljiu.
Borrowed from Latin palatum, Italian palato. Compare păraț, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin palaestra.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin pallium.
Borrowed from Latin pallium or French pallium.
Borrowed from Latin palmatus or Italian palmato or French palmé.

parole.significato: palm (the inner concave of the hand)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂. Compare Aromanian palmã.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plātinus, from Latin platanus (“plane tree”), itself from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos); same change of meaning in Albanian panjë (“sycamore maple”). See also Romanian platan, an etymological doublet stemming from the same Greek word.
Borrowed from Latin paludosus or Italian paludoso. Doublet of păduros.
Borrowed from Latin palūs (“swamp”), judging by the retention of /-l-/. Doublet of pădure (“forest”), which was inherited via a metathesized form.
Borrowed from Latin palla (“a lady's outer garment”).
From Latin pāla (“shovel”).
Borrowed from Latin panaricium.
Borrowed from Latin pancreas.
Borrowed from Latin pancreaticus or French pancréatique or Italian pancreatico.
Borrowed from Latin pandectes or Greek πανδέκτης (pandéktis) or French pandectes.
Borrowed from Latin panicula or French panicule.
From the older form peană, from Latin pinna, penna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).

parole.significato: an offering or dole made for the dead at a funeral (in the form of wine mixed with honey and water sprinkled on the bod…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pausum, from Latin pausō.
Borrowed from Latin papalitas. By surface analysis, papal + -itate.
Borrowed from Latin papilla.
Borrowed from Latin papyrus or French papyrus. Doublet of papură.
Borrowed from Latin papula.

parole.significato: rush, bulrush, club-rush, cattail, reed mace (Typha)
parole.testo: Inherited from a Vulgar Latin *papura, from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of papir and papirus. Compare Megleno-Romanian papră.
Borrowed from Latin pappus.
