Borrowed from Latin promontorium.
Borrowed from Latin promovere.
Borrowed from Latin promulgatio.
Borrowed from Latin pronuntiare or French prononcer.
Borrowed from Latin propagatio or French propagation. Equivalent to propaga + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin propositum.
Borrowed from Latin proprius.
Borrowed from Latin proponere, French proposer, with conjugation based on pune.
Borrowed from Latin propagatio.
Borrowed from Latin prorector or German Prorektor.
Borrowed from Latin proruptio.
Borrowed from Latin proscenium or French proscenium.
Borrowed from Latin proscriptio.
Borrowed from Latin prospicere.
Borrowed from Latin prostituta.
Borrowed from Latin prostratus.
Borrowed from Latin prostratio.
Borrowed from Latin prōtēctor or French protecteur.
Borrowed from Latin protestatio. By surface analysis, protesta + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin proverbium, French proverbe.
Borrowed from Latin providentia or French providence.
Borrowed from Latin provincialis. By surface analysis, provincie + -al.
Borrowed from Latin provincia or French province.
Borrowed from Latin provisorius.
Borrowed from Latin proximus.
Borrowed from Latin proximitas. By surface analysis, proxim + -itate.
Inherited from Latin prūnus, from Ancient Greek προύνη (proúnē).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pueruncus, from Latin puer (“child”) + diminutive suffix -unculus. In Balkan Latin, a popular, syncopated variant of the suffix -unculus was *-unclus, hence words like unchi, rărunchi, genunchi, etc. This *puerunclus was hypercorrected by analogy with Latin iuvencus ("ca
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neuter plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).
Inherited from Latin prandium, of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Italian pranzo, Aromanian prãndzu.

parole.significato: to lunch, lunch on, eat lunch, dine
parole.testo: Probably from Latin prandēre, with change in conjugation, or from prânz. Compare Italian pranzare, Calabrian pranziare, Logudorese Sardinian prandere, Vegliot/Dalmatian prandar, Aromanian prãndzu, prãndzescu.

parole.significato: to plunder, pillage, sack, rob, loot, ravage, ransack
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *praedāre, from Latin praedārī.
Inherited from Latin praedātiōnem, accusative singular of praedātiō. By surface analysis, prăda + -ăciune.
From prăda + -ător or from Latin praedātor.
Borrowed from Latin Pterosaurus.
Borrowed from Latin pubes or French pubère.
Borrowed from Latin publicare.
Borrowed from Latin publicanus.
Borrowed from Latin pudicus or French pudique.
Borrowed from Latin pudicitia.
Definite form of pulă, probably from Latin pulla, feminine of pullus (“offspring, child, cub, chick, etc.”)
Inherited from Latin pulverem, accusative of pulvis, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Doublet of pudră, taken from French.
Borrowed from Latin pulmō, pulmōnis. Doublet of the inherited plămân.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin pulpitum.
Inherited from Latin pulpa, from Old Latin *pelpa, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
Borrowed from Latin pulsāre.

Probably from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of Latin pullus (“offspring, child, cub, chick, etc.”). Compare Aromanian pulã, Catalan and Spanish polla, also Dalmatian pula. An alternate, and less likely, etymology derives it from a Vulgar Latin root *pūbula, from pūbes.
Inherited from Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, *puḱnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Borrowed from Latin punicus.
Borrowed from Latin pūnctum (18th century). Cf. also the doublet pont, which arrived through the intermediate of Hungarian.
Inherited from Latin pōnere, from Proto-Italic *posnō.
Borrowed from Latin punicus or French punique.
Borrowed from Latin punitio or French punition.

Inherited from Latin pontem m. Compare Aromanian punti. Based on the Aromanian and Megleno-Romanian cognates referring to all bridges in general, it is probable that older Romanian also did. This change may have come about due to centuries of Slavic administration preferring the Slavic derived term

From a Vulgar Latin *puppāre, from puppa (“breast, teat, nipple”), from Latin pūpa; or perhaps formed from a hypothetical, now lost noun *pupă in early Romanian, from this Latin word. Compare Italian poppare (“to suckle”), poppa (“boob, breast”), Catalan and Occitan popar (“to suckle”), popa (“boob,

parole.significato: pupa (stage of the life cycle of certain insects)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pupa, from specialized use of Latin pupa (“doll, puppet; girl”).
Borrowed from Latin pūrus, French pur.
Variant of por. Probably from Latin porrum.
Inherited from Late Latin porcella (“female piglet”), from porcellus (“piglet”), from Latin porcus (“pig”). Compare Aromanian purtseauã.

parole.significato: to proceed, begin, start, set out
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin prōcēdō, prōcēdere, possibly preserved as an inherited term only in Romanian. Compare also the doublet proceda, borrowed from French.
Inherited from Late Latin porcellus, diminutive of Latin porcus. Compare Aromanian purtsel.

parole.significato: act of leaving, going (e.g. on a journey)
parole.testo: From the past participle of purcede; possibly corresponds to Latin processus (and hence a doublet of the borrowing proces).
Borrowed from Late Latin pūrgātōrium (“cleansing”). Compare to Italian and Spanish purgatorio.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *pūlicāre, from Latin pūlex, pūlicem. Compare Aromanian puric, puricari, Logudorese puligare, Sardinian pulicare. Superficially, and semantically, resembles Vulgar Latin *pilūc(i)cāre and its reflexes.
Inherited from Latin pūlicem, singular accusative of pūlex, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plus-.
From purpură + -iu, from Latin purpura.
Learned borrowing from Latin purpura (19th century). See also the archaic porfiră, directly from Greek.
Inherited from Latin portāre (“to carry, bring”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”). Compare Neapolitan purtà.
Unknown. Probably from Latin porro + suffix -re. Other theories include per hora, *pororsus, from prorsus, or purus.
Borrowed from Latin pustulosus or French pustuleux.

parole.significato: to be able to; can, could, may
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse.
From putea (“be able to”) + -re; from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse (“can, be able to”).
Inherited from Latin potentia, equivalent to putea + -ință. Doublet of potență, a borrowing.

parole.significato: a foul odor or stench; stink
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin putor, putōrem. Equivalent to puți + -oare
Inherited from Latin putridus. Doublet of the borrowing putrid.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *putricālium, from Latin putridus, the same source as putred (“rotten”). Formed similarly to mucegai.

parole.significato: a blister, sore, or pustule in the mouth, particularly on the tongue
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *pustulella, diminutive from Latin pustula. The early loss of the second /u/, and then change of /tl/ to /kl/, are regular.

parole.significato: well (both for water and oil, gas, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin puteus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *paw- (“to strike”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *putīre, from Latin putēre.

Uncertain, as with a number of similar words across the Romance languages. Probably from Vulgar Latin *putīnus, a blend/alteration of Latin pisinnus, pittinnus and putillus, pusillus, all meaning “a teeny boy”. Compare Aromanian putsãn; further Albanian picërr, Italian piccino and piccolo, French pe
From pâine + -ar, or perhaps from Latin panārius.
Inherited from Latin pānis, pānem, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”). Compare Aromanian pãni.
Inherited from Latin pantex, panticem.
From pântece + -os or from Latin panticōsus, from pantex. Compare Aromanian pãnticos.

parole.significato: Optionally preceding și (“even”, adverb) for emphasis or clarification.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin paene ad (“almost to”). Compare Aromanian pãnã.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pergla, from Latin pergula, with the meaning of a stall outside of a hut or a support for vines changing to that of a small girder or beam.

parole.significato: fuzz, lint, fluff; flock (coarse tuft of wool)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pettia, from Late Latin pettia. Compare Albanian pjesë, French pièce, Spanish pieza, Catalan and Portuguese peça, Italian pezza, pezzo.
Inherited from Latin peccātum (“sin”). Compare Aromanian picat.
Inherited from Latin pecuīna, from pecuīnus, from pecus or less likely from Vulgar Latin *pecorina.
Inherited from Latin pecorārius. Compare Aromanian picurar.
Inherited from Latin pecus, having developed from the plural of the older variant păc, pecuri.
Inherited from Late Latin picula, from Latin pix. Compare Italian pegola, Dalmatian pecla, Provençal pegourë.

From the form păduchi, from Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus (it was already attested to be used in a form peduclus by Petronius), diminutive of pēdis (“louse”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-. Compare Aromanian piduclju, Megleno-Romanian piducľu, Istro-Romania

Inherited from Late Latin padūlem (“swamp”), from Latin palūdem via metathesis. Cognate with Albanian pyll (“forest”), which also shares the change in meaning. Compare also Italian padule. Doublet of paludă (“marsh”), an apparent borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Late Latin pāgānus. Compare Aromanian pãngãn. Doublet of pogan.
From păgân + -ătate, possibly from Latin pāgānitās, pāgānitātem. Compare Aromanian pãngãnãtate, pãngãnãtati.
Inherited from Latin post. Cognate with Spanish pues and Portuguese pois.

Possibly from Latin pānic(u)lus (cf. pānicula), or from a derivative of pānicum. Obsolete and found in an old Slavic-Romanian gloss. Its form was either altered by influence from pâine, or a result of an incorrect transcription. Cf. also Old French panil.
Inherited from Latin paliūrus, from Ancient Greek παλίουρος (palíouros).

Inherited from Latin pavīmentum (“floor composed of small stones beaten down”), possibly through attested Vulgar Latin paumentum. Compare Italian pavimento, Aromanian pimintu, Istro-Romanian pemint, Logudorese Sardinian pamentu (“floor”), pomentu, Friulian palment. Doublet of paviment.

parole.significato: a rough homespun woolen fabric (used to make coats, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin paenula, from Ancient Greek φαινόλη (phainólē).
Inherited from Latin paenitēre (“regret, be sorry”), with a change in verb class. Found in 16th century texts.
Inherited from Latin pappāre.
From a diminutive derivative of Latin pūpa (“doll, puppet; girl”) (cf. the Romanian suffix -ușă). Compare Aromanian pupushi.
Inherited from Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-.
Inherited from Latin pirus.

parole.significato: the palate, roof of the mouth
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin palātum (“palate”), probably confused with or influenced by palātium (“palace”) phonetically (or perhaps through a Vulgar Latin *palātium). Compare French palais (“palate”), in which the same evolution took place. Doublet of palat, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

From an unattested early Romanian singular form *păresimă, though a derivative is attested; părăsimă. From Vulgar Latin *quaresima, from Latin quadrāgēsima (“the fortieth part; Lent”), substantive of quadrāgēsimus (“fortieth”).
Inherited from Latin parentem, accusative form of parēns. Compare Aromanian pãrinti
From păr + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin pilōsus. Compare Italian peloso, Aromanian piros.
Inherited from Late Latin particella. By surface analysis, parte + -cea. Doublet of parcelă.
Inherited from Latin pānicum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palanga, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Compare Italian and Spanish palanca, French planche. Doublet of palancă and falangă.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum (“weight”).
Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh carefully”), frequentative of pendere.

parole.significato: to go, to leave, to walk, to pass
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun). See also the neologism pasa, a doublet borrowed from French.
From a lost verb *păsa + -re, ultimately from Latin pausāre. Most used in 16th century.

parole.significato: ground seeds or grains of millet or corn or the meal/porridge made from them
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pinsatum, from pinsāre. Another origin may possibly be quassatum.

Most likely from Vulgar Latin *pistālia, from Latin pistāre, from pinsō (“stamp, pound, crush”); also hypothesized to be (due to the -aie ending) from various other possible Latin sources, including *quassitālia, from quassāre, or *pyxitālia, from pyxis. Compare Albanian bishtajë and Aromanian pãsta
Inherited from Latin pāstor, pastōrem. Doublet of pastor.

parole.significato: deposit of pollen from flowers by bees on honeycombs, used as food
parole.testo: Probably from Latin pastūra, from pastus. Other theories include Vulgar Latin *pestula, diminutive of pestis. Compare Aromanian pãsturã.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *pictāre, a verb based on Classical Latin pictus (“painted”). For the semantics, cf. Spanish pinta (“stain”) < pintar (“paint”, verb). The normal outcome of /kt/ is /pt/ in Romanian, but the loss of /p/ in this case can be explained as the result of dissimilation from the
Inherited from Latin plantāginem, accusative singular of plantāgō, undergoing metathesis in standard Romanian (cf. also the original, now regional variant above).
Formed from patru (“four”), based on Latin quadrātus, Italian quadrato, German Quadrat, etc. Doublet of cvadrat.
Inherited from Latin pertundere, with metathesis.
Ultimately from Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon, “parsley”), from πέτρος (pétros, “rock, stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patubulum, from Latin patibulum (“crossbeam”).
Either from Vulgar Latin *pittula, diminutive of *pitta, or from paturi, the plural of pat ("bed").
Inherited from Latin pāvōnem.
Borrowed from Latin pausare.
Inherited from Latin pastiō, pastiōnem, from pastus. Compare Aromanian pãshuni, Friulian passon, French paisson.

parole.significato: to have something, chiefly negative or sometimes neutral, happen to oneself
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī.
Borrowed from Latin quidditas or French quiddite.
Borrowed from Latin rabies, Italian rabbia.

parole.significato: to shave (someone or something, respectively oneself)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin rādere.
Borrowed from Latin radix.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin ragĕre. Compare French raire, réer; cf. also French railler, Italian ragliare.
Inherited from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
Borrowed from Latin ramificare or French ramifier. Equivalent to ram + -ifica.
Either a diminutive of ram formed from the plural ramuri or from Latin rāmula, from rāmulus, diminutive of rāmus. Compare also Old Italian ramora.
Inherited from Latin rārus (“seldom”).
Borrowed from Latin rāritās, rāritātem. Equivalent to rar + -itate.
Inherited from Latin rāsus.
Borrowed from Latin ratificare or Italian ratificare or French ratifier.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *radia, from Latin radius. Doublet of radius. Compare Spanish raza.
Borrowed Latin ratio, French ration. Doublet of rațiune.
Borrowed from Latin ratiocinium.
Borrowed from Latin rationabilis. Equivalent to raționa + -bil.
Borrowed from Latin rationabilis and French rationaliser. By surface analysis, raționaliza + -bil.
Borrowed from Latin ratiō, ratiōnem (19th century). Doublet of rație.
Borrowed from Latin re-. The form ră- only appears in a few inherited words.
Borrowed from Latin reagens.
Inherited from Latin recēns, possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *reces. Doublet of recent, which was borrowed.
Learned borrowing from Latin recipere.
Borrowed from Latin recrementum.
Borrowed from Latin rectangulum.
Borrowed from Latin recte.
Borrowed from Latin rectitūdō, French rectitude.
Borrowed from Latin rēctor or German Rektor or French recteur.
Borrowed from Latin recursus or German Rekurs or French recours.
Borrowed from Latin requiem.
Borrowed from Latin requisitor.
Borrowed from Latin redhibitio.
Borrowed from Latin reducere, French réduire, based on duce. Compare the inherited doublet arăduce.
Borrowed from Latin reduplicare.

Unknown. Proposed etymologies include Latin refricāre (compare Portuguese refegar, refregar), a Vulgar Latin *orificāre, from ōrificium, or a root *reficcāre, from ficcāre (compare Italian ficcare). Less likely of Slavic origin. Cf. also Aromanian arufec, aruficari, with the same meaning.
Borrowed from Latin referendarius or French référendaire.
Borrowed from Latin referendum, French référendum.
Borrowed from Latin reformatio or German Reformation or French réformation. Equivalent to reforma + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin rēgālis. By surface analysis, rege + -al.
Borrowed from Latin regalitas. Equivalent to regal + -itate.
From rege (“king”) + -at, from Latin rēx.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin rēgem, accusative of rēx (19th century). Doublet of rigă.
Borrowed from Latin regifugium.
Borrowed from Latin rēgīna.
Borrowed from Latin regius.
Borrowed from Latin regressus.
Borrowed from Latin rēgulāris. By surface analysis, regulă + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin regulatio or German Regulation. Equivalent to regula + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin rēgula. Doublet of riglă.
Borrowed from Latin reiectare.
Borrowed from Latin renegare.
Borrowed from Latin repatriare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *repausum, from Latin repausō. Compare Aromanian arãpas, Italian riposo, French repos, Catalan repòs, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso.

Inherited from Latin rapidus and Latin rapidē. The -e declension derives from the adverb, the two having been conflated at some point. The rarely used western Transylvanian variant rapăd preserves the adjectival declension. Thus there must have been two distinct forms for the adjective and adverb or
Borrowed from Latin repens.
Borrowed from Latin repositio.
Borrowed from Latin repressor.
Borrowed from Latin reprobare.
Borrowed from Latin reprobabilis.
Borrowed from Latin repudium.
Borrowed from Latin rescissorius.
Borrowed from Latin respiciens.
Borrowed from Latin respirium.
Borrowed from Latin restitutorius.
Borrowed from Latin rhetoricus.
Borrowed from Latin rhetorica or Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ) or French rhétorique.
Borrowed from Latin rheumaticus or Italian reumatico or German rheumatisch. Equivalent to reumă + -atic.
Borrowed from Latin reumaticus or German rheumatisch.
Borrowed from Latin reverenda.
Borrowed from Latin revocatio. By surface analysis, revoca + -ție.

parole.significato: to pour out/forth, overflow, gush out, spout, flood
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Late Latin reversāre, from Latin versō, and modeled after vărsa.
Borrowed from Latin residuum.
Borrowed from Latin resolutus or German resolut.
Borrowed from Latin resolutorius or French résolutoire.
Borrowed from Latin resolvere.
From a Vulgar Latin root *retella, a diminutive of Latin rēte, retis. Compare Abruzzo Italian dialect ritedda, compare also French réseau.
Borrowed from Latin ricinus or German Rizinus.

parole.significato: to lift, elevate, raise, hoist, suspend
parole.testo: Probably from Latin ērādīcāre (“root out, eradicate”) (and thus a doublet of the borrowing eradica). Another possibility is Late Latin or Vulgar Latin ridicāre (“tie a vine, e.g. in a vineyard”) (attested from a late gloss), from ridica (“stake; prop; vine-prop”); cf. also Spanish rodrigón. The sema
Inherited from Latin rādīcula (“little root”) (with early loss of /u/), diminutive of rādīx (“root”). Compare Albanian radhiqe.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *reniclus, from Latin rēniculus (“little kidney”), from rēnēs (“kidneys”), from ren. Compare Aromanian arniclju, Sardinian arrigu.
Inherited from Latin rōdere, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”).
Inherited from Latin rota, from Proto-Indo-European *Hret- (“to roll”).
Inherited from Latin rubeus. Compare the doublet ruj, borrowed from French.
Inherited from Latin rubia.
Borrowed from Latin rōmānus. Doublet of român (“Romanian”), rumân, and aromân (“Aromanian”), which was inherited. By surface analysis, Roma + -an.

Inherited from Latin Rōmānus. The variant rumân also meant peasant, or a serf who worked the land (in feudal medieval Wallachia). In popular speech, it also had the meaning of a husband or man in general, but this is now archaic. Doublet of aromân and roman, a later borrowing.
Inherited from Latin rōsus.
Inherited from Latin rōstrum. Compare Aromanian arostu. Compare also related meanings in Albanian rast.
Per most sources, borrowed from Latin rotundus, but alternatively may represent a crossing of older Romanian rătund (inherited from the Late Latin variant retundus) with words like roată (“wheel”).

parole.significato: to dew, moisten, to form, cover in, or let fall dew
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin rōrāre.

Inherited from Latin rōs, rōrem, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *rovem through analogy with other words like bos, whence bovem. Another theory suggests an initial early Romanian form *roor, resulting in a plural *rouri which was reformed into a singular analogically. Compare also the change of
Borrowed from Latin rosa, Italian rosa, French rose, German Rose.
Inherited from Latin russus, or less likely from Latin roseus. Compare Aromanian arosh, Italian rosso.
Borrowed from Latin rubia.
From Latin rogus, probably borrowed in the 19th century or semi-learned. The linguists Candrea and Tiktin believed it to be inherited.

Inherited from Latin rubus (“bramble, briar”), from Proto-Italic *wruðos, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo- (“sweetbriar”). Compare Italian rovo, dialectal rogo. For the sound shift of Latin -b- to -g- in Romanian, compare neg, negură.

parole.significato: to ask politely, to say please
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin rogāre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-, ablaut of *h₃reǵ-.
Inherited from Latin rugīre. Compare Aromanian arujescu, arujiri (“neigh”).
From rugină + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin aerūginōsus or alternatively rūbīginōsus.
Inherited from Latin rogātiōnem, accusative singular of rogātiō. By surface analysis, ruga + -ăciune.
Reconstructed from the plural of rugământ, from the verb a ruga + suffix -ământ, -mânt, possibly from Latin rogāmentum.
Inherited from Latin rūmigāre.

Inherited from Latin rōmānus. Variant of român. As this now obsolete form of the word was mostly used before the language's orthographic reform and shifting of script to the current Latin-based one, it would have been represented mostly with the old Romanian Cyrillic alphabet. The sense of "serf" or

parole.significato: a deforested area used for pasture or cultivation
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *runcus, from Latin runcō. Compare Latin runcātio and Italian ronchio.
Inherited from Latin rumpō, rumpere (“to break”).
Inherited from Latin ruptus. Compare Aromanian aruptu.
Either from rupt + -ură or directly from Latin ruptūra. Compare Italian rottura, French roture, Spanish rotura.
Probably a 17th-century learned borrowing from Latin rūta; ultimately from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).

Unknown. Compare Latin roseus. Probably from the verb rușina, itself from roși (“turn red, blush”), from roșu. Other explanations derive it from a Vulgar Latin root *rōsīnus (“rosy”), *russiō or *rōsiō. May possibly be also from a Romanian *rușiciune, from roși. Compare Aromanian arushini, arusheni,
Inherited from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. Compare Aromanian arãd.
Inherited from Latin rimāre.
Inherited from Latin rancidus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rhonchizāre (“to snore”) (compare Old Italian roncheggiare, Istriot ronchizea), from Latin rhoncō, rhonchāre (compare Spanish roncar), denominative of rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hirundinella, diminutive of classical Latin hirundō, hirundine. Compare also French hirondelle.
From rândunea + -ică, from Vulgar Latin *hirundinella, diminutive of classical Latin hirundo.

parole.significato: each of the two sides of the body
parole.testo: Probably from Latin rēn, rēnem (“kidney”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin word *rēna).
Inherited from Latin rīpa, from Proto-Italic *reipā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁réyp-eh₂ (“steep slope”), from *h₁reyp- (“to tear, tear down”).
Inherited from Latin rīsus. The plural was formed from that of the word râset, itself having the same meaning and deriving from râs + -et.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rius (river), from Latin rīvus (“brook, small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós.

Probably from an earlier form *arăbda(re), from a Vulgar Latin *ēlib(ī)dāre (“to force oneself not to desire”), from Latin ē in privative sense + libīdō, with a later apheresis of the initial a-. Compare Aromanian aravdu, arãvdari. Another theory is that it derives from a Vulgar Latin root *reemendā
Inherited from Late Latin rādīcīna, from Latin rādīx, rādīcis (“root”), from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from *wréh₂ds. Cognate with Aromanian (a)rãdãtsinã, French racine, Sardinian radichina.

Unknown. Probably linked to repede or Vulgar Latin *rapicāre. Also possibly from Vulgar Latin *repicāre (a root), from Latin rēpēns or *repigāre, from Latin rēpō.

parole.significato: to get lost, become lost, lose oneself.

From rășină + -os or from Latin resīnōsus.
Inherited from Latin resīna, from Ancient Greek ῥητῑ́νη (rhētī́nē). Compare Albanian rrëshirë.

parole.significato: his/hers (that which is his or hers)

Inherited from Latin suīnus.

Borrowed from Latin sardius.
Borrowed from Latin sardonyx.

parole.significato: fluffy woolen mantle worn by peasants, especially shepherds in mountain regions
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *sarica, from Latin sērica.
Borrowed from Latin sarissa.

parole.significato: the sensation of being full/satisfied/sated; satiety
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *satium, from Latin satis.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre, from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiāre from the older form scâmba. Compare Albanian shkëmbej, Italian scambiare.

parole.significato: to burn; to heat sour milk to make cheese
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin excoquere, from ex + coquō. Compare Spanish escocer.
Inherited from Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría). Doublet of the borrowing scorie, as well as the more common zgură, taken from Greek.
Inherited from Latin scortea, feminine noun form of scorteus (“made of skin or leather”).

parole.significato: to remove, take out, subtract, bring out, pull out, throw out
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excotere, from Latin excutere.

parole.significato: a hollow (sunken area in something solid, such as in the trunk of a tree)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin scrobis through a Vulgar Latin form *scorbis after metathesis. The final result in Romanian may be explained through a root *scorbula or through a lost Romanian word *scorb and its plural scorburi. Compare Aromanian scrob, cf. Italian scroba.

parole.significato: to strain or exert oneself, to push (used especially in the context of the effort of defecation or occasionally of givi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expremere, from Latin exprimere, possibly influenced by excrementum phonetically. Compare Aromanian mi-sprem, sprimeari, mi-spreamit. Doublet of exprima, borrowed through French.
Inherited from Latin scrībere, from Proto-Italic *skreiβō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ-.

parole.significato: script (of a film, play, show, etc.)
parole.testo: Initially inherited from Latin scriptum as the past participle of scrie, which was later replaced by scris. The current meaning is borrowed from English script.

Inherited from Late Latin excurare, from cūrāre (“to look after”). Compare Catalan escurar, Old French escurer.

parole.significato: to rise, come, spring, appear, flow
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin excurrere.

parole.significato: to scratch, scrape, poke, disturb the earth or ground, in order to take something out or dig a hole (often of animals)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *excorrimare. Another possibility (perhaps more likely) is a relation to scrum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excurtus, from Latin curtus (“short”); the initial s- may also have been added later in Romanian, or appeared as a result of the influence of scurta, from excurtare. Compare also Aromanian shcurtu. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Inherited from Late Latin excurtāre, from Latin curtāre.

parole.significato: hard modified leaflet that protects the buds, receptacle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin squāma (“scale”). Compare scamă, an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Latin scandula (“roof tile”). Doublet of șindră.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scantilia, from Latin scintilla.

parole.significato: to decrease, diminish, shrink, mitigate, reduce
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *excadēre (“fall out”), from Latin ex- + cadere. Compare Aromanian scad, scãdeari.
Inherited from Late Latin excaldāre, from Latin cal(i)dus (“hot”). Compare Aromanian ascaldu.
From scamă + -os or from Latin squāmōsus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”). Compare Aromanian scap, scãpari.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excarmināre, from Latin ex- + carminō (“to card”), from carmen (“card for wool, flax”). Compare Aromanian scarmin, scãrminari, Calabrese scarminare, Spanish escarmenar, Italian scarmigliare.

parole.significato: to scratch (to rub a surface with a sharp object)

From scaun + -el, or possibly from the older form scăuel (cf. also scăuieș), perhaps from Latin scabellum. Cf. also Venetan scanèl.
From Latin sē.

parole.significato: one who is the same as another

parole.significato: a small and mischievous mythical creature roughly synonymous with a kind of elf, imp, goblin, fairy, pixy, or gremlin
