parole.testo: Inherited from Latin trāma, probably through the intermediate of a Vulgar Latin verb *extrāmāre, and perhaps a lost early Romanian verb *străma (compare Aromanian strãmedz, strãmari, Sardinian istramare). Cf. also destrăma and tramă.
Borrowed from Latin strangulare.
Inherited from Latin strātum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oestricula, derived from Latin oestrus. Compare Aromanian streclji.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *extracōlāre or *transcōlāre, from Latin cōlāre (“filter, strain, purify”). Compare Aromanian stricor, stricurari. Less likely from s- + trece (“pass”), and with influence from verbs like spânzura, vântura, etc.

parole.significato: to have the unpleasant feeling on the teeth and mouth when eating something sour
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extorpidire, from torpidus (“benumbed”).
Inherited from Latin extricāre.
Borrowed from Latin stridor or French stridor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *strigāre (“scream like a screech owl”) from Latin strix (“screech owl”). Compare Megleno-Romanian strig, strigari.

parole.significato: In Romanian folklore, a spirit that can transform into an animal or some ghostly appearance and cause problems for thos…
parole.testo: From strigă + -oi, from Latin striga (“hag, evil spirit”), from strix (“screech owl”). Compare Italian strega (“witch”).

parole.significato: barn owl (An owl of the genus Tyto)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin strīga, from strix, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx).
Borrowed from Latin structūra, French structure.
Inherited from Latin struppus, stroppus, from Ancient Greek στρόφος (stróphos, “rope”), from στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist”).
From Latin struthio, probably through the Italian intermediate struzzo. The Megleno-Romanian equivalent, ştruş, may be inherited directly.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin strabus, from Ancient Greek στρᾰβός (străbós), akin to Aromanian strãmbu, Albanian shtrembër, Italian strambo, Friulian stramp, Spanish zambo.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strinctus, from Latin strictus. Compare Aromanian strimtu. A similar nasal infix occurred in old Italian and Neapolitan strinto, Friulian strent, Venetan strento, Logudorese Sardinian istrintu, French étreint. Doublet of strict, ultimately borrowed from the same source.

parole.significato: a narrow pass or strait, tight or narrow passage, enclosed area
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *strinctura, from Late Latin strictura, from Latin strictus. Doublet of the borrowing strictură.
Inherited from Latin stringere (“tighten”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.

parole.significato: Shows intensification of verb, superiority, age or remoteness of noun or adjective; also used to show passage or penetr…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin extra, though numerous instances of the prefix seem to derive from Latin trāns- (inherited in Romanian as tră-), the distinct meanings probably having become confused at some point.

parole.significato: to pass through go through or over, penetrate, traverse
parole.testo: From stră- + bate, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *extrabattere, from Latin battuere. Compare Aromanian strãbat, strãbatiri.

Inherited from Latin extrāneus, through a Vulgar Latin intermediate form; the expected normal phonetic result in Romanian from the base Latin word would be *strâi, so it must have come from a derivative form. It is likely that Latin extraneus produced several popular altered variant or derived forms

parole.significato: to shine, to sparkle, to radiate, to glister, to beam, to flare; to be bright
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrālūcīre, from Latin lūcēre. By surface analysis, stră- + luci.
From stră + Latin mater.

parole.significato: a goad (long pointed stick used to prod animals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *stimulāria, from Latin stimulus (the archaic variant form strămur may derive directly from stimulus). Compare Aromanian strimburari, Megleno-Romanian strămulari.

parole.significato: to shift, change places, dislodge, displace, move
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin root *extrāmūtāre, instead of Latin trānsmūtāre. Equivalent to stră- + muta. Compare Aromanian strãmut, strãmutari, Friulian stramudâ, Sardinian stramudai.
From stră- + nepot or less likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrānepōs, extrānepōtem. Compare also Albanian shtërnip.
Inherited from Latin sternūtāre, frequentative of sternuō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrāpungere, change of prefix from *trānspungere, from Latin pungere. Compare Aromanian strãpungu, strãpundziri, cf. also Friulian strapongi, Venetan straponzer.
Borrowed from Latin studium. Doublet of studio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *stypus or *stupus, from Ancient Greek στύπος (stúpos, “stem, stump, block”).
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *stupire, formed from a crossing of Vulgar Latin *scupire (compare Romanian scuipa) and Latin spūtō.

parole.significato: tow (untwisted bundle of fibers such as hemp or flax)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē).
Uncertain. Possibly from Latin stylus, stilus.

parole.significato: thrush (any of several species of songbirds of the family Turdidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin turdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. The initial s- may be due to influence by Latin sturnus, and the final -z may be due to the word being reformed from the plural *turzi, or less likely through a Vulgar Latin root *turdeus. Compare Aromanian sturdzu, strudz.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stirparia, from stirps.

From a Vulgar Latin root *stancus, from a contraction of Vulgar Latin *stānticus (“tired”), from Latin stāns, stantis. Compare Aromanian stãngu, also Old Italian mano stanca (“left hand”); cf. also the etymology of Italian manco (“left; originally 'maimed', 'faulty' 'imperfect'”).

parole.significato: a winter stable for sheep or other animals
parole.testo: Probably from staul n + -ină f; another proposed etymology was a Vulgar Latin *stabulīna f, from Latin stabulum n.
Inherited from Latin subtus, from sub. Compare Aromanian sum.
See sub, from Latin sub.
Borrowed from Latin subiectum.
Borrowed from Latin subligaculum.
Borrowed from Latin submersus.
Borrowed from Latin subordinatio or French subordination. Equivalent to subordina + -ție.
From sub- + braț, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *subbracchium, from Latin sub- + bracchium; compare Galician sobrazo.
Borrowed from Latin subscriptio.
Borrowed from Latin substituere.
Borrowed from Latin substractio or German Subtraktion or French substraction.
From sub- + *suoară, from Late Latin subāla, from Latin sub (“under”) + ala (“wing; armpit”); the preceding sub was added later in (early) Romanian. Compare Aromanian sumsoarã, soarã.
Borrowed from Latin subtribus.
Borrowed from Latin suburbanus.
Borrowed from Latin suburbium.

parole.significato: to thin, become/get thinner, make thin
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin subtīliāre, from Latin subtīlis.
Inherited from Latin subtīlis, subtīlem. Doublet of subtil.
Borrowed from Latin sūcus through French suc. See also usuc, which may be an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Latin sūdōrem. Equivalent to asuda + -oare (the "a" prefix is a later innovation).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.
Borrowed from Latin sufficiēns.
Inherited from Latin sufflāre.

From a Vulgar Latin root *sufflitum, from Latin sufflō, from flō (“to breathe”). Compare Aromanian suflit, derived from the same Vulgar Latin root. Compare also the Latin word animus, anima ("soul, also breath") deriving from the Proto-Indo-European root for "to breathe", as well as Latin spiritus (
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *subfronticella, from Latin sub + frontis + diminutive suffix -ella, possibly with influence from cilia. Compare Aromanian sufrãmtseauã, sufrãndzeauã.
Inherited from Latin sūgere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūgillum, from Latin sigillum (“seal”) crossed with sūgillāre (“to bruise”). Compare Italian suggello. See also the borrowed doublet sigiliu.

From an earlier hypothetical form *sughiuța, from Vulgar Latin *suggluttiāre, probably from an alteration of Latin singultō, singultāre, from singultus, with the prefix sub-. The (Vulgar) Latin was probably influenced by gluttiō, gluttīre (cf. înghiți). Compare Aromanian sugljits, sugljitsari, Sicil
Inherited from Latin subīre (“approach”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sublum, from *sūbulum, from Late Latin insūbulum, from Latin insuō + -bulum, or related to sūbula. Compare Italian subbio.

parole.significato: furrow of earth (alternating with a ditch or pit)
parole.testo: Probably from Latin sulcus, corresponding to Proto-Indo-European *solk-o- (“furrow”), *selk- (“to pull, drag”).
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *sublicidus, from Latin sublica.
From a Vulgar Latin root *sulfīna, from Latin sulphur, sulfur.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subla, from Latin sūbula, from Proto-Indo-European *syuh₁-dʰleh₂, which consists of the root *syewH- (“sew”) and the suffix *-dʰlom (“tool suffix”).
Borrowed from Latin summarius or French sommaire.

parole.significato: to roll up (one's sleeves, hem, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin summittere.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin summum.

From Latin summa. The word was probably originally inherited and popular, as evidenced by its appearance (also in an older form somă) among the earliest Romanian texts from the 16th century, and the popular nature of some of its derivatives and related terms. However, the modern version of the term
Probably from Latin sonus, or from the verb suna.

parole.significato: to ring or produce a sound in general
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). First attested in 1581.
Inherited from Latin sonitus.

Related to sănătate. Possibly from Vulgar Latin (herba) sanatōria, from Late Latin sanatōrius, from Latin sanō. This form came to be influenced by the verb suna (cf. sunător) in Romanian, altered through popular etymology deriving it from that verb.
Borrowed from Latin superbia.
Borrowed from Latin superfluus or French superflu.
Borrowed from Latin supinum or French supin.
Borrowed from Latin supplicium or French supplice.
Borrowed from Latin superficialis or French superficiel.
From Latin superponere. By surface analysis, supra- + pune.
Inherited from Latin suctus.

parole.significato: to subject to, subdue, subjugate, force, oblige, coerce
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin suppōnere.

Inherited from Latin superāre (“surpass, exceed; overflow”). The meaning in the Romanian arose from the idea of exceeding or going beyond what can be taken or tolerated. Compare Aromanian shupãr, shupãrari, meaning "to ridicule, make fun of". Compare also the semantic development of French outrer (“

parole.significato: (of women, often in the countryside) good friend; a friendly and familiar term used to address a fellow woman
parole.testo: Probably formed from soră as fârtat was from frate, analogically. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *sororiāta, from a verb sororiāre.
From a gender shift of surcel, from Vulgar Latin surcellus, variant of Latin surculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin surcellus, variant of Latin surculus.
Inherited from Latin surdus, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”). Compare Aromanian surdu.
suroră + -itate, correspond to Latin sororitas.

From a Vulgar Latin root *subrūpāre, from Latin rupes (“cliff”). Compare Aromanian surpu, surpari, old Abruzzese dialect surrupare, Sicilian sdirupari. Compare also Italian dirupare, Galician and Portuguese derrubar, Spanish derribar.
From sub + râs, based on French sourire (cf. also Italian sorriso) or Latin subrisus.
Inherited from Latin sūsum.
Borrowed from Latin suscitare.
Borrowed from Latin suspectio.
Borrowed from Latin suspiciosus.
From suspina, or from Latin suspirium; compare Aromanian suschir, Italian sospiro, Spanish and Portuguese suspiro, Occitan and Catalan sospir, French soupir.
Inherited from Latin suspīrāre.

Borrowed from Latin susurrō through French susurrer. The presence of shushuredz, shushurari in Aromanian prompted some to attribute it directly to Latin, though this is improbable, and the Aromanian is probably an onomatopoetic expression.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *suta, see which for more.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sambata, from Vulgar Latin *sambatum, from Latin sabbatum. The Latin is derived from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), ultimately from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath, Shabbat”). Compare French samedi (“Saturday”), itself also from *sambatī diēs. Compare als
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *summicēlla, from Latin summa.
Inherited from Latin sinus. Compare Aromanian sin, French sein, Italian seno, Romansh sain, Spanish seno.

parole.significato: to wake up in the morning
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *sānicāre, from Latin sānus. Less likely from a root *signicāre (“make the sign of the cross”), referring to one’s morning prayers. Preserved only in popular spells.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, accusative of sanguis. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare Catalan sang, French sang, Italian and Portuguese sangue, Spanish sangre, Aromanian sãndzi, sãndze.

parole.significato: Common dogwood (Cornus sanguinea), a tall bush with reddish branches
parole.testo: Either a back formation of sângera or from Latin sanguineus. Compare Portuguese sanguinho, Spanish sangüeño, Catalan sanguinyol, Italian sanguinella, and Friulian sanzit, all meaning "dogwood."
Inherited from Latin sanguināre.
From sânge + -os. From Late Latin sanguinōsus, from Latin sanguis. Compare Aromanian sãndzinos.
Inherited from Latin sānctus. Mostly replaced by the more common sfânt, but preserved in popular saint names.

parole.significato: several plants of the genus Galium (Galium verum, Galium mollugo, Galium rotundifolium)
parole.testo: Unknown. Probably from Latin Sancta Diana or *sanctae Dianae, indicating a pre-Christian deity. (compare Calabrian curse expression santu Diana). Other theories include Sanctus dies Iohannes or a confusion with it. Also, compare the related cosânzeană and zână.
Inherited from Latin sī (“if”). The semantic function might have been influence from Paleo-Balkan; compare Albanian të.
Inherited from Latin secrētus. Compare the change of meaning also in Albanian shkretë, whence Aromanian shcret. Cf. also the neologism secret.

parole.significato: purse or pouch worn around the neck
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *sacculeus, from Latin sacculus. Compare Aromanian sãculj.
Inherited from Latin sagitta (“arrow”).

parole.significato: to shoot or hit with an arrow
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sagittāre.
From săgeată + -ar, possibly corresponding to Latin sagittārius (thus possibly a doublet of the borrowed sagitar).
Inherited from Latin silvāticus, from silva (“forest”). Compare Italian selvatico, French sauvage.
Inherited from Latin salicētum. Equivalent to salcie + -et.
Inherited from Latin saltāre.

Inherited from Late Latin sementia, plural of sementium, neuter form derived from Latin sēmentis, itself derived from sēmen (“seed”). Among certain rural areas the singular is used for both single and plural. Compare Aromanian simintsã, Italian semenza, French semence, Portuguese semente, Spanish se
Inherited from Latin sānitās, sānitātem. Compare Aromanian sãnãtati.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sānitōsus, from Latin sānitās + -ōsus. Compare Aromanian sãnãtos, cf. also Albanian shëndoshë.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sappāre, from Latin sappa. Compare Aromanian sap, sãpari, French saper, Italian zappare, Sicilian zappari, Spanish zapar, Friulian sapâ, Venetan sapar.

Inherited from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), from septimus (“seventh”). Cognate with Italian settimana, French semaine and Spanish semana. Compare Aromanian siptãmãnã.
Inherited from Latin sāpōnem, accusative singular of sāpō, taken from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ. Less likely through the intermediate of Greek σαπούνι (sapoúni). Compare Aromanian sãpuni, sãpune.
From săpun + -are. Calque of Latin saponaria.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *salāre, from a change in conjugation of Latin salīre (“to salt”), from sal. Compare Italian salare, French saler, Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan salar, Friulian salâ, also Aromanian ãnsar, ãnsãrari.
Inherited from Latin salīre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥-ye-. Cognate with Italian salire (“to go up”).
Borrowed from Latin sepullum.

parole.significato: ground salt mixed with bran, given to sheep
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *salōnem, from Latin sal (“salt”).
Inherited from Latin salūtāre. Compare the borrowed doublet saluta.

parole.significato: full (in regards to eating), sated, satiated
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin satullus, a diminutive of satur.
Inherited from Latin saturāre. Doublet of satura (“to saturate”).
Past participle of sătura, from Latin saturare, from satur (“full”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *seus or *sous, from Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé (“self”).
From Vulgar Latin *ta, from Latin tua, feminine of tuus.

parole.significato: table (grid of data in rows and columns)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tabella.

parole.significato: table (grid of data in rows and columns)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tabella or German Tabelle.
Borrowed from Latin tabernaculum.
Borrowed from Latin tabularium.

Inherited from Latin tālem, accusative of tālis. The sense of "distinguished" or "so great / excellent" in Latin probably eventually became "strong" in earlier Romanian, finally taking on the more literal meaning of "hard" or "tough". Compare also atare.

Inherited from Latin tata, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tatás. Compare Aromanian tatã, Dalmatian tuota (“father”), Neapolitan tata (“father”); cf. also Albanian tatë. It was possibly reinforced by the similar South Slavic term (e.g. Serbo-Croatian tata (“dad”)).
Inherited from Latin taurus, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.
Borrowed from Latin taxodium.
From Latin tē (accusative of tū), from Proto-Indo-European *twé, *te, accusative of *túh₂ (“you”).
Inherited from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”).

parole.significato: fear (uncountable: emotion caused by actual or perceived danger or threat)
parole.testo: From the verb teme (“to fear”) or possibly from a Vulgar Latin tima. Compare Italian tema, Romansh tema, temma.
Inherited from Latin tēla.
Borrowed from Latin Te Deum.
Inherited from Latin tilia, turned masculine in assimilation to other tree names, or through Vulgar Latin *tilius. Compare Italian tiglio and Friulian tei.
Inherited from Latin timēre, through a Vulgar Latin intermediate *tīmĕre.
Inherited from Latin timōrem. Equivalent to teme + -oare
Borrowed from Latin temperies.
Borrowed from Latin tempestas.
Borrowed from Latin tempestuosus.
Borrowed from Latin tentamen.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin tepidārium.
Borrowed from Latin terrarium or French terrarium or English terrarium or German Terrarium.
Borrowed from Latin thermae.
Borrowed from Latin termen, with senses from French terme. Doublet of țărm.
Borrowed from Latin terminātiō. Equivalent to termina + -ție.

parole.significato: that is in its third year
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tertius, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *tertīvus or with -iu added (as the normal result in Romanian would have been *terți). Compare the borrowed doublet terț; compare also the related term anțărț.
Borrowed from Latin testamentum.
Borrowed from Latin testiculum or French testicule.
Borrowed from Latin testimonium.
Borrowed from Latin tetrarches or Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs) or French tétrarque.
Borrowed from Latin thesaurus.
Borrowed from Latin thymia or English thymia.
Inherited from Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stetch, string”).
Inherited from Latin temporivus (“early, early in the season”), ultimately from tempus.
Borrowed from Latin tinctura (19th century).
Inherited from Latin tendere, from Proto-Italic *tendō, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

parole.significato: rods over which cloth or canvas are stretched over a surface
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tendicla, syncopated form of Latin tendicula.

From a Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Italian tenda, Spanish tienda, Friulian tinde.
Inherited from Latin tē, as with mine, sine.

From tânăr (“young”) + -ețe, from -eață, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *teneritia, from Latin tener. Compare Aromanian tinireatsã, Italian tenerezza, Old Sicilian tinirizza, Catalan tendresa, French tendresse, Spanish and Portuguese terneza.
Inherited from Latin tensus.
Borrowed from Latin titanium.

Inherited from Latin autumnus, with a change in gender as with iarnă through analogy with vară or primăvară, possibly through an intermediate aphaeretic Vulgar Latin *tumna < Vulgar Latin *otumna, with the rare lowering of stressed -u- into -o- and subsequent diphthongization. Compare Aromanian toam
Inherited from Latin toxicum, from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón, “arrow poison”), from τοξικός (toxikós, “pertaining to bows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre. Compare Aromanian toartsiri.

Inherited from Latin torta, feminine of tortus, perfect passive participle of torqueō. Or from the feminine of Romanian tort as the past participle of toarce, as early handles may have been made from twisted string, fiber, or rope. Compare Calabrian torta ("thread used to connect the yoke and the ma
From toca (“to chop, mince”) + -ană, from Vulgar Latin *toccare (“to knock, strike”).
Borrowed from Latin toga
Inherited from Late Latin (in)toxicāre, from Latin toxicus. Compare Italian intossicare, Venetan intosegar, tosegar, Friulian intosseâ. Doublet of intoxica.
From Latin torus.
Inherited from Latin tortus.
Borrowed from Late Latin tortūra (itself from Latin tortus) through French torture.
Inherited from Latin tōtus. Compare Aromanian tut, Catalan tot, French tout, Italian tutto, Portuguese todo, Spanish todo. First attested in the Hurmuzaki Psalter, dated to circa 1500–1510.

parole.significato: always, ever, all the time, at all times
parole.testo: From tot, from Latin totus + de + a + una. Compare Aromanian tutdiunã.
Borrowed from Latin thracius.
Borrowed from Latin thracicus.
Borrowed from Latin Tradescantia.
Borrowed from Latin trādūcō, French traduire.
From Early Medieval Latin tragere, from Latin trahere (“to draw, drag”).
Borrowed from Latin trajectus or French trajet.
Originally from Latin trāma, now used only with modern senses borrowed from French trame.
Borrowed from Latin transcendere or French transcender.
Borrowed from Latin transcriptus.
Borrowed from Latin transigens or French transigeant.
Borrowed from Latin transylvanus.
Borrowed from Latin translocatio.
Borrowed from Latin transmontanus. By surface analysis, trans- + montan.
Borrowed from Latin trānsubstantiō.
Borrowed from Latin trānsiēns and English transient.
Borrowed from Latin transitorius or French transitoire.

parole.significato: step (on a stair or ladder), stair
parole.testo: From a nominalization of Latin trāiecta, from trāiectum.

parole.significato: to pass through (enter and then leave a region in space)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin trāicere.
Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Aromanian trei.
Inherited from Latin tribulāre.

parole.significato: to tremble, shake, shiver, shudder, quiver
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin tremulāre, from Latin tremulus (“trembling”), from tremere (“shake, tremble”).
Inherited from Latin trepidāre. Doublet of the borrowing trepida.
Borrowed from Latin tribus.
Borrowed from Latin tribunus.
Borrowed from Latin tribunicius.
Borrowed from Latin triclinium.
Borrowed from Latin triennium.
Inherited from Latin trifolium. Compare Aromanian trifolj, trifoljiu.
Borrowed from Latin Trifolium.
Borrowed from Latin trimestris.
Inherited from Latin trāmittere, variant of trānsmittere. Doublet of the borrowing transmite.
Borrowed from Latin triplicatus or French triplicate.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis.
Borrowed from Latin triumphus. Possibly a doublet of trufă.
Borrowed from Latin triumphare or French triompher.
Borrowed from Latin triumphalis or French triomphal.
Borrowed from Latin triumphator.
Borrowed from Latin triumvir or French triumvir.
Borrowed from Latin triumvirātus or French triumvirat.
Borrowed from Latin trivium.

parole.motivo_incerta: Unknown; Possibly; ipotesi scartata nel testo
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *trufa, or also suggested to be from Ancient Greek τροφή (trophḗ), though this is unlikely. More likely is a feminine derivation ultimately from Latin triumphus, which would make it a doublet of triumf (compare Italian tronfio).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trunclus, from syncopation of Latin trunculus, from truncus.
Inherited from Latin trādere, with a change of conjugation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tradimentum or Italian tradimento. Equivalent to trăda + -ământ.
From Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.
Borrowed from Latin tuberosus or French tubéreux.
Inherited from Latin tūfa.
Inherited from Latin tonus (the original meaning being "thunderclap", as with the Romance cognates). See also the doublet ton (“tone”), borrowed through French.
Inherited from Latin tonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”).

parole.significato: to crop, shear, clip, trim, prune, mow
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tondĕre, a variant of Latin tondēre, from Proto-Indo-European *tend-, from *temh₂- (“to cut”).
Inherited from Latin tonitrus (“thunder”) and possibly influenced by the Romanian noun sunet (“sound”).
Past participle of tunde, possibly corresponding to Latin tōnsus.
From tuns + -oare; cf. also Latin tonsōria.
From tuns + -ură, or possibly directly from Latin tōnsūra.
Inherited from Latin turbāre.
Probably from Latin turbātiō, turbātiōnem. By surface analysis, turba + -ăciune.
Inherited from Latin turma.
Inherited from Latin tornō, tornāre.
Borrowed from Latin turpitudo or French turpitude.
Inherited from Latin turta. Thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”), which yielded toartă in Romanian. Compare Aromanian turtã.
Inherited from Latin tussis, tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).
Inherited from Latin tussīre (“to cough”).
From a Vulgar Latin *tōnsionāre, from Late Latin tōnsiō, tōnsiōnem, from Latin tondeō.
From tâmplă + -ar, from Latin templa, from templum.
From Latin templum, possibly through a Byzantine Greek intermediary τέμπλον (témplon). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *t(e)mp-lo-s, from *temp-. Doublet of templu. Compare Aromanian templu.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tando, a demonstrative form to Latin quandō (“when”) (whence Romanian când), after the model of Classical Latin quālis ~ tālis, quantus ~ tantus. Compare Neapolitan tanno, Sicilian tànnu, Corsican tandu, Sardinian tando.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tenerus, from Latin tener, tenerum. Compare Aromanian tinir, tiniru, tinãr. Doublet of tandru, which was borrowed from French.

parole.significato: a rough fabric made out of horse or goat hair
parole.testo: Likely from Late Latin trassenna, a variant of Latin trānsenna (“net, trap”), either directly or via the mediation of Bulgarian тръсина (trăsina). See also Albanian tërsirë.
Inherited from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus. Compare Aromanian tãrdziu.
Inherited from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tak- or *tHk-.
From tăcea + -re. From Latin tacēre.

parole.significato: smoldering brand, piece of wood or coal that is burning without flames
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tītiō. Compare Italian tizzone.
Inherited from Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”). Compare Aromanian talj, tai.
From a Vulgar Latin root *thȳmānea, from Latin thȳmiāma, from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama). Compare Sardinian timanza, timagna, Old French timoine; cf. also Aromanian timnjamã.
Possibly from the variant form trăgăna, from Vulgar Latin *tragīnāre, from *tragere, ultimately from Latin trahō. Compare French traîner, Spanish and Portuguese trajinar.
Inherited from Latin tata, tatanis.
Inherited from Latin tuus, probably through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *tous or *teus. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *towos.
Borrowed from Latin ubique.
Inherited from Latin occīdere. Compare Italian uccidere.
Inherited from Latin occisus, equivalent to the past participle of ucide.
Inherited from Latin ūdus (“wet”).
Inherited from Late Latin ūdāre, from Latin ūdus (“wet”).

Inherited from Latin ūber, from Proto-Italic *ouðer, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”). The change of the Latin consonant -b- to Romanian -g- is also witnessed in rug, neg, etc. In this case, it may also have been influenced by suge (“to suck”). The regional variant may have been influen

parole.significato: territory (area you can see); used in the expression "în uib"
parole.testo: From a substantivization of Latin obvius (“exposed, lying open; known, familiar”). Compare also the Megleno-Romanian verb nuib.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre (“forget”), a frequentative based on Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus). Compare Aromanian ultari. The second sense of "to look at", used reflexively, may have arisen through its use in an expression "a se uita pe sine", to forget oneself, by ext
From a Vulgar Latin root *ollicella, diminutive of Latin olla.
Borrowed from Latin ulcus or French ulcus.
Inherited from Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
Borrowed from Latin ultimus or Italian ultimo.
Borrowed from Latin hūmānus.
Borrowed from Latin umbella or French ombelle.

From older îmbla, from Vulgar Latin *amblāre, syncopated form of Latin ambulāre; compare Aromanian imnu, imnari, Megleno-Romanian amnu, amnare, Istro-Romanian omnu, Old Italian ambiare, Occitan amblar.
From umbră + -atic, or possibly from Latin umbrāticus.
Inherited from Latin umbrōsus, corresponding to umbră + -os. Compare Aromanian aumbros.
Inherited from Latin umbra (“shadow”), probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-. Compare Aromanian aumbrã.
Inherited from Latin hūmidus or ūmidus.

parole.significato: to inflate, swell, puff up, blow out
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin inflāre. Compare Romansh and Catalan unflar, Sicilian unchiari.
From umfla + -ciune, or possibly Latin inflātiō, inflātiōnem, and therefore a doublet of inflație. Compare Italian enfiagione, dialectal French enflaison, Spanish hinchazón, Portuguese inchação.
Borrowed from Latin humilis.
From Vulgar Latin *implĕre, from Latin implēre. Compare Catalan omplir, Aromanian umplu, Sardinian umprere.
Inherited from Latin humerus, from umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”).
Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin avunculus, probably through an intermediate Vulgar Latin *unclus.
Borrowed from Latin uncialis.
Borrowed from Latin ū̆ncia.
Borrowed from Latin uncinatus.

parole.significato: to undulate, wave, make move like a wave
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin undāre. Compare Aromanian undedz, undari.
Inherited from Latin unde. Cognate with Sardinian unde and Sicilian unni.
From undă + -os, or possibly from Latin undōsus.
Inherited from Latin unda (“wave”).
Inherited from Latin unae.
Inherited from Latin ungere, from earlier unguō, from Proto-Italic *ongʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”). Compare Aromanian ungu.
From Vulgar Latin anglus, from Latin angulus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng-, *ang- (“corner, hirn”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin unguentum.
Borrowed from Latin ungulata.
Inherited from Latin ūnīre.
Borrowed from Latin ūnifōrmis.
Borrowed from Latin unimanus.
Borrowed from Latin unisyllabus.
Inherited from Latin ūnōrum.
Inherited from Latin ūnctum (“ointment”). Compare Aromanian umtu.
Inherited from Latin unctūra. Compare Aromanian umturã.

Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one, single”). The reason why unu was exempt from the widespread dropping of word-final /u/ at the time was because the word’s use is reserved for counting only, whereas its doub
Inherited from Latin ōrāre.
Borrowed from Latin urbem.

parole.significato: to climb, ascend, go up, rise
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *oricāre, derived from Latin orior (“rise, appear”).
Inherited from Latin urceolus.
Inherited from Latin hordeolus. May have been confused with or influenced by the other definition above phonetically.

parole.significato: to go often to someone or somewhere, to take the same road repeatedly
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ōrdināre. Compare Aromanian urdin, urdinari. Doublet of ordona.
Inherited from Latin ōricula, variant of auricula. Doublet of auriculă, which was borrowed.
Probably from a Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia). Doublet of orgie.
Inherited from Latin ululāre, through Vulgar Latin ūrulāre, ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.
Inherited from Latin ornus, influenced by ulm. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-.

parole.significato: to follow (go where someone else goes, not in pursuit)
parole.testo: From urmă, perhaps connected to a Vulgar Latin root *osmāre, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Italian ormare, ormeggiare, also Spanish husmear, husmar, Old French osmer, Venetan usmar. Also compare adulmeca.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *orma or Late Latin osma, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) . Compare Aromanian urmã, Megleno-Romanian urmă, Istriot urma, Italian orma, also Spanish husma, Venetan usma and Friulian olme.
Inherited from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos.
Borrowed from Latin ursa or French ourse.

parole.significato: to hatch (a plot), devise, brew, plot
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ōrdīre, collateral form of ōrdīrī.
From a Vulgar Latin root *urdīca, from Latin urtīca. Compare Aromanian urdzãcã. Sense 2 has been popularised by influencer Vlad Obu since the early 2020s.

From a Vulgar Latin root *horrīre, from Latin horrēre (“to be afraid”) (other forms or parts of the verb from horrēscere, horrēscō as with many other 4th conjugation verbs); compare Aromanian urãscu; compare change in meaning also in Albanian urrej (“to hate”), Occitan orrir (“to hate, despise”). Se
From an antecessor shared with mentionable variant urușnic, probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *holoserinicus (“silken”), based on Latin holosēricus.

Most likely inherited from Latin exsūcāre, or less likely, from a Vulgar Latin root *usticāre, from ustus, from ūrō, although the normal phonetic result in Romanian would have been *usteca or *utsca, after which the intervocalic -t- disappeared; in this view, the form usuc is a modern one that repla
Inherited from Latin ustulāre. Compare regional Italian/Tuscan ustolare; cf. also bruciare and French brûler.
From ustura (“to burn, itch”) + -oi, from Latin ustulare (“scorch, singe”).
Borrowed from Latin uterus, French utérus.
Borrowed from Latin usus.
Borrowed from Latin usufructus.
Borrowed from Latin usufructuarius.
From the older form iușor, from a hypothetical (perhaps Proto-Romanian) intermediate *lieu, from Latin levis (“light”), + the diminutive suffix -șor. Compare Aromanian li(c)shor, ljiushor.

parole.significato: Either of the two vertical poles or columns that support a door or gate on the sides.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ostiolum, a diminutive of ostium (“door”). Equivalent to ușă + -or.
From a Vulgar Latin root *ustia, from Latin ostia, plural of ostium (“door, entrance”). Compare Aromanian ushã, Italian uscio (Old Italian plural form uscia), Old French huis, Occitan ussa.

parole.significato: only used in mai va (see usage notes).
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vādit, third person singular present active indicative of vādō. It is also rarely used as a second person singular imperative form, meaning "go", from Latin vāde (and plural form vați from vāditis). 16th century Transylvanian documents also display respective variant forms vă an
Borrowed from Latin vacatio or French vacation.
Borrowed from Latin vacillatio or French vacillation.
Learned borrowing from Latin vacuus.
Borrowed from Latin vacuum.
Inherited from Latin vacca.
Inherited from Latin vadum (“shallow, ford”), from Proto-Italic *waðom, from Proto-Indo-European *wh₂dʰóm, from *weh₂dʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin vade-mecum.

parole.significato: earth rampart which served in antiquity as a military stronghold
parole.testo: From Latin vallum (“wall, rampart”), probably a later borrowing; cf. German Wall, Italian vallo, also English wall.
Inherited from Latin vallis, vallem. Compare Aromanian vali / vale.
Borrowed from Latin valetudinarium.
Borrowed from Latin vānus, Italian vano.
Inherited from Latin virga, probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgā (“flexible rod or stick”).
Borrowed from Latin varius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virdia (see for cognates), from Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis (“green”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vēra, from Latin vēr (“spring”), from earlier *veror, from Proto-Italic *wezor, from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥ (“spring”). Cognate with Aromanian vearã; more distantly related to Spanish verano and Portuguese verão.
Inherited from Latin (consobrina) vēra.

parole.significato: vessel (including blood vessels), general term for receptacle or container (such as a bowl, basin, dish, bucket, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vāsum (“vessel”).
From vas + frângere. Calque of Latin naufragium.
Borrowed from Latin vaticinatio or French vaticination.
Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus. Compare Aromanian vitsin.
Inherited from Latin vaccinus. Is preserved today only in the name of the plant limbă vecină (“hart's-tongue, Scolopendrium vulgare”). Doublet of vaccin, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin vīcīnitas, vīcīnitātem, equivalent to vecin + -ătate. Compare Aromanian vitsinãtati.
Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Compare Aromanian ved, videari, Italian vedere.

parole.significato: to watch, to monitor, be on the lookout, keep vigil
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viglāre, from Latin vigilāre.
Borrowed from Latin vehicularius or French véhiculaire. By surface analysis, vehicul + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin velarium or French vélarium.
Borrowed from Latin velox, velocem.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcitās. By surface analysis, veloce + -itate.
Inherited from Latin venīre, from Proto-Italic *gʷenjō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥yéti, from zero-grade of *gʷem- + *-yéti.
From Latin venēnum, either directly or via the later form venīnum.
From venin + -os. From the Late Latin adjective venēnōsus, from Latin venēnum (“poison”).
From Latin verbum.
Inherited from Latin verbēna. Doublet of vervenă, which was borrowed from French.
Inherited from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Related to English verdure.
From verde + -eață or Vulgar Latin *virditia. Compare Italian verdezza, Aromanian virdeatsã.
Inherited from Late Latin virgella, diminutive of Latin virgula, itself a diminutive of virga. Compare Aromanian virdzeauã.
From vergură (“virgin”), from Latin virgō, virginem, or through Vulgar Latin *virgula, an intermediate form. Doublet of virgin.
Inherited from Latin virgō, but the phonetics remain unclear. A diminutive Vulgar Latin *virgula has been proposed. Compare Aromanian virghirã, Albanian virgjër. Doublet of virgină.
Borrowed from Latin verificatio or French vérification. Equivalent to verifica + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin vermiculatio.
Borrowed from Latin veronica.
Borrowed from Latin verosimilitudo. Equivalent to verosimil + -itudine.
Borrowed from Latin verrucosus or French verruqueux. By surface analysis, verucă + -os.
Borrowed from Latin verruca. Possibly a doublet of boroacă.
Borrowed from Latin vesania or French vésanie.
Borrowed from Latin vespertilio.
Borrowed from Latin vespera.
Borrowed from Latin veto or French veto.
Borrowed from Latin vexillatio or French vexillation.
Borrowed from Latin vēsīca (“bladder”). Compare the inherited doublet bășică.
Inherited from Latin vestīmentum.

parole.significato: to have life; to live, exist
parole.testo: From an older form vie, from Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).
Inherited from Latin vesper.
Borrowed from Latin viaticum.
From Vulgar Latin *vīvitia (cf. Aromanian yeatsã). Synchronically viu + -eață.
Borrowed from French vice- and Latin vice-.
Borrowed from Latin vitium.
Borrowed from Latin victōria.
Borrowed from Latin victoriosus. Equivalent to victorie + -os.
Inherited from Latin vīnea.
Inherited from Latin verrēs.
From vie (“vineyard”), or from Latin vīneārius.
Inherited from Latin vermis, vermem, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

parole.significato: wormy, full of or eaten by worms
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin verminōsus. Compare Aromanian yirminos, yirmãnos.
Inherited from Latin versus. Cf. also the borrowed neological doublet vers.
Unknown. Possibly derived from Latin versiō, versiōnem (probably from the sense of "change"). Old word found in writings of Dosoftei in the 17th century.
Borrowed from Latin villa or French villa or Italian villa.
Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.
Probably from Late Latin vīnāceus, from Latin vīnum.
Inherited from Latin vēndere (“sell”). Compare French vendre.
Inherited from Latin vindicāre (“avenge, claim”).
Inherited from Latin (diēs) Veneris.
Inherited from Latin vindemiārius, from vindemia.

parole.significato: rich in wine, full of wine; vinous, winy
parole.testo: From vin + -os, possibly corresponding to Latin vīnōsus. The sense of wine-colored was taken from French vineux.
Inherited from Latin venter, ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.
Inherited from Latin viola.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *vīvula, from Latin vīvus.
Inherited from Latin vīpera. Compare Aromanian vipirã.
Inherited from Latin vīctus.

parole.significato: virgin, that which has not had sexual intercourse, chaste, maiden, virginal
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin virgō, virginem. Doublet of vergură.
From virgin, from Latin virgō, virginis. Doublet of vergură.
Borrowed from Latin virīlitās, French virilité, equivalent to viril + -itate.
Borrowed from Latin virtūs, virtūtem. See also the older inherited form, vârtute.
Inherited from Latin vīsum.
Borrowed from Latin viscera.

parole.significato: step- (as in not a blood relative but related through the marriage of a parent), half-
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vītricus.
Borrowed from Latin vituperativus or French vitupératif.

Generally taken as inherited from Latin vīta (“life”), from Proto-Italic *gʷītā. In this view, the shift toward the meaning “animal” is sometimes explained as Slavic influence; compare Bulgarian животно (životno, “animal”) alongside живот (život, “life”). Another possibility is a back-formation from
Inherited from Latin vīvus, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós.
Borrowed from Latin vivat or French vivat.
Borrowed from Latin vivificus or French vivifique.
Borrowed from Latin vivificator or French vivificateur.
Borrowed from Latin vivificatio or French vivification.
Borrowed from Latin Visigothus or French wisigoth.
Borrowed from Latin visitatio or French visitation or German Visitation. Equivalent to vizita + -ție.
Borrowed from Latin visio.
Borrowed from Latin visualitas. Equivalent to vizual + -itate.
Inherited from Latin viēscere (“wither”), from vieō.
Inherited from Latin vitella, diminutive of vitula (“calf, young cow”). Compare Aromanian yitsauã, Italian vitella, French velle, Catalan vedella.
Inherited from Latin vitellus. Compare French veau, Italian vitello.

parole.significato: vine - often used as viță de vie (grapevine)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vītia, from Latin vītea, from vītis f.

parole.significato: yours (that which belongs to you (plural- group being addressed))
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vostra(m), feminine of voster.
Borrowed from Latin vocalis, German Vokal.
Borrowed from Latin vōx, vōcem, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs. Compare French voix, Italian voce, Spanish voz. Replaced the older inherited form boace (a doublet).
Inherited from Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs.
Formed on the basis of voi, the variant first person singular of vrea (normally vreau), possibly from Late Latin voleō for Latin volō. Compare Aromanian voi. See also further information at va.
Borrowed from Latin volaticus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *volvula, from Latin volvō. Compare Aromanian vãrvurã.
Inherited from Latin vomere.
Borrowed from Latin vomitāre.
Borrowed from Latin vomitorium.

Maybe from Latin verbum (“word”) through *vărbu, subsequently *vărbă by singularization of the supplanted neuter plural up to vorbă in analogy to the change from [ə] to [o] in the imperative vino from vină. The intermediate form *vărbu is strengthened by related Aromanian vãrghescu (“to quarrel, sco
Inherited from Latin voster, vostrum, from vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.
Inherited from Latin vōbīs, dative plural of tū.

Inherited from Late Latin volēre, remodeled from Latin velle, from Proto-Italic *welō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. The word passed through an older form *vurea/*vureare in early Romanian before reaching its current state (compare the phonetic evolution of durea). The 1st, 2nd, and 3

parole.significato: peasantry, commoners, the common people, plebians
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vulgus.
Borrowed from Latin vulnerare.
Borrowed from Latin vulneratio. By surface analysis, vulnera + -ție.
Inherited from Latin vulpēs, vulpem, from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p- ~ *h₂ulp- (“(red) fox”).
Inherited from Latin vultur, vulturem (“vulture”) or vulturius. The standard pronunciation has the accent on the first syllable, but there is a variant with it on the second.

parole.significato: small or narrow valley, dale, or dell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vallicella, diminutive of Late Latin vallicula (“small valley”), diminutive of Latin vallis.
From the past participle of vâna or from Latin vēnātus.
Inherited from Latin vēnōsus. By surface analysis, vână + os. Compare Aromanian vinos. Piecewise doublet of venos.
Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts < *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
From vânt + -os, or from Latin ventōsus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ventulāre, from Latin ventilāre. Compare Aromanian vintur, vinturari, Sardinian bentulare, vinturà. Compare the borrowed doublet ventila.
From the verb vinde + -tor, possibly from Latin vēnditor. Compare Italian venditore, French vendeur, Spanish vendedor.

parole.significato: vein, or blood vessel in general
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of venă, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin venetus (“blue; sea blue; Venetian”). Doublet of venet.
Inherited from Latin vēnātōria, from vēnātor.
Inherited from Latin vēnātor; equivalent to vâna + -ător.
Inherited from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. Compare the borrowed doublets virtuos and virtuoz.
Inherited from Latin virtūs, virtūtem. Compare the neologism virtute.
Inherited from Latin viscum.
Inherited from Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum. Equivalent to vâsc + -os.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin vaccārius. Compare Aromanian vãcar.
Inherited from Late Latin vaccāricia, from Latin vacca (“cow”). By surface analysis, vacă + -ăreață. Compare Aromanian vãcãreatsã.

parole.significato: that which has or is full shallows or fords
parole.testo: From vad + -os or from Latin vadōsus.
Derived from the dated/regional form văduu, which is Inherited from Latin viduus (“widow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂.
Probably adapted from Latin vēlum or Italian velo. If inherited the regular shift of an intervocalic "l" to "r" would be expected. Less likely from Vulgar Latin *vēllum.

Inherited from Latin (cōnsobrīnus) vērus (“true cousin”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros, from *weh₁- (“true”). Cf. Aromanian ver and cusurin. For the semantic evolution compare Spanish and Portuguese primo.
Probably from Latin virgātus, or from vargă + -at.
Inherited from Latin versāre (“turn, twist”).

parole.significato: pie filled with cabbage, onions, various other vegetables, or fruit
parole.testo: From varză, or less likely a Vulgar Latin root *virdiāria, from *virdia, from Latin viridia. Compare Aromanian virdzari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vituleus, from Latin vitulus. Compare Aromanian vitulj.

parole.significato: to harm, damage, wound, hurt, injure
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin victimāre. Compare Aromanian vatãm, vãtãmari. While ct in Latin usually results in pt in Romanian, this underwent dissimilation, as with păta, boteza, etc.
Past participle of vedea, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Aromanian vidzut, Italian veduto, French vu (Old French veü).
Inherited from Latin daeda, variant of taeda.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exbattere. Compare Aromanian zbat, Italian sbattere, Venetan sbàter, sbàtar, Sicilian sbàttiri, Friulian sbati.
Inherited from Latin exbibere, from ex- + bibō, or within Romanian from s- + bea.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvolāre, from Latin ex- + volāre. Compare Aromanian azboair.

It could be directly inherited from Latin zema (“saucepan”). However, it is more likely that the word is from Ancient Greek ζέμα (zéma, “decoction, something boiled or fermented; extract; essence”), through a Vulgar Latin intermediate *zema. The current meaning in Eastern Romance is closer to that o
Inherited from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.
Unknown. One proposed etymology was a Latin set(u)la, diminutive of seta, and another was a Vulgar Latin *dec(u)la, from Latin decus, but these are improbable.
From zeu + -itate, modeled on Latin deitas.
Inherited from Latin dextrae or dexterae, plural of dextera (“pledge, promise”), from dexter.
Inherited from Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós. Doublet of zău.
Inherited from Late Latin scabia, from Latin scabiēs. Compare scabie, a borrowed doublet.

parole.significato: to goggle, ogle, stare at intensely and with wide eyes
parole.testo: From zgău, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *excavīre, from Latin cavum.
Probably from Latin cavum with an s- added later in Romanian or a remnant of a Latin ex-. Compare gaură, căuș, găun, găoace.

Inherited from Classical Latin diēs (“day”), back-formed from the accusative diem (whose vowel e was once long), from Proto-Italic *djēm, the accusative of *djous, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). May have been inherited from an intermediate Vulgar Latin *dilla , hence why the defini
Inherited from Latin dīcere, present active participle of dīcō, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

parole.significato: May God be with you; God bless you
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin deus te constet.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exventāre, from Latin ventus (“wind”). Compare Aromanian zvintu, zvintari.

Inherited form of Latin Diāna. Compare Aromanian dzãnã (“fairy”), Asturian xana (“child-exchanging nymph”), Sardinian giàna, Old French gene (“fairy”); compare also Albanian zanë. Other survivals of ancient god names in Romance include Spanish huerco, from Latin Orcus, and Old French netun (“marine
Inherited from Latin jacēre, iacēre (“lie prostrate”). The shift from the expected initial -j- in Romanian to -z- is due to dissimilation from the following consonant.

Inherited from Latin deus (“god”), or simply a variant of Romanian zeu ("god"), a simple doublet which kept the original meaning. The semantic evolution may be due to the act of "swearing to God" to affirm something is really true.
Inherited from Latin illī, dative common singular of ille.
Inherited from Latin illum, accusative masculine singular of ille. Was originally l in earlier Romanian, with an initial prothetic î- added for ease of pronunciation.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ambi, from Latin ambae as the plurals of ambo. Replaced by the neologism ambii, ultimately from the same source.

parole.significato: to dress up, to get dressed
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbrācāre, from Latin brāca (“pants, trousers”). Compare also Italian imbracare, Spanish embragar, cf. Latin brācātus.

parole.significato: to eat quickly, gobble up, tongue, swallow, lap
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca (“cheek, mouth”). Compare Aromanian mbuc, mbucari, Italian imboccare, French emboucher, Portuguese and Spanish embocar.

Unknown. Several theories have been proposed. One was a derivation from a Vulgar Latin root *imbubiāre, from bubia, but this was later abandoned. Another possibility is Latin imbuere, through a root *imbuviāre, or Latin bubīre (“swell, inflate”).
Maybe from a Vulgar Latin *ambagella, from Latin ambages.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbibitāre, derived from Latin bibere (“to drink”). Compare Aromanian mbitari.
Unstressed form of mie. From Latin mi, dative singular of egō.

parole.significato: to hinder (to make it difficult for someone to do something), impede
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin impedicāre.

parole.significato: to press (down upon), step on, tamp, compress
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *impillāre, from Latin pilāre (“ram down, fix firmly”).

parole.significato: to push (transitive: apply a force to (an object) so that it moves away), thrust, shove
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin impingere.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *implenīre, from Latin plenus (“full”). Compare Aromanian mplinescu, mpliniri, Romansh emplenir, amplanir, Venetan inpinir, inpienir, Catalan emplenar. Compare also Old French plenir.

parole.significato: to stick or thrust a weapon
parole.testo: From în- + Latin plantāre, or from Latin implantāre. Doublet of implanta. Compare Aromanian plãntu.
From împrejur. Another etymology derives it from a Vulgar Latin *pergȳrāre, from Latin per + gȳrāre, with the addition of the prefix în later within Romanian.

From în- + Vulgar Latin *pressurāre, from Latin pressura, or from the Vulgar Latin root *impressoriāre, from Latin pressorium, or ultimately from pressus through a resulting hypothetical lost word in Romanian, *pres and its plural *presuri.
From un through the intermediate preună, probably from a Latin composition *in per una. Compare Aromanian mpriunã.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.

parole.significato: to lend (to allow to be used temporarily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprūmūtāre, from Early Medieval Latin imprōmūtuāre, from Latin prōmūtuārī. Compare Aromanian mprumut.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *impungere, from Latin pungere, or with the în- prefix added later in Romanian. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *pungō, from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
From the old verb împuta + -ciune (compare the modern doublet imputa), or possibly corresponding to Latin imputātiō, imputātiōnem.

parole.significato: to make up, reconcile, conciliate, come to agreement
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *impācāre, from in + pācāre (“make peaceful, pacify”); or, more likely, the îm- was added later within Romanian to an older form păca.
Inherited from Late Latin impālāre, from Latin pālus. Compare Aromanian mpãrari, mpar.
Inherited from Latin imperātor, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *imperātus. Compare Megleno-Romanian ạmpirat, and also Albanian mbret. Doublet of imperator.

parole.significato: to share, apportion, assign, dole, impart
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin impartīre, impertiō, from Latin partiō. By surface analysis, în- + parte + -i.

parole.significato: to happen or occur to someone (something negative, surprising, unpleasant)
parole.testo: Probably from Latin pātrāre, with senses probably from Latin impetrāre.
Inherited from Latin in. Cognate with English in.
Inherited from Latin in-, a prefixation of in (“in, into”); see în.
From în + ainte (obsolete synonym), from Late Latin ab ante. Compare Aromanian nãnti.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inaltum, from Latin in + altus (or perhaps from the phrase in altō). The preposition may have been added by influence of înălța (“raise”).
Inherited from Latin in ad post.
Borrowed from Latin incarcerare. Compare French incarcérer.
Inherited from Latin incipere (“to begin”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *incircāre, from Latin circāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quetus, from Latin quiētus with the prefix în- added later in Romanian from the variant cet. See also the doublet chit, which came later through French.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētāre, from Latin quiētor, with the prefix în- added in Romanian. Compare also Latin inquiētō.

parole.significato: to conclude, end, wrap up, wind up, close
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre or *inclāviāre, from Latin clāvis (“key”) or clāvus (“nail”) (see also clāvāre (“to nail”)). Probably influenced by cheie. Compare also Friulian inclavâ, French enclouer.
From încheia + -tură. Another proposed etymology was în + Vulgar Latin *clautūra, but this is less likely.
Inherited from Latin inclūdere. Compare Aromanian ncljid, ncljidiri, French enclore, Italian chiudere. Doublet of the borrowing include.
Inherited from Latin inclīnāre (“incline”) (compare Aromanian ncljin, ncljinari, Italian inchinare). Doublet of the borrowed înclina.
Inherited from Latin inclīnātiō, inclīnātiōnem. Compare Aromanian ncljinãciuni. Doublet of the borrowed înclinație.
Past participle of închide (“to close”), perhaps corresponding to Latin inclūsus. Doublet of inclus.

parole.significato: to take fire, heat up, flare up, run hot, enkindle
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin incendere.
Inherited from Latin incingere, from in- + cingō (“to surround, encircle”).
Past participle of încinge; possibly corresponding to Latin incensus.

parole.significato: hither, here, this way, in my direction
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin in-(ec)cu(m) *hocce, from Latin hoc. Compare Megleno-Romanian ạncoatsi, coa, Dalmatian cauc.
Inherited from Latin congȳrāre, with the prefix în-.
Borrowed from Latin corōnāre, with the prefix in-, or from Romanian în- + coroană. Cf. the inherited doublet cununa, and also încununa.
Inherited from Latin in- contra ubi.
From crunta (“to frown”) (with the prefix în-), from Latin cruentāre (“make bloody”). Compare Aromanian ncruntu, ncruntari (“to bleed”).
From a Vulgar Latin root *incuneāre, from Latin cuneāre, ultimately from cuneus (“wedge”). Compare Albanian ngujoj. First attested in 1581.

Inherited from Latin committere as *cumete, later prefixed (equivalent to în- + Latin committere) and with change of conjugation (cf. the prefixed original, now regional, form încumete). Doublet of the borrowed comite.

parole.significato: to drive, goad (a horse); to chase away
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *incurrāre, from Latin incurrō, incurrere, from currō.
Either from Vulgar Latin incolicāre, from colus, or from a root *curricāre, from currō. Less likely from descurca, which is more likely derived from this word instead. First attested in 1581.
Inherited from Latin umquam.
Probably from Vulgar Latin incallare, from Latin callēre (“be calloused, hardened, grow hard”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incaballicāre, from Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus (“nag, jade”). Compare Aromanian ncalic, ncãlicari or Albanian ngalkoj.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incalidīre. Compare Aromanian ncãldzãscu. Possibly also influenced by Latin incalēscō (whence încări).

parole.significato: to put on shoes or other footwear
parole.testo: From în- + Latin calceāre. Compare Aromanian ncãltsari.
Probably from în- + the plural of the older form călțământ, from Latin calceamentum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre, ultimately from Latin carrus. Compare Aromanian ãncarcu, ãncãrare, cf. also Albanian ngarkoj.
Inherited from Latin incalēscere, changed to a fourth conjugation Vulgar Latin root *incalīre for the infinitive form, as with all inchoative verbs in Romanian.
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *indemināre, from inde + minārī.

parole.significato: to stuff, cram, jam, pack, press in
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indensāre, from Latin densāre.

parole.significato: to persuade, usually towards a more merciful course of action
parole.testo: From în- + dupleca (now obsolete), from Latin duplicāre. Compare Aromanian ndpulic, nduplicari.

Inherited from Latin indūrāre. The original, now obsolete meaning of “be hardhearted”, a continuation of the Latin, was a negative polarity item whose sense reversed after simplification of its negative construction. This semantic reversal had already occurred by the earliest attestations of the wor
From în + Late Latin dē retrō. Compare Italian indietro.

From în + the variant neca (“to kill”), from Latin necāre, present active infinitive necō (“kill”); cf. also ēnecāre. Compare Italian annegare, Spanish anegar, Aromanian nec, nicari, French noyer. The specialized sense of "to drown" seems to have arisen in Late or Vulgar Latin and can be found in th
From fierbinte. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *inferventāre, from Latin fervens.

Unknown. Possibly from în + a Vulgar Latin root *fervidiāre, from Latin fervidus. Only appears in the 17th century writings of the scholar Dosoftei, who was known to have created some words, so the etymology is still uncertain.

parole.significato: to thrust, push into, stick in, dig into, insert into
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin īnfīgere (“fasten, fix”).

From a Vulgar Latin *infebrizō or later Balkan Romance equivalent, derived from Latin febris. Cognate to Aromanian nhiuredz, nhiurari. The -ez type conjugation is likely the older variant due to the pronunciation of "io" in the root, as this pronunciation is an outcome of the intonation falling else
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *īnfīctus, from Latin īnfīxus. Doublet of infix.

parole.significato: to flower (to put forth blooms), bloom
parole.testo: From în- + Late Latin flōrīre. Compare Aromanian nfluriri.
Inherited from Late Latin infocāre, a verb derived from Latin focus ("fire", originally "hearth"). By surface analysis, în- + foc + -a.
Inherited from Latin īnfrēnāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *infrangere, from Latin infringere, from in- + frangō. Equivalent to în- + frânge. Compare Italian infrangere.
Unknown. Possibly from în + fărma, variant of fărâma, or from a Latin informāre or formāre. Another hypothesis is in + Latin firmāre.

From a Vulgar Latin *infasciāre or în + Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia. Compare Aromanian nfash, nfãshari, Italian fasciare, Occitan faissar, French fesser, Portuguese enfaixar, Spanish fajar, Friulian infassâ, Venetan infasar, Istriot infasà, Sardinian fasciai.
Inherited from Latin ingemināre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingenuclāre < *ingenuculāre, from Latin geniculum. Compare Aromanian ndzinuclju, ndzinucljedzu, ndzinucljari, Italian inginocchiare, French agenouiller, Portuguese ajoelhar, Spanish ahinojar, Catalan agenollar.
Inherited from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Doublet of Anghel.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inglaciāre. Synchronically în- + gheață + -a.
From an intermediate earlier form *înghiuți, from Late Latin ingluttīre, from Latin gluttiō, from gluttus. Compare Italian inghiottire.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingrevicāre, a verb based on early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem. Compare Aromanian ngricari.

parole.significato: to make or become heavy, burden
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ingrevināre, from grevis, from Latin gravis. Compare Aromanian ngriunedz, ngriunari.

From gras or a Vulgar Latin root *ingrassiāre, from grassus, from Latin crassus (“thick, fat”). Compare Aromanian ngrash, ngrãshari, French engraisser, Dalmatian engrassur, Italian ingrassare, Spanish engrasar.
Inherited from Latin angustus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰu-, from *h₂enǵʰ-.
Inherited from Latin angustāre.

parole.significato: to imitate, mimic (a voice, etc), to echo
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (“trick, deceive, mock”) (attested in a gloss), from Latin *ganno or ganniō. Compare Aromanian angan, angãnari (“call”), Italian ingannare (“deceive, cheat”), Spanish engañar, Portuguese enganar, Catalan enganyar, Albanian gënjej. Cf. also Medieval
Inherited from Latin iniectāre, frequentative of iniciō through its perfect passive participle iniectus. Doublet of the borrowing injecta.
From jug or possibly from în + Latin iugāre. Cf. also Spanish enyugar.
From în- + junghia, from Latin iugulāre (“slay, slit throat”).
Either from nod (“knot”) or Latin innōdāre, or from the dated or regional variant form noda, from nōdāre. Compare Aromanian nod, anod.
From în- + nota, the latter from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Aromanian (a)nutari, Italian nuotare.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ipsus or Latin ipsum, masculine accusative of ipse, with a nasal infix from Latin (compare attested inpsuius). Cognate with Aromanian nãs, Old French esse, Italian esso, Portuguese esse, Spanish ese, see more cognates at ipse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin insignāre (also later attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin signō.

parole.significato: to marry, wed (become married or wedded)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(in)uxōrāre, a verb based on Latin uxor (“wife”). Compare Aromanian ãnsor, ãnsurari.

parole.significato: to repair the sole of a shoe
parole.testo: From în- + Vulgar Latin *solāre, from Latin solum.
Inherited from Latin ipsa, with a nasal infix.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intītiō, from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”).
Inherited from Latin intendere, or possibly în + tinde.

parole.significato: to soak or moisten food (e.g. bread) by dipping in some liquid or other food
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin intingere, from Latin tingō.
From întinde or Latin intensus. Doublet of intens, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intorcĕre, from Latin torquēre (cf. also intorquēre).
Inherited from Latin intortus.
Inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intreguāre, itself from Classical Latin interrogō. Doublet of the borrowing interoga.
Inherited from Latin integer, integrum (“whole, entire”). Compare Sardinian interu, intregu, Italian intero, Spanish entero, Portuguese inteiro. Doublet of integru. See also: Aromanian ntreg, ãntreg.
Inherited from Latin intrō.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intunicāre, from Latin tunicāre (“cover with a tunic”), from tunica (“tunic”). Compare Aromanian ãntunic, ãntunicari. Compare also Italian intonicare, Spanish entunicar (which were internal formations). Not related to întuneric.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *intenebricāre (attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin tenebricus. The original form may have been *întenerica before being influenced phonetically by or confused with the probably unrelated but coincidentally similar întuneca.
From în + tuneric, probably ultimately from Latin tenebricus through a hypothetical intermediate form *teneric, and then influenced by întuneca within early Romanian. Compare Aromanian ãntunearic.

parole.significato: to do or endeavor with diligence or effort
parole.testo: From în- + veghea or from Latin invigilāre.

parole.significato: to stiffen, harden, make obstinate, rigid, inflexible
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *inversionāre, from Latin versiō, versiōnem (“turning, change”). Probably related to vierșun. Another proposed etymology is Hungarian verseny.
Inherited from Latin investīre, with a shift in conjugation (see also variant învești). Compare Aromanian nvescu. Doublet of the borrowed investi.

parole.significato: to resurrect, revive, raise or awaken from the dead
parole.testo: From în + viu or more likely a variant of via, from Latin vīvere (with a change in conjugation from the older form învie). A less likely origin is Vulgar Latin root *invīvāre or *invīvere. Compare Aromanian anyedz, anyeari.
From în- + vince (now archaic), from Latin vincere. Replacement of /t͡ʃe/ with /d͡ʒe/ likely by analogy with other verbs, like încinge, înfrânge, împinge, etc.
Inherited from Latin invītāre. Almost completely replaced by the modern doublet from French, invita.
Inherited from Latin involvere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus. Doublet of involut.

From a Vulgar Latin *invitiāre, a variant of *vitiāre (“accustom, habituate, familiarize”), or formed from in- + Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Aromanian anvets, nvets, anvitsari, Istro-Romanian ănmeţå, Italian avvezzare, invezzare, Spanish avezar, vezar, Portuguese vezar, Occitan envezar, Old Frenc
From în- + zestre (“dowry”) + -a, from Latin dextrae. Compare Spanish adiestrar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Aromanian analtsu, anãltsari, Italian innalzare, Occitan enauçar, Old French enhaucier (where English enhance).
Unknown. Possibly from Latin in illac intro, or in ad intro. The original form in Romanian was likely *înăîntru. Compare Sicilian 'n dintra.
From șir. Alternative etymologies include a link with Latin inserere, although this is less likely.
Inherited from Latin intelligere, variant of intellegere (“to understand”); compare Aromanian ntsileg, Megleno-Romanian ạnțileg, cf. also Albanian dëgjoj (disputed), Romansh encleger.
Inherited from Late Latin intellectiōnem, accusative singular of intellectiō, from intellēctus, from Latin intellegō.

Inherited from Late Latin intellēctus, from Latin intellegō. Was originally also the past participle of înțelege, replaced by înțeles through analogy with other -e ending third-conjugation verbs (i.e. merge > mers, drege > dres, scrie > scris). Doublet of intelect.

parole.significato: to cut down a tree incompletely, making it easier to take down afterward
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin tenuāre, with în- added.
Inherited from Latin illum, from ille.
Inherited from Latin ille (“that one”) + hāc (“over here”), equivalent to ăl + -a. Compare acela, ăsta, acesta.
Inherited from Latin iste (“that one”) + hāc (“over here”), equivalent to ăst + -a. Compare ăla, acesta, acela.
From an older form șea, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-. See also șale.

parole.significato: the part of the backbone or spine near the lumbar region of the back
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sella. See also șa.
Inherited from Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin serpis, from Latin serpēns, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. Compare Aromanian sharpi.
Inherited from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

Inherited from Late Latin sclavus or Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos, “Slav”); see there for more. Compare Aromanian shcljau, Albanian shqa. The Romanian word seems to have preserved the original ancient ethnic meaning before it took on the sense of "slave" later on, which is the mean
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excloppus (compare Aromanian shcljop, Albanian shqep, Occitan / Catalan esclop), from cloppus (compare Old French clop, also Italian zoppo).
Either from șchiop or from Late Latin root *excloppāre, from cloppus. Compare French écloper, (éclopé).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *excloppitāre, from Late Latin excloppus, from cloppus. Cf. also Aromanian shcljoapic, shcljupicari.
Inherited from Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From șa + -ar, or from Latin sellārius, from sella.

Inherited from Latin servus, from Proto-Italic *serwos (“guardian”), from Proto-Indo-European *serwos (“guardian”), possibly from *ser- (“watch over, protect”). Doublet of serv, which was a borrowing.

parole.significato: to work or serve as a serf or slave
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin servīre. Doublet of servi, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin serpentis, the genitive singular of Latin serpēns, apparently having been substantivised at some point in the development of Romanian.
Inherited from Latin sessus (“seat”) (compare Albanian shesh, Aromanian shes), from sedeō (“to sit”); change in meaning also in Albanian shesh (“plain; flatness”).

Inherited from Latin sīc (“thus, so, like, in this way”). Compare Aromanian shi, Megleno-Romanian și. Possibly related to Italian sia (originally a subjunctive form of essere “to be”) as in the construction sia … sia … (“both … and …”), which is equivalent to Romanian și … și ….

parole.significato: string, line, chain, series, succession, row
parole.testo: Back-formation from șire, plural of șiră. Or more likely just an expressive creation. Alternative theories include Latin series.
Inherited from Latin sōricem, accusative singular of sōrex (“shrew”). Compare Aromanian shoaric, French souris and Italian sorcio.
Inherited from Latin spurius.

parole.significato: (usually wooden) rod or bar, especially those used to hold together or form a net
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin schidia, from Ancient Greek σχίδια (skhídia).
Inherited from Latin stercus.

parole.significato: to wipe, clean, clear (either an object or a substance off an object)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin extergere, from tergō.
Inherited from Latin scīre. Compare Sardinian ischire.
Inherited from Latin scientia or ști + -ință, with the modern meaning of "science" based on French science. Compare Aromanian shtiintsã.
Inherited from Latin sciurus.

parole.significato: feeble, flimsy, frail, weak, fragile, unstable
parole.testo: Unknown. The -ed ending indicates a Latin etymology. Possibly from Latin hybridus, from hybrida (compare also Ancient Greek ὕβρις (húbris)), with the addition of the prefix s- (from Latin ex-) in Romanian. The transition of -și- to -șu- also occurs in șuiera (compare also jur, from gyrus). The meani
Inherited from Latin suscitāre.
Inherited from Latin terra. Compare Aromanian tsarã, Dalmatian tiara.
Inherited from Late Latin testa (“skull”), from Latin testa (“brick, tile, pot”).
Borrowed from Latin circinus.
